“Finish the story,” Phainon prompts, and it comes out kind of quiet, kind of weird.

“He fell in love with a warrior in Okhema,” Mydei tells him, sliding a hand under his pillow. “They were equals in just about everything, and that’s… significant to a Kremnoan. He died sacrificing himself to buy that warrior time to save the city.”

“That sounds like something a hero would do to me.”

“Maybe,” Mydei grumbles. “A real hero wouldn’t leave the one he loves to fight alone.”
|

Chapter Notes

Grief and death are going to be pretty prominent themes (we're digging into phainon's trauma with this one :D) that said, I don't think this fic will be too sad, hugs WILL be received when needed.

if you're ever curious what they're listening to on the journey, I made a playlist for this fic.

The shower in their apartment makes this sound like the pipes are groaning. Sometimes the walls seem to shake with it. Rumbling plumbing, the scream of a loose washer in the faucet, and then the hiss of water running. These are the sounds Mydei wakes up to, too hot and swaddled in sheets that are due for a wash. He kicks them off and rolls onto his back, peeling his eyes open to stare at his hideous popcorn ceiling and listen to Phainon shower.

Four months into this life, he doesn’t know why he doesn’t regret it. 

As he peels himself out of bed, Phainon starts to sing. His voice is thin and muffled through the walls; Mydei doesn’t recognize the song.

When he gets to the kitchen, he smells the remains of three charred eggs before he finds them in the trash. There’s a crusty pan left to soak in the sink, crumbs all over the counter, and a small puddle on the ground that Mydei steps in whilst trying to fill a glass of water. He curses and drops a towel, mopping it up with his foot, making a mental note to make Phainon come back and clean the kitchen properly.

Later, with a protein shake and two pieces of toast with honey butter, Mydei hears the bathroom door open, Phainon’s bedroom door shut. The pipes have stopped screaming. Mydei takes a sip. A little longer, the door clicks open again. Phainon comes out, dressed in black sweats and a polo, hair still wet and limply lying atop his head.

“Mydei,” he says, smiling a little. Something in his eyes isn’t right. “Good morning.”

Why do you seem sad? Mydei wonders. Out loud, he says, “What’s wrong with you?”

Phainon only blinks. “Nothing in particular,” he says, wetting his lips, shifting from foot to foot, bagel printed socks on scuffed faux hardwood laminate. “Listen, Mydei, I’m going to be gone for a week or so, visiting my sister. I’m almost done packing, so I’m—”

“Visiting your sister,” Mydei interrupts. “Since when? Are you flying?”

Now, he avoids eye contact, gaze tracing the pictures lining their walls, friends and family, inoffensive blue paint. “Driving,” he answers, lingering on a photo of himself and Cyrene, him in his graduation gown, her in a knee-length pink and white dress. They’re leaning into each other, and Phainon’s smile is big enough to split his face in half. The slightest twitch in his brows. “It was an impromptu decision, I’d have told you earlier if it was planned, of course. But I’m leaving in an hour and I—”

“She lives across the country,” Mydei reminds him. “It’s like a thirty hour drive. Were you planning on taking your car? Do you have somewhere booked to stop for the night? Are you even—”

“Okay!” Phainon says, holding up his hands. “I’m totally unprepared, I get it. It’ll suck, but I’ll sleep in the car. And you know Chartonus worked on it a little while ago; it’ll survive the trip. I’ll knock it out in two days, and—”

“You are not driving for fifteen hours each day, you idiot, you’ll—”

“Can you stop interrupting me?” His voice raises. His next exhale comes out shaky. Mydei goes quiet, a little shocked by his reaction and trying to hide it by leaning back on their brown, second hand upholstery couch, propping his chin on his hand, raising an eyebrow in expectation. Phainon continues, wet hair and all. “Have a little faith in me to not get myself killed, please. I’ll take breaks, and if I need to I’ll stop early. I’m not… I’m not that much of an idiot, okay?”

Mydei holds his gaze. After a breath, he sighs, makes this decision before he has time to decide if he’ll regret it or not. He will, but he won’t. Most things with Phainon are like that. “Alright,” he says. “Are you already packed? Give me a minute.”

“Give you—” Phainon blinks. “What?” And then he’s tailing Mydei back to his room like a stray dog in his stupid socks with his stupid face, and Mydei just—

“We’re taking my car; yours is going to get us killed,” he says, rolling his closet open and pulling down the duffle bag he has stuffed up there. It’s hot pink and nearly torn at one of the straps, but he’s had it since high school. A week long summer camp in the mountains with a couple dozen other boys. The first time he followed Phainon on some stupid journey. 

And there he is, standing in the doorway, a hand on either side of the frame, brows slightly furrowed. He inhales, lips parting, and Mydei looks away in favor of pulling a few shirts off their hangers and tossing them onto his bed.

“Mydei,” Phainon says.

“Go finish your shit,” Mydei replies. A laugh or a puff of air. In his peripheral, Phainon leans his head against the doorframe.

“I can’t decide if I should be upset that you don’t think I can go on my own or flattered that you’d drop everything to come with.”

And yet, it still seems he doesn’t have a clue. This isn’t the first time Mydei has thrown everything else to the wind to follow him to the ends of the earth. It probably won’t be the last. “Not that second one,” he says, reaching for pants next. “Maybe I want to see Cyrene too.”

The pause between them stretches a little too long. When Mydei looks, Phainon’s expression is complicated. Still a little pinched until it softens and he sighs again. “Alright, if you’re sure,” he says. “It’ll be nice not to be the one driving the whole time at least.”

“I’m sure,” Mydei says, arms full of fabric. He shoos Phainon out.

△

In the next hour, Mydei packs, forces Phainon to clean the kitchen, argues quite a bit, and books a hotel for each night they’ll be driving because he has no interest in sleeping in his car after sitting in it for ten hours straight. Phainon sits cross-legged on the couch with a rolling carry-on in front of him and his phone open to a map by his thigh. There’s a sleeve of crackers in one of his hands and a can of spray cheese in the other. He’s dressed the same as he had been—that is to say terribly—and he’s clearly upset. Mydei pays him no heed as he draws a frowny face with angry eyebrows on a cracker.

“Did you pack your toothbrush?” he asks. Phainon makes a face, hair dried and sticking up atop his head.

“Yes, mom,” he says.

“Extra socks? A jacket in case it gets cold? Deodorant?”

“I’m not completely helpless, Mydeimos.” Phainon looks at him tiredly. Not annoyed, not quite, not really. It’s something else, like he’s pretending. Mydei exhales.

“Alright,” he says. “We can go whenever you’re ready.”

Phainon pushes the frowning cracker into his mouth and puts the cap back on the cheese. He brushes past as he gets up to put the food away, and then he rustles around in their tiny kitchen before he comes out with a paper grocery bag in arms. He sets it on the couch and disappears, skidding in his bagel socks down the hall. Mydei hooks a finger on the edge of the bag to pull it down. Chips, a box of protein bars, cookies, licorice, fruit leather… It’s stuffed with junk food for the ride. He slips into the kitchen himself to pack a cooler. As he zips it up, the floor creaks, and there’s Phainon leaning against the stove, a tote bag on his shoulder and gray slip on sneakers on his feet. The bagel socks peek out from under them.

“Let’s go,” he says coolly. One side of his collar sticks up.

Mydei straightens up, taking the cooler with him, filled to the brim with drinks and all the fresh fruit and veggies from the fridge that might go bad while they’re gone. He pauses in front of Phainon to fix his stupid polo, hearing his breath, nearly skimming his fingers over the sun tattoo he got in college, backing away before his face has a chance to heat. “Come on, then,” he says. “I bet you can’t carry all your shit in one trip.”

Phainon scoffs, and that’s how they end up stumbling down three flights of stairs with their arms full, all but racing each other, each of them almost tripping as they take their turns too fast. But Phainon has never made Mydei smart. He brings out his best and his worst. Weakness and strength. Fondness and frustration.

“I win,” Phainon pants as they stagger to Mydei’s butter yellow hatchback. His carry-on clacks as he sets it down, the snack bag on his hip crinkling as Mydei shifts his duffle to the same hand as the cooler to open the trunk.

“Win what?” Mydei asks, hefting the cooler into the car and shoving it into one corner to make room for the rest of their stuff.

“The bet,” Phainon answers.

Despite him, Mydei’s mouth twitches upward. “Where’s your phone?”

Bewildered, Phainon pats his pockets, comes up empty. “You’re kidding,” he says. “You did this?”

“You left it on the couch,” Mydei laughs. “I just didn’t say anything.” He puts his duffle in next. Phainon sets the snacks down and storms back to their apartment. Mydei just chuckles again as he finishes loading everything in the car, leaving the snacks and a couple of waters between the seats in the back so they won’t have to pull over to get to them.

He leans against the car as he waits for Phainon to come back. Listens to the wind sift through the trees and wonders what he’s doing, following Phainon at the drop of a hat again and again and again. He has the next two days off, but he sends a quick email to work saying there’s been an emergency and he’ll be out. An emergency. Laughable.

Phainon comes jogging down the creaking metal steps leading up to their landing, Phone in one hand, middle finger flipped up on the other. Mydei barks a laugh. “Get in, fucker,” he says, slipping around to the driver’s side. His car is hot from the sun and stinking of the lemon scented air freshener dangling from the rear view mirror. Phainon slides into the passenger seat. “We have to stop for gas,” Mydei tells him.

“Figured,” Phainon says. He buckles his seatbelt and digs around the center console until he finds the right cord. “I call aux.”

“Who won the bet?”

“You never set stakes, Mydei. That’s on you.”

“Shut the fuck up.”

△

Phainon has a strange taste in music. Kpop girl groups, old folk music, and musical soundtracks take the forefront. Most of it is bearable, some of it could even be considered good, and everything else—everything he plays for Mydei, that is—is the most god awful, ear splitting stuff known to man. He does it on purpose, obviously, gleefully tapping his foot and his fingers on the back of his phone in his lap. Mydei’s burnt orange aux cord connects it, spelling his doom. He takes a big inhale, palms sliding down the steering wheel, thumbnails digging into the leather, and merges onto the freeway.

One song passes, two, three. Phainon leans all the way back, head tipping against the seat like he’s trying to look through the sunroof. And then he lets out this little huff. A moment later, the song changes to something palatable, something Mydei may have mentioned liking at one point. Something soft, a girl with beautiful vocals and beautiful lyrics to match.

“You let me get away with too much,” Phainon tells him.

Mydei spares him a glance. The line of his jaw, choker, collar. Higher, one ice blue eye, white hair that stirs slightly in the breeze from the air conditioning. Mydei turns back to the road. “I find that the more I complain the worse it gets,” he says. “You like the reaction.”

A half laugh. “Figured me out,” Phainon says. His fingers are still tapping. His phone case, blue and orange in halves, a beach scene. “When you just sit there and suffer like that, I feel bad for you.”

Silence. Another verse, another chorus. Mydei gets over to pass a semi truck. “Why now?” he decides to ask. Cyrene is probably Phainon’s most important person. The only family he has left. They call every other week, text at least three times as often. He visits twice a year, but those trips are always planned months in advance. He’s never just up and gone like this.

Another glance, brief. Phainon’s lips part. Ahead, a car attempts to merge without signaling. He’s quiet for too long.

“I… missed her,” Phainon says. “I wanna see her while I can.”

Mydei chews on the inside of his cheek. He’s reminded of the way Phainon is overly wary of candles, a bit more frugal than he needs to be. “You’re not just going to up and go broke one day, Phainon.”

This too earns a laugh, though it shouldn’t. “That’s not something you can promise,” Phainon says, sardonic. “Not in this economy.”

It’s true. Neither of them lives paycheck to paycheck, but their bills seem to get a bit bigger every time they have to pay them. If something went south, it wouldn’t take long at all for Phainon to burn through his meager savings. Same for Mydei. “You have people you could fall back on,” he points out.

“Who, Cyrene?” Phainon asks. It comes out almost bitter. “Maybe an uncle I’ve only spoken to a couple of times?” The song fades out as it ends. It’s a handful of seconds before the next plays. A little softer, a little slower. A voice clear as glass and an acoustic guitar. As it would turn out, a song Mydei showed Phainon. “Can you imagine that? ‘Hey, you remember when I was this tall, right?” He waves his hand about level with his stomach. “‘But now that I’m this tall—’” He passes a hand over the top of his head. Mydei gives him half a glance and scoffs. “‘—I’m a bit strapped for cash. You think you could help a nephew out?’”

“You’re an idiot,” Mydei says. He checks his rear-view mirror. A flash of yellow. He checks a second time and reaches over to punch Phainon firm in the arm. “Slug bug.”

“Ow— what?” Phainon clutches his arm to his chest, then checks every which way in search of the car.

“Behind,” Mydei directs him. Phainon twists in his seat to look, and then laughs.

“God,” he says, settling back into his spot, still rubbing his arm like it hurts. Mydei didn’t even hit that hard. Phainon takes much worse from him when they spar and gets right back up after. He once chipped a tooth on the floor in high school because Mydei punched him so hard, only to keep fighting like it was nothing. “I haven’t seen one of those in forever.”

“Double points, then?” Mydei asks, making like he’s going to punch Phainon again. He gets a fist bump for his troubles, and then Phainon shoves his hand away.

“I hate you,” he says, but he’s smiling when Mydei checks. Silence falls between them. Just the sound of the road and the chorus of this song that they both like. Hours to go. Between the heat of the car and the uncomfortable feeling in his chest, Mydei starts to sweat.

A little longer, he tests his tongue against the points of his teeth. “I’d help out,” he says, clearing his throat. “If worse came to worst.”

Phainon’s fingernails against his phone case. He reaches for the drink he’d gotten from the gas station—lemonade, the kind in a glass bottle—and screws off the cap. “I appreciate that,” he says softly, just when Mydei is expecting another joke to punish him for trying to be serious. But this time, Phainon meets him in kind. “I would too, if it were you.”

Face warming, Mydei grunts. The lid clinks at Phainon returns it to the glass bottle. He puts it back in the cup holder and says, “But hopefully it never comes to that for either of us.”

△

Phainon goes quiet after a point. He leaves one of his more inoffensive playlists on shuffle and takes to leaning against the window, cheek propped on his fist, eyes shut, expression smooth.

He has an interesting sort of face. If he were an entirely different person who wore it, he could make himself look like an asshole just by breathing, or paint a convincing picture of the collected, stoic type. As it is, Phainon wears his heart on his sleeve. He feels so many things, so obviously. He reminds Mydei of a goddamned dog. He so rarely looks like this. Something just off from peaceful, a step too strained to be relaxed, somehow expressionless all the same. Mydei turns his gaze back to the road.

They’re three hours in at this point. His car has burned through a third of its gas tank. They’ve crossed the first of five state lines along the way. Phainon’s eyes are still closed.

One year, when Cyrene was spending the holidays with her partner at the time, Mydei took Phainon to his home so he wouldn’t be alone. On arrival, his mother had taken Phainon by the chin and tipped him this way and that, seeing how he’d grown up, how he’d lost the baby fat and the acne, how his hair was still unruly as ever, how he’d gotten that stupid sun tattooed on his neck. A strong placement, she’d said later, because the more a tattoo hurts the more worthy it’s wearer is to Mydei’s dying culture. He grew up beautiful, she’d said just to Mydei, because it wasn’t the first time she’d met Phainon, but it was the first time since he was an awkward teen coming over after school to play games.

Mydei still thinks about that. He shouldn’t, but he does. Glances at Phainon every now and then and remembers his chin in his mother’s hand. The panic in his eyes as he was helpless to do anything but comply with her scrutiny. His embarrassment and bewilderment later, tucked up in Mydei’s childhood bedroom, rubbing his own jaw, the tiny pinpricks of stubble there, because he can’t grow a beard but these tiny patches under his jaw always try anyway.

He remembers that, Phainon’s stupid expressive face, and he remembers his mother calling him beautiful. Over and over he hears it, until sometimes he looks at Phainon and wonders if she’s right.

An inhale, like the first upon waking, but he knows Phainon was never asleep. His fingers were still tapping to the beat. He struggles to sleep anywhere but a bed anyway, and even then, sometimes he’s lying awake for a long time before he gets anywhere close. Mydei has woken up too many times to the hollow sound of their faux hardwood as Phainon paces to have something to do with himself.

“Do you want to swap?” Phainon asks. “You’ve been driving for a while.” He flips his phone face up, clicks the power button to check the time. “Are you tired yet?”

“I guess my ass is getting numb,” Mydei concedes. His shoulder is aching too; old injury or unconscious tensing. He isn’t dumb enough to turn this into one of their competitions. He’ll fuck around with his safety, but not everyone else’s. “We can stop for lunch, and then you can take a turn.”

Phainon pulls up his maps and asks, “Where to, Your Highness?”

“Shut up,” Mydei tells him. “Somewhere cheap.”

△

Between the two of them, Mydei is the better driver. It isn’t that Phainon is bad, but he has a habit of taking turns too fast and getting confused by his own directions. He’s never been in a crash, and he’s never been more than five minutes late from taking the wrong route, but Mydei is better. He’s steady, calm, stable. Nothing on the road scares him. He never gets lost. Sometimes he makes Phainon a tired, aching sort of envious.

They stopped in the middle of nowhere for gas station pizza and a piss, and now they’re on the road again. Phainon is at the wheel, and he realizes after pressing on the brake and scaring himself with how sensitive it is, that this is the first time he’s ever driven Mydei’s car.

“Don’t crash it,” Mydei warns him. It isn’t a nice car by any means. Mydei bought it off a cousin in his last year of high school, but he’s taken good care of it since. It’s nicer than Phainon’s by a long shot. And yet, he didn’t even need to adjust the seat. All it means is that he and Mydei are the same height. For some strange reason, it gives him an odd, almost possessive feeling. It’s a goddamn car.

“No guarantees,” he laughs. “Just try to be nice to me while your life is in my hands.”

“Shut up.” Mydei takes the aux; his turn now that he’s in the passenger seat. He likes old rock and pop ballads, and doesn’t particularly care what language they come in. This first song he plays sounds like it might be in Chinese. “Try to kill me and you’ll just kill yourself too.”

“Maybe I’ll only crash on your side,” Phainon retorts.

A scoff. “And then the momentum will turn the car and your side will get hit too, dumbass.”

He hums, tapping the steering wheel. It’s leather, shiny and soft, part of it pocked with dents where Mydei usually rests his thumbs. He must dig his nail in as he drives. Phainon’s never noticed. “Not if I get the speed and the angle just right.”

“You know dogshit about physics, don’t give me that,” Mydei tells him, so he laughs again and gives up this line of conversation. There’s a hollow feeling in his stomach. Sticky like sap covered hands run through dirt. Earthworms and wheatgrass. The stink of old fire.

“I’d never kill you anyway,” Phainon jokes. Tries to joke; it comes out too sincere. He’ll make Mydei gag. To save it, he adds, “Who would pay the other half of my rent?”

“You know that conversation we had earlier about how I’d help if things went downhill for you financially?” Mydei asks him, scrolling absently through his phone. “I take it back, since it’s pretty obvious I’m being used.”

Fields and fields of nothing. A long, empty stretch of road. Phainon is going over a hundred miles an hour without realizing. He eases his foot off the gas. “Wasn’t it your car getting crashed in this scenario? Doesn’t that make you the broke one?”

“That would make me dead,” Mydei says. “And you as well. You’re just fucking dumb.”

Phainon laughs, then pretends to be offended. “I feel like you used to be nice to me.”

“And you’re wrong about that too.”

“Hah…” Phainon takes a breath. It comes out as a sigh. He’s still… he doesn’t know. He wants to see his sister. 

“Phainon.” He must take too long to reply. Must show something in his face. Mydei hardly ever calls him by name. “You’ve been weird all day.”

“I know,” Phainon admits. That pit in his stomach. Like sand slipping through fingers. Rocks on the beach. He wishes he were better at pretending, but he’s not. He doesn’t want to be watched as he crumbles. “You don’t need to worry about me.”

“Wasn’t planning on it,” Mydei tells him. A lie. He’s probably worrying right now, but Phainon doesn’t have the words to make him stop. Not when he can’t figure out how to stop himself.

“I should’ve figured,” Phainon says. “You’ve never done nice things like that for me anyway.”

△

It’s a joke, and it’s funny because Mydei does loads of nice things for Phainon. Not with his words, rarely with his words, but he’s… very nice, actually. He drives Phainon home when he’s drunk. He cooks meals for him without being asked, he takes over chores when Phainon doesn’t feel well. Sometimes the things he says make it seem like he’s a bad friend, but his actions make it seem like “how can I make life easier for Phainon?” is a question that runs through his head daily.

He always asks if Phainon needs anything when he goes to the store and doesn’t ask to be repaid if he picks something up. He picks outfits when Phainon is going somewhere important, like a date or an interview or a party. He shares his own things—clothes, food, skincare, workout routines—and doesn’t act entitled to Phainon’s in return. He never asks for anything in return ever, really. Strange.

The rumble of the road. Mydei put rock on a few songs ago, but he plays it pretty quietly. They’re both starting to get sick of listening to so much music, but they’re barely halfway through their drive for today and it feels wrong to drive in silence. Mydei would probably disagree, but he’s better at focusing on one thing than Phainon will ever be. Phainon always needs background noise, movement, touch, something. He’s… A glance at Mydei. Why is he here?

He’s never tagged along on Phainon’s visits before. He hasn’t seen Cyrene since they were all in high school. And yet, here he is, donating his car, his paid leave, his time to the cause. He… Maybe he just wanted to get out for a while.

“Do you need to swap?” Mydei asks out of the blue.

Phainon kind of flinches. “What? No, it hasn’t even been two hours. You drove like three and a half.”

“You’re restless,” Mydei points out. Phainon’s free leg is bouncing, and it isn’t even in time with the music. He stills it. “This isn’t a competition, don’t be stupid. If you need to swap, we can swap.”

The road is straight and basically empty. Phainon has enough presence of mind to drive, he’s just… thinking. Overthinking. But he’s not distracted, not dangerous. “I’m fine, Mydeimos,” he says. “Just… have stuff on my mind.” Mydei just grunts, shifts in his seat to pull a leg under him. Phainon’s knee is bouncing again. “Seriously. Talk to me if you’re so worried. My brain is just going a mile a minute.”

A low hum. “What are you thinking about?”

Phainon opens his mouth. Exhales. Gets over to pass as he approaches a car going quite a bit slower than he is. “I don’t know,” he says, because saying you would be super weird. “I was kind of… wondering why you’re here.” That never ending pit in his stomach. The words of a phone call playing on repeat. Over and over. The mind is a prison. Stop thinking about it.

“That’s what has you chewing up the inside of your cheek?” Mydei asks. Phainon relaxes his jaw, not having noticed he was doing that. His tongue traces the sores he’s made. “I’m due for a vacation anyway. And even if I haven’t seen Cyrene in years, I know she’s cool. She’s your sister, idiot, why are you shitting your pants?”

“I—” His throat tightens. Helpless, Phainon swallows, clears it. “I’m not,” he says. “You’re really just coming along to see her?”

Mydei makes an indignant sound and pulls Phainon’s empty lemonade bottle out of the cup holder so he has something to brandish. His gaze could light something on fire. “Are you seriously asking if I have bad intentions with your sister? Your sister, Phainon?”

“No!” Phainon exclaims. “No, what the hell? Why is that even where your mind went? Maybe you really do— Ow!” Mydei pinches the meat of his upper arm and huffs, sitting back. The lemonade bottle clinks as he puts it back. Phainon lifts his other hand from the steering wheel to rub the spot. “What was that for?”

“Being an idiot,” Mydei answers. “Eyes on the road.”

Phainon turns back to the road, huffing. Still, a lump in his throat. “You suck and I hate you,” he says, anything but sincerely, and Mydei barks a laugh and crosses his arms over his chest.

“Sure,” he says. “That’s why we’re taking my car and splitting the costs of this trip. Because I suck and you hate me.”

“True,” Phainon says, nodding, trying to smile. He pulls the inside of his cheek between his teeth again, and it’s already sore. That fucking hollow feeling. A thistle in a flower garden. “Listen, Mydei. When we get there…” His words stumble to a halt. He wets his lips and takes too long to finish the thought.

“Cyrene probably doesn’t have room for me, does she? You know I can sleep pretty much anywhere, though. I don’t mind the couch.”

“No, that’s… Why would you be on the couch? You can just share with me. But that’s beside the point. I was trying to say that… well…”

“Yes?”

A lump in his throat. Insurmountable. Phainon swallows and his Adam’s apple rolls against his choker. “You’ll have to cook for us,” he says. “Cyrene’s just as hopeless in the kitchen as I am.”

Mydei laughs through his nose. In the corner of Phainon’s eye, his hair slips free from behind his ear, shines slightly in the sun as he shakes his head. “Why am I not surprised at all?”

△

They check into the hotel just past nine. It isn’t fancy or particularly nice, but it’s quiet, passably clean, and air conditioned. After all that driving, Phainon is glad to be anywhere but the inside of the car. Mydei was right about getting a hotel.

The room is tiny, with a little cubby in the wall by the entryway that houses a coffee maker and supplies to go with it, a bottle of water, and two glasses. Below that is a mini-fridge that he puts the dregs of a gas station cola in. Just past that, the bathroom, the rolling door to the closet. On the other side of the room is a desk with a single chair, and inside a little further is a dresser with a TV perched on top. Across from that, the bed. One, because it was a few hundred dollars cheaper than two. Phainon struggles out of his shoes as Mydei tosses his bag on the floor and pokes his head into the bathroom. Water runs as Phainon drops his shoes in the entryway, sighing as his feet can finally breathe.

“You can’t steal the soaps,” Mydei informs Phainon as he comes back out. “They’re mounted to the shower wall.”

Phainon rolls his bag next to Mydei’s and sits heavily on the bed. He rubs his thumb between his eyebrows, eyes slipping shut. “Hah,” he says, a bit weakly. “What a shame.”

“Do you have a headache?” Mydei asks, taking the other side of the bed like breathing. He’s closer to the window, Phainon the bathroom. It’s one of the only arguments they’ve never had to have.

“A bit,” Phainon admits. He can still hear the phantom of tires on the road. It feels like there’s cotton in his ears. He should’ve just taken the red-eye and flown. “The sun was in my eyes for a while.”

Mydei grunts and kicks off his shoes. When he sits, he pulls one leg up onto the bed, ankle under thigh. “Come on, then,” he says, and his jeans are a bit wide legged, riding up to show the black band of his sock, half an inch of his shin. Phainon sighs and leans back, resting his head in the dip there, legs hanging off the bed. His collar flips up in the process. Mydei fixes it for him for the second time that day, and then presses his small knuckles into Phainon’s temples, massaging a firm circle there.

As he does, Phainon looks up. The hotel light is a rather nauseating shade of yellow. It casts weird shadows on Mydei’s face, tipped down, expression neutral. Phainon has always thought that Mydei has a unique face. No one can assign him a celebrity doppelganger. Something about the set of his eyes, the bridge of his nose, the shape of his jaw. He’s a rare combination. Sometimes he wears makeup too, red eyeliner to match the red tattoos that cover most of his body. He’s… no one really looks like him.

“How many times do I have to tell you not to stare at me while I do this?” Mydei asks, folding a hand over Phainon’s eyes. He smells like hotel hand soap, and the thumb of one hand is rough and calloused from playing the guitar, same with the fingertips on the other. “It’s like you’re counting my nose hairs or something.”

Phainon laughs a little, reaches up to pull Mydei’s hand away. Maybe Phainon’s fingers are cold, but his wrist is warm, heart thrumming beneath his touch. “All clear,” he says, “I haven’t noticed any.”

Mydei chuckles. “Shut up,” he says, and pretends to poke Phainon’s eyes out until he laughs weakly and squeezes them closed. Behind them, his head throbs. He’s so tired, body heavy. He goes quiet as Mydei rubs a firm line from his temples to his hairline and traces it a few times, pausing to rub circles into pressure points. Even if it’s only temporary, the throb eases up as Mydei chases it away.

“You’re oily,” he comments after a while.

Phainon cracks his eyes open only to squint against the light. It burns red through his eyelids. “Shut up,” he parrots. “When am I not?”

“Wash your face, fucker,” Mydei tells him, but he still takes the care to do this right. Another nice thing he does for Phainon. He’ll sit down after hard workdays or stressful interactions and work the pain out from behind Phainon’s eyes. He says his mother did it for him as a kid, that she would pull him into her lap and massage his head while she told him stories and legends of the old Kremnoan warriors. People who built their culture on war. He’s shared some of those stories with Phainon too. Men and women who wore tattoos and braids in their hair, who fought side by side with someone as an act of love, who taught their children to fight as they learned to walk. He hadn’t taken kindly to Phainon comparing them to ancient Spartans. They weren’t violent, he’d say. They were protective. They showed love with their strength.

Mydei probably does too. He’s steady, calm, stable. Strong in a lot of ways. In body and in this. He makes a good rock. He’s been anchored as long as Phainon can remember.

“Wash your mouth, Mydeimos,” he says back. Mydei flicks him softly in the forehead.

“The light is in your eyes, isn’t it?” he asks when Phainon flinches.

“Yeah,” Phainon answers, so Mydei sighs and gently lifts his head to slide out from under him. He flicks the light off and turns on his bedside lamp instead. It’s a soft, dull glow. Still yellow, but it doesn’t hurt Phainon’s eyes so much. He pushes himself up so Mydei can settle back into place, fingers carding through hair as he pushes it out of Phainon’s face. They meet eyes, just for a moment, and Mydei looks almost as tired as Phainon feels. Still, “thanks,” Phainon tells him, that lump crawling back up his throat.

And Mydei shrugs it off like he always does, averting his gaze and clearing his throat. “Whatever,” he says, and probably goes red at the tips of his ears. Phainon can’t tell in this light. He chuckles, and silence falls between them like a blanket of ash.

chapters.title: Chapter 2
chapters.html:
Mydei wakes second, as he tends to. Phainon’s side of the bed is vacant and rumpled, cold when he slides a hand through the sheets. The bathroom door is shut, but there’s no sound of water running or the buzz of an electric toothbrush. Just silence.

Pushing the blankets off, Mydei sits up. A breath in turns into a yawn, and he stretches his arms over head. His eyes stay closed a little after he’s done, clinging to the last bits of sleep before he wipes a crust from the corner of his eye and drags himself upright. As he digs through his stuff for his water bottle—a scratched, dented old thing lacquered red and covered in peeling stickers—the faucet runs, shuts off. The door creaks softly as Phainon pulls it open. The ends of his bangs are wet.

“Morning,” he says, a little rough from sleep. He’s still in his pajamas, so he can’t have been awake for long. A blue t-shirt with a hole in the armpit and old basketball shorts. Mydei sits without a shirt, swishing a mouthful of water through his teeth. Groggy, he blinks, swallows.

“Morning,” he rasps back. Phainon inhales.

“We’re up a bit late,” he says. “Breakfast is over in an hour, so we should probably get ready and head down.”

Mydei grunts and leans forward to rest his elbows on his knees. He takes another sip, yawns again. Phainon steps out of the doorway and goes for his suitcase, turning it onto its side and unzipping it. He digs around a bit before he picks a set of clothes for the day. Gray cargo pants and a folded shirt in a suspiciously familiar shade of purple. As Phainon slips by, Mydei grabs his wrist.

“Do not wear that shirt,” he says. Phainon blinks and looks down at the bundle of fabric in his hands.

“Didn’t you buy it for me?” he asks.

Mydei winces. “You were never supposed to wear it. Not in public, at least.”

Phainon huffs a laugh and unfolds the shirt to look at it. It’s a frankly offensive shade of purple, with a giant fish emblazoned on the front. Behind it is a man with a fishing pole, the string along the top of the graphic and the hook in the fish’s mouth. Around are some cartoon splashes, spreading out evenly above the bold, large printed words Master Baiter.

It was a gag gift. Or, was supposed to be, because Mydei had been on vacation in Alaska and Phainon unironically enjoys fishing. He thought it would get a couple laughs and be forever banished to pajama duty, but here it is, haunting him, just like the rest of Phainon’s fashion sense.

“It’s funny, though,” Phainon protests. “What’s wrong with it?”

“Look at it,” Mydei says tiredly. “Literally just look at it.”

Phainon does. “It’s pretty bad,” he admits. “But it’s not like anyone is going to take it seriously. It’s a joke. People like jokes.”

“Okay,” Mydei says, snagging a plain brown muscle tee from his open duffle bag and pulling it on. “I’m not sitting with you at breakfast.”

“You’re so rude,” Phainon laughs, but he tosses the shirt back in his luggage and picks a new one—a Star Wars tee, the graphic cracked and fading. God knows how long it’s been since Phainon even saw the movies. He sits on his side of the bed, back to Mydei, and pulls off his pajama shirt to change. Mydei stays quiet, still looks at him. The hair curling around the nape of his neck, his shoulder blades, the dimples in his lower back. He has this mole a third of the way down his spine. Muscles he’s grown into since Mydei started dragging him to the gym. He pulls the shirt on.

“I hope you realize you’re only pushing it off,” Phainon continues, standing and hooking his thumbs in his waistband to change his pants. Now, Mydei looks away, finding his jeans in his bag, listening to fabric rustle as Phainon gets dressed. “I only packed so many shirts. I have to wear that one eventually.”

“You can wear it for Cyrene,” Mydei tells him, slipping into his pants and bending for fresh socks too. A yawn builds; he hides it in his hand as the bed creaks when Phainon sits back down. Back to back, they put on their socks. 

“Maybe I will,” Phainon muses. “I’ll be sure to let her know it was a gift from you.”

“Goddamnit.” Maybe she’ll find it funny now. The Cyrene Mydei remembers was a bit of a prude, frowning when Mydei swore, scolding him for making inappropriate comments. He always worried he looked like a bad influence in her eyes, but she’d always been kind to him.

“Heh.” The mattress shifts. Phainon comes to his side, tossing his old clothes on top of his luggage. “Listen, Mydei…”

A glance at him. Dark circles under his eyes. Did he sleep? Mydei did. Blurry, dreamless. He remembers staring at Phainon’s shoulder under the blanket until his eyes fell closed on their own. It’s warmer with two bodies instead of one. “I’m listening.”

Phainon is quiet for a little longer. He swallows visibly, throat smooth and uninterrupted because he hasn’t put his choker on yet. Odd, it’s like seeing him naked. He curves a palm over his sun tattoo and averts his eyes. “I know,” he breathes. “I’m just having some trouble saying what I need to say.”

“I can see that in your face.” Phainon’s eyes meet his again. Ice blue, dilated because they never turned on the light. “Spit it out, HKS.” An old Kremnoan word. It’s meant as an insult, but it always comes out too soft when he uses it for Phainon. Too fond. Four months into a life right next to him, a decade into a life in his orbit, this is why Mydei can’t regret it.

A shaky breath. Phainon breaks eye contact. “I’ll tell you later,” he finally says, standing up and stuffing his feet into his shoes. “We’re going to miss breakfast.”

They won’t. Mydei stares after him. The slope of his shoulders, the hang of his head. The way his hand curls into his fist as he supports himself on the wall. “Phainon,” he says.

“I know,” Phainon says back. “I’m sorry. Let’s just go.”

△

Breakfast is probably powdered eggs, slightly soggy sausages, and roasted potatoes. Mydei mixes a plastic cup full of half apple, half cranberry juice from a dispenser, and Phainon makes himself a coffee with two sugars. It sits in front of him as he eats, steam curling off the surface. He hates coffee. That’s how Mydei knows he didn’t sleep well at all, but he doesn’t comment.

Instead, he busies himself with mapping the drive to the next hotel on his phone as he attempts to saw through his sausage one handed with the side of his fork. “Eight hours’ drive today,” he says. The meat slips, and his fork collides with the plate in a hideously loud sound. He sets down his phone to cut it properly.

“Better than yesterday,” Phainon notes, sliding Mydei’s phone over so he can look. He lowers the brightness first. Mydei spares him a glance. The dark circles. He’s a little pale too, isn’t he? 

“Tomorrow’s the longest,” Mydei says. “Eleven hours and some change. Is your headache back?”

A snort. “More like it never left,” Phainon says. “I’m fine, though. Took some pain meds.”

Mydei purses his lips. Phainon isn’t even looking at him, too busy pinching and dragging the screen around, inspecting their route, a furrow between his eyebrows. “I’ll drive first,” Mydei says, extending his hand until Phainon passes the phone back. “Try to take a nap in the car or something.”

Phainon smiles wryly, lifting his paper coffee cup. “That defeats the point of the devil’s liquid, dear Mydeimos. I’ll be too awake by then.” He takes a sip to punctuate the statement, making a face and licking his teeth as he puts the cup down.

“So don’t drink it,” Mydei tells him, scraping eggs, potatoes, and a piece of sausage together into one bite. As he chews, Phainon mournfully shakes his head.

“I already got it,” he says, “and I’m not going to drink it cold. My mama didn’t raise me to waste food.” And it’s true, now that Mydei thinks about it. Phainon will sooner lick his plate clean and make himself sick than leave a few bites behind. He sighs and reaches for the cup. Phainon just watches. Mydei isn’t a fan of coffee either, but he downs the cup, swallowing it fast so he won’t have to taste it.

“There,” he says, bitter on the back of his tongue, ignoring the delighted incredulity alighting on Phainon’s face. “Now you can take a goddamned nap.”

“The things you do for me, Mydeimos,” Phainon laughs. “If you keep it up, people might start to think you’re nice to me.”

Mydei just crushes the paper cup and flips his middle finger toward Phainon, swallowing a mouthful of potato to wash the bitterness back.

Phainon laughs and goes quiet. “I’ll try, at least,” he says. “Thanks, Mydei.”

△

The beginning of the drive is quiet. They stop for gas again, and while Mydei pumps, Phainon goes inside to buy himself another lemonade—strawberry this time—and a pack of mini chocolate donuts. As they pile into the car, he offers one to Mydei, who wants to scold him but has too much of a sweet tooth to refuse. He chooses to say nothing, even as Phainon pulls up the map to direct him to the freeway entrance. As they climb up the ramp, he shuts his phone off and shoves it beneath his leg.

“Cruise here for another three hundred miles,” he says. “Let me know when you want to swap.”

Mydei just grunts in acknowledgment. The crinkle of plastic. Phainon extends the donuts to him again, and he spares a brief glance to take one. Only two are gone. Phainon took neither. This too, Mydei doesn’t comment on. “Try to sleep,” he reminds Phainon, stuck thinking of the shadows beneath his eyes, the exhaustion in his smile. Without looking, he opens the center console compartment and digs around until he finds his sunglasses. Plain black frames with orange polarized lenses. He holds them out. 

A laugh, more air than sound. Phainon takes them. “Thanks,” he says, probably gearing up to add something stupid to punish Mydei for thinking of him, but he just inhales and leaves this weird little pause between them.

“Whatever,” Mydei tries to fill it.

And then, “You’re a good friend, Mydeimos,” Phainon tells him out of the blue. And he is. Mydei is a great friend to Phainon and they both know it, but they’re not supposed to say it out loud.

“And you’re fucking weird these days,” Mydei says back. “But… thanks, I guess.” In his peripheral, Phainon puts the glasses on and settles in, head against the back of the seat, arms crossed. His neck will hurt if he falls asleep like that. Mydei sucks the inside of his cheek between his teeth and wishes he didn’t care so much. But no, he doesn’t. Because he cares, and if he didn’t, who would? Phainon’s the type with a hundred friends but only a few who really know him. And Mydei has always fit best by his side anyway.

It’s silent but for the sounds of the road; they turned off the music about an hour away from the hotel the night before, since Phainon’s headache was brewing and neither one of them had anything left to play. Mydei loves music, but it’s easy to get sick off too much of it. Now, though, he turns the radio on at half the volume he’d listen to on his own and starts the air conditioning at the first setting.

Half a song plays, and Phainon stirs.

“You’re supposed to be sleeping,” Mydei points out as he plugs his phone into the aux and scrolls for a moment before selecting something.

“I know,” Phainon says, tapping a bit more before he settles back again, phone in his lap, leaning against the window this time. His neck is at a better angle. God knows why Mydei notices. “I just needed to set the mood.”

“Needed to make me listen to more shit, more like,” Mydei retorts, though the opening chords of this song are a lot sweeter than what Phainon often plays for him. Two days in a row, he’s chosen not to make Mydei suffer. What is there to say about that?

“Nah,” Phainon says, probably shutting his eyes behind the glasses. He shifts a bit more, and when Mydei glances at him, he almost looks comfortable. “I think you’ll like this one.”

So Mydei stays quiet and listens to it. Acoustic guitar. The intro is tapped, and as the verse starts, it becomes clear that this song doesn’t have any vocals. It’s soft, until the chorus builds into something stronger, emotional, beautiful. The song is almost six minutes, but about halfway through he has to murmur, “I like it.”

Phainon’s lips curl up. “You could learn it.”

“I’m not that good,” Mydei scoffs.

“Not with that attitude,” Phainon tells him, and his voice is a little soft, a little sleepy. “You’re plenty good. Remember when you first started learning?”

“Sleep, Phainon,” Mydei sighs.

“You talked to me first,” Phainon says, because he always needs to be right. But he goes quiet, and maybe if Mydei drives for long enough, he’ll fall asleep.

△

It’s three hours before they swap. Phainon leaves a playlist full of acoustic instrumentals on, and sleeps a bit. When he does, it’s fitful, shifting, sighing, but he doesn’t fuss or complain. Sometimes he wakes and looks at the view or starts short conversations before he tries to fall asleep again. At the gas station, he stirs on his own, taking the sunglasses off and stepping out of the car to stretch, yawning, working a crick out of his neck. Mydei leans against the car, watches him, and breathes.

It’s hot out, and the asphalt of the parking lot is cracked and tarred, cracked and tarred over again, the sun beating down like it wants to burn everything to a crisp, and Mydei just… Exhales. Tears his gaze away from the tuft of hair that sticks up atop Phainon’s head.

“I’m going to run in and buy a coffee,” Phainon says once he’s finished his pandiculation. God knows if he really slept, but he looks like he feels better. The sun always does that, so long as it’s high overhead and not in Phainon’s eyes. He’s funny like that. He could probably photosynthesize if he weren’t so light sensitive, but his eyes were born blue. “Do you want anything?”

“I’m good,” Mydei says, and watches his back. He could go in too, at least to get out of the heat, but he doesn’t. He just stands, stretches out each of his stiff muscles in turn, and waits. On the road, cars pass by. Closer, a sedan pulls up to one of the gas pumps. A moment longer, he follows Phainon inside.

“Changed your mind?” Phainon asks, fitting a lid onto his coffee cup. The air conditioning in the store is bitter cold, but maybe Mydei has just grown used to the warmth. He likes road trips. He likes the smell in the air.

“No,” he replies.

Phainon scratches under his shirt. “Alright,” he says, and leads the way to the cashier. His cup makes a soft sound as he sets it down. The woman manning the counter offers a half-hearted smile as she rings him up.

“Are you still tired?” Mydei asks as they walk back to the car.

“A little,” Phainon admits. He gestures with the coffee. “I’m good to drive, though.” An awkward pause. He hesitates. They look at each other over the top of the car, him on the driver’s side. He hasn’t unlocked it yet. The door doesn’t budge when Mydei tests the handle. “Thanks for letting me rest.”

“You were dead on your feet.”

Phainon chuckles, a little weak. His dark circles are still there, but that sort of thing doesn’t go away fast. “Did no one ever teach you to say ‘you’re welcome?’”

“Unlock the car, dumbass.”

A dry smile. “Yeah, yeah.”

△

It’s a bit odd, playing passenger in his own car. Phainon drives a little faster than he does, always in the left lanes, ten or fifteen over instead of Mydei’s five. The leg that isn’t working the pedals is always bouncing, his fingers tapping out rhythms on the steering wheel. He’s a restless person in general, but ask him to focus on driving for hours and it’s glaringly obvious.

Mydei controls the music now, and he puts on some older rock classics. The beat Phainon taps matches to them; he’s infinitely distracted whenever there’s music playing, always listening to it no matter how loud or how quiet it is, no matter what he’s doing or who he’s talking to. Not dangerously distracted, obviously, but he listens more than anyone else in the room. 

“You know,” he says, still tapping, still bouncing his leg. He doesn’t even like this song much, it’s just that music infects him. “You can eat the rest of those donuts.”

Four left in the package, the chocolate coating a little bit muddy from sitting in the sun. Outside, they leave the city behind for a road winding into the mountains, all green, rustling trees and slabs of reddish rock. Sunlight on everything. The polarized glasses make Phainon look like some sort of bug. Mydei watches the leaves of aspens quiver in the wind, their trunks blurring by as they drive past.

“You haven’t had any,” he says. “Now they’re all melted.”

“Eh,” Phainon says in reply. “They were for you anyway. You can put them in the cooler if you want.”

“Then they’ll get wet,” Mydei points out. They’d filled the cooler with ice during one of their stops; it’ll be half-melted and soupy in there by now. All he gets is another noncommittal sound in reply, and then something makes him think it over again. They were for you. Weird. Phainon has been so fucking weird lately. “What do you mean they were for me?”

“Uh… Exactly what it sounds like.” The sound of Phainon’s palms sliding on the leather steering wheel. The road twists a bit, each stretch taking them a little further into what seems like the mouth of a canyon.

“I know that much,” he says. “I want to know why?”

“Why is that so accusatory?” Phainon asks, glancing over, bug-eyed instead of blue. Mydei’s reflection in orange lenses. “It’s not like I poisoned them or anything.”

“And suddenly I have my doubts.”

Phainon laughs. He has that kind of laugh you hear two rooms over. Like light through a crack in the curtains. Right in Mydei’s fucking eye.

“You haven’t had like, any snacks this whole trip,” Phainon says. “And I know sweets are your weakness, but you have too much self control unless they’re offered to you or about to be wasted. So. It’s not like I’m going to eat those donuts; they’re all melty and gross.”

Looking at him is like looking into a mirror just to find it’s been glass all along, and some loser on the other side is making faces. “What the fuck,” Mydei says. All he gets is another laugh and a hand blindly groping for a mushy pack of mini chocolate donuts and tossing them into his lap. Phainon’s other hand is still tapping. His leg is still bouncing. Mydei still can’t see his eyes.

△

Somewhere down the road, Mydei rolls down the windows. Maybe it’s a bad idea, considering how hot it is out, but the air is sweet and fresh and a handful of degrees cooler when they crawl into the shade from one of the mountains. It’s so green here, so colorful. They drive through slabs of rock cut for the road to go through, marbled with reds, browns, blues. They drive past forests and old, gnarled trees, wildflowers and rivers along their path.

It’s beautiful. Phainon was raised with beaches and wheatfields, maybe that’s why he’s so awestruck by this. Mydei, when they first met so long ago, had been raised with forests and mountains. That’s why he was so awestruck by the beach the first time Phainon took him.

The car jostles as he pulls it off the road and onto a wide gravel shoulder. The river roars now that they’re stopped to hear it. Wind whisks in through the open windows and ruffles Mydei’s bangs. He’s tied the rest of his hair back, and it makes his face seem sharper, stronger. The slant of his eyes could cut, given the chance. He doesn’t ask why Phainon pulled over, doesn’t question it as he undoes his seatbelt and steps out of the car.

Gravel crunches underfoot. Two doors slam. Phainon walks around the car, and there’s Mydei, grabbing him by the wrist and pulling him along a scarcely worn trail in the foliage flanking their drive, ignoring the way he stumbles over roots and rocks, tugging him out of the trees until the only sound is the river and the breeze is damp and almost cool enough to give him chills.

“This is what you wanted to see, isn’t it?” Mydei asks, voice raised over the rush of the water over rocks. It’s so fast, so loud, though the river itself can’t be wider than a few yards. It’s full of stones coated in algae and swept up sticks, the flow churning it to a froth as it rushes over them, light dancing in the shallow parts, the blissfully calm edges that Phainon can’t help but stoop to dip his hand in. It’s so much colder than he expected. He laughs, and then it cuts off in his throat. Cyrene would love to see this.

Phainon wraps his cold, wet hand around Mydei’s exposed bicep, laughing again at the way he scowls and flinches. “It’s freezing,” he says, and Mydei flips him off. “No, seriously, feel it!”

So Mydei does, bending to touch the stillest part of the river, crystal clear and softly lapping at the muddy shore, digging out a palmful of tiny rocks the water has pained sunset orange or rich, glimmering gray. He tosses the pebbles back and turns to Phainon, the breeze stirring his hair again, the tips of his ears exposed to the sun dappled by tree leaves.

“Oh, no,” Phainon says as he steps closer. His smile is killer. He could push Phainon in and Phainon would probably be okay with it, just to see him laugh a little. It’s a curse, being willing to bleed out dry for the tiniest things. But this, perhaps, could be tantamount to a loss, and Phainon is still terribly competitive. He takes a step back, two. Mydei darts forward to smear a wet hand along the side of his neck, and he falls in by his own making, a single, critical misstep.

Or, he would have, but Mydei catches him by the shirt and hauls him upright, still cupping his neck, smile shifted into something like fear and annoyance at once. “Watch where you’re walking,” he scolds, and he’s close because he’s still holding on. “That’s the type of shit that’ll get you killed one day.”

Phainon’s belly sinks and soars in equal measure. “Your fault,” he breathes, eyes wide, water rushing in his ears, soaking his left foot.

A scoff. His breath or a breeze. “Seriously?” Mydei asks, fist tightening in his shirt. He steps back, Phainon forward, and then he lets go completely. Thump, thump, thump. A heartbeat. The sound of water like static. Mydei turns his back, makes his way back to the car. Phainon’s shoe is caked in mud. His shirt is all wrinkled. Why are you here? he thinks. What is this?

Mydei drives. Phainon takes off his shoe, wrings out his sock out the window, and apologizes for being an idiot. And somehow there it is, that laugh he’d tear apart worlds for.

“You are,” Mydei agrees, “but you’re right, though. That was partly my fault.”

△

They stop for a meal that’s too late to be lunch but too early to be dinner at an Indian restaurant. Phainon eats unreasonably cheap curry that both burns his mouth and makes him feel like moaning obscenely aloud for how good the flavor is. They argue about white rice versus brown rice, and then they’re on the road again, Phainon at the wheel for this last stretch, shoe mostly dry, the sun hanging just barely too low to make driving westward even remotely comfortable. But It’s in their eyes for only as long as it takes them to get gas and get lost in the town before they’re back on the freeway heading East.

“How’s your head?” Mydei asks, and his song of choice this time seems to be in Japanese this time. Piano and guitar, a man and a woman, a little bit soft.

“Good, surprisingly,” Phainon answers. He’s the type to get migraines at the drop of a hat, the slightest bit of heat, ten minutes of squinting, reading in the dark. Mydei always says it’s because his eyes are so blue, but that can’t be scientific, can it? His dad’s eyes were the same, and he didn’t suffer with any of this. “The sunglasses helped.”

“Wear them tomorrow,” Mydei says. Or, grunts it more than says it, because he’s always like that.

“Alright,” Phainon says. He’s speeding again, ninety-five in a sixty-five, bouncing his leg to the beat. He eases his foot off the gas, sets cruise control at eighty just to be safe. The girl singing has a beautiful voice. He has no idea what she’s singing about, but it sounds like nostalgia. A bit more sweet than sad. He might need this one for his playlist. “Thank you.”

“Whatever,” Mydei replies, because god forbid he says something like you’re welcome. Phainon feels kind of happy, and then kind of guilty for feeling kind of happy. He laughs.

“You’re the worst, you know that?” he says. His shoe is still damp, but he can’t even fathom driving barefoot, so he’ll suffer it with that squirming glow in his chest.

“I’m literally letting you use my sunglasses?” Mydei says incredulously.

“Yeah,” Phainon agrees, “but the way you reply to thank you, my God. It’s not going to kill you if you acknowledge that you make people feel cared about.”

He looks over. Mydei’s hair is still pulled back. The tip of his ear is red, or maybe that’s just the weird tint of the glasses. “Shut the fuck up,” is the only reply he can muster.

△

Their hotel tonight is a little run down, but it’s nice enough. The floors squeak, the room is small, and the air conditioner far too loud for how little cool air it produces, but the water pressure is surprisingly okay and the bed is neatly made and soft. The sun goes down. They eat fried chicken for dinner, despite Mydei’s complaints that they need at least one nutritional meal per day.

And then it’s dark outside and there’s not much left but the sound of cars out the window, the too loud a/c, his heart in his ears, the pit in his stomach now that the sun’s gone.

“Tell me a story, Mydei,” Phainon says a bit later, freshly showered and dressed in the same pajamas from last night. He packed two sets, one for each direction of the trip. For now it’s a t-shirt he’s had since the beginning of high school and some basketball shorts he’s always found a bit too breezy to wear in public.

His stomach feels full of rocks, so before he can sink under the weight of them, he asks for this. 

Mydei looks up and clicks off his phone, bending to plug it in on the nightstand. He won rock, paper, scissors, so he got to shower first, but his hair is still damp, that little braid he wears by tradition undone. He sleeps without a shirt, but for now he has a loose tank top on as some semblance of modesty. “A story,” he repeats, rather dryly.

Phainon tosses his dirty clothes with the rest of his luggage and sits at the foot of the bed, falling back until his shoulders connect with the mattress and the frame creaks. “Yeah,” he says, staring at the ceiling, smooth and untextured and entirely uninteresting, so he looks at Mydei instead. “One of your ancient Kremnoan legends, or some crazy tale from youth, I don’t care.”

Mydei meets his gaze with a flat expression. “You were there all of my youth; what crazy tales would I have to tell that you haven’t already heard?”

“Fair enough,” Phainon concedes. “Option one, then.”

Mydei does this thing where he closes his eyes and sighs. When he opens them again, his gaze finds the spot where Phainon’s shirt has ridden up an inch, then his face. “Did I ever tell you about my namesake?” he asks, and it sounds like he’s admitting defeat. “Crown Prince Mydeimos?”

Phainon’s eyebrows climb his forehead. “You’re named after a prince?”

“A lot of people are named after legends if you trace the roots back,” Mydei tells him. “It’s nothing special.”

“Crown Prince Mydeimos,” Phainon echoes, rolling it on his tongue, propping his arms behind his head and turning to the ceiling again. A dim blue glow seeps out the top of the curtain rod. The window is on Mydei’s side, as it always is. Their view today is the side of another building and half a parking lot. “It has a nice ring to it. Crazy that sometimes I call you Your Highness.”

“Don’t start,” Mydei grumbles, stretching out a socked foot to kick his hip. Mydei, who sleeps in socks but not in shirts. This, unlike the side of the bed thing, is an argument they have had. “This is why I haven’t told you this one.”

“Sorry,” Phainon laughs, liking the light feeling it gives him, if only for a moment. And then he thinks of why they’re here, and the rocks settle again. “I’ll restrain myself. Tell me about this crown prince.”

Again, Mydei sighs. “He was destined to kill his father, so the king threw him in the River of Souls,” he starts, stretching his legs over Phainon’s stomach. “But he didn’t die like he was supposed to. He fought his way out and gained an immortal body, but for one weakness.”

“Like Achilles,” Phainon says. Mydei’s face pinches, as it does, when Phainon compares his legends to other things.

“Not like Achilles,” he protests. “Mydeimos wasn’t lovingly dipped, he was thrown in to die.” He pauses, then, daring Phainon to interject again. He doesn’t, just turns his face a little so he can watch Mydei speak.

Mydei swallows, Adam’s apple bobbing before he continues. “But he didn’t. He fought his way out, and killed his father as an act of justice.”

Phainon lays a hand on Mydei’s ankle, hooking a finger in his sock, taking a breath like it’ll fill the hole in his chest. Listen, he thinks. Just listen to this. Don’t worry about anything else. “Was it revenge?”

“Justice,” Mydei repeats. “Eurypon was a terrible king. He led to more bloodshed and suffering than any five Kremnoan kings combined, but that’s another story. Mydeimos had personal reasons to kill him, sure, but it wasn’t just revenge.”

“He was a hero, then?” Phainon asks.

Mydei laughs, a little gruff. “A hero?” he asks. “Not really. He led the Kremnoans to Okhema instead of taking the throne. He brought the fall of Kremnos.”

“Fall makes it sound like everyone died.”

A grunt. Mydei kicks him softly when he pulls his sock halfway down his ankle. “Quit that,” he says, so Phainon fixes his sock and pats him on the shin until he huffs and continues. “Maybe he didn’t kill the people, but he killed the culture when he forced everyone to assimilate. That’s why I hesitate to call him a hero.”

“Oh,” Phainon says. “Maybe he thought he wouldn’t make a good king.”

Mydei shrugs. “Maybe.”

“So how’d he die?”

“That’s your question?”

Phainon huffs a laugh. “They always die at the end of your legends, Mydei. You can’t blame me.” Another kick. Mydei digs his heel into Phainon’s stomach until he shoves him off and bowls over, laughing and pained at once. “Mercy,” he wheezes. Again, that light, fleeting feeling. Mydei lets up, so Phainon rolls over to lay by his side rather than at his feet. The bed rocks and groans, and Mydei watches him the whole time. When his head hits the pillow, he turns on his side and meets his eyes. “Hi,” he says.

Mydei’s gaze flicks between his pupils, up to his still damp hair, down to the collar of his shirt. “Hi,” he says back, moving onto his side to mirror him, a little gravelly.

“Finish the story,” Phainon prompts, and it comes out kind of quiet, kind of weird. His heart climbs his throat to sit under his tongue.

“He fell in love with a warrior in Okhema,” Mydei tells him, sliding a hand under his pillow. “They were equals in just about everything, and that’s… significant to a Kremnoan. The old words they used for falling in love translate pretty close to ‘to meet one’s reflection’ and they actually used the word equal instead of husband or wife, it…”

“I like that,” Phainon murmurs.

Mydei looks away. “Anyway. He died sacrificing himself to buy that warrior time to save the city.”

“That sounds like something a hero would do to me.”

“Maybe,” Mydei grumbles. “A real hero wouldn’t leave the one he loves to fight alone.”

Phainon tries to laugh, but it’s all air. He can taste his own heartbeat. “Cut him some slack, Mydei, he was trying to save the world.” A shrug. “How’d he get killed, if he only had one weak spot?”

“Stabbed through the back,” Mydei replies. “Tenth thoracic vertebra.”

“Tenth thor— Where even is that?”

“Thoracic spine starts at the base of your neck. Just count the vertebrae down from there, it’s not that complicated,” Mydei tells him. He reaches out, shoves at Phainon’s shoulder. “Turn around,” he says.

“What are you doing?”

“Showing you, fucker,” Mydei answers, and presses a finger to the top knob of his spine when he complies. “One,” he says, and then drags his finger down to feel through his shirt. “Two.”

“That tickles,” Phainon says, squirming a little. Mydei blows on the back of his neck.

“Shut up. Three. Four,” Mydei continues. Here, the vertebrae don’t poke out so much, so he wiggles his finger into Phainon’s back to feel for them, ignoring the way he shakes with near laughter. “Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine.” He stops at the middle of Phainon’s back, pressing into the dip of his spine, thumb rubbing a circle into the right spot. “Ten.”

A shiver climbs up Phainon’s spine. “Alright,” he says. “There, then.”

“There,” Mydei agrees. A pause. His hand falls away. Phainon rolls onto his back, shoulder skimming Mydei’s chest, closer than he expected. He should have figured, with the breath on his neck, the nearness of his voice. That brush of contact is terribly warm. Neither of them bothers to move away.

“That warrior,” Phainon starts, eyes following the lines of his tattoos, climbing partway up his neck. “The Okheman one. What was his name?”

And Mydei looks back, amber gaze enough to pierce through metal. “I forget,” he says. “Probably something stupid, like Phainon.”

Chapter End Notes

small tidbit on my characterization: Mydei comes from a fairly wealthy family but he's very frugal and anticonsumeristic. Phainon's family Was comfortably middle class until their house burned down and his parents died. He and Cyrene share a trust with the death benefit and everything their parents left behind, but he refuses to spend a penny of it. Aside from that, he struggles a lot with saving money, but he tries his best. He just spends way more than he should on snacks

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.html:
Sometime, too early, three or four in the morning, the mattress squeaks and shifts, a door closes, a light flicks on and creeps under the gap at the base. It’s negligible with his eyes closed, but Mydei cracks his eyes open and notices, and just the fact that he knows that bit of light is there makes it so he’s irremediably disturbed. He can sleep through the sun rising and lighting the room enough to see, and he can nap midday with the lights on, but this… this is too much.

He waits a little while. If Phainon is just using the bathroom, it’ll be no more than a handful of minutes before he comes back out and the light turns off again. For now, he turns his back to the light, tries to ignore it. He can make out silhouettes and shapes, bends in the curtains, the box of the heater. That tiny bit of illumination somehow spilling over it all. Shifting a little more, he pulls the comforter up so it blocks his eyes at the cost of stale air and too much warmth. This is better; he slips into a half sleep.

And then, for some reason, he wakes again. The light is still there, and Phainon is either taking a very difficult shit, jerking off, or doing some mysterious third thing that likely involves some measure of emotional distress and his weirdness from the last few days.

He gets nightmares. Mydei is well aware of this much.

Tiredly, he pushes the blanket off. Sits up. Rubs his eyes and then sits there with them closed for a solid five breaths, because there’s nothing he’d rather do than go right back to sleep, but he doesn’t. He pushes himself up to stand in front of the bathroom door and knocks twice with the second knuckle of his index finger. A moment, an inhale, the door cracks open.

“Did I wake you?” Phainon asks, tired eyed and caught between the light and the dark. Mydei winces against the brightness.

“You aren’t sleeping,” he grumbles.

The dregs of a smile. “When am I ever?”

Mydei grunts. “Turn that light off,” he says, and shuffles back to bed, pulling the blankets back on Phainon’s side. A moment passes, the light flicks off, but there’s nothing else. When Mydei cranes his head to look, Phainon is just standing there, his silhouette a solitary blur in the dark. “Phainon.”

Softly, “Alright.” The bed creaks as Phainon settles back into place, lying face up, hands folded over his chest. His eyes might be open, Mydei can’t tell in the dark. He reaches out and flicks Phainon in the shoulder.

“Why’re you up?” he asks, muffled into his pillow, hand softening but staying where it is, fingers hooking in Phainon’s sleeve.

“I don’t know,” Phainon answers. He’s warm where Mydei skims his arm. Living warm, so much body heat for someone who gets cold so easily. “I don’t want to be.”

He’s the type that will sleep seven hours when he gives himself nine. He takes a long time to fall asleep and is never able to sleep in, but he’ll at least stay in bed and try. Rarely does he give up and venture into another room to do… something. Every now and then, Mydei will wake to find him on the kitchen floor with a package of cookies and cat videos on his phone, but never has he seen him so… resigned to his sleeplessness.

Under the blanket, Phainon’s foot bounces, restless and creating this horrible hiss of fabric on skin, skin on fabric. Mydei yawns, half-asleep, body frustrated by disturbance after disturbance. He flicks Phainon again and mumbles, “Want the bed to yourself?”

“No,” Phainon says, catching his hand. “Where would you go?” Their room only has the one bed and they don’t have a sofa, just a desk with a stiff rolling chair and an out of place ottoman stuffed into the corner.

“Dunno,” Mydei murmurs, yawning again, prodding Phainon’s palm, his other arm sliding beneath his pillow. “The floor.”

“No,” Phainon says, spreading his fingers out, bending his fingertips over Mydei’s, though his fingers are only a fourth of an inch longer than Mydei’s at best. Mydei bats his hand away, and he chuckles. “I’ll survive.”

His foot is still bouncing. Mydei rolls onto his stomach, arms folding under his head, one of his legs sliding under the sheets to pin Phainon’s in place. “Stop that,” he says, and the sound cuts off. Phainon goes still, and Mydei shifts into a more comfortable position, bare arm against Phainon’s shoulder, leeching his body heat. He falls asleep through whatever Phainon says next.

△

Breakfast today is make-your-own waffles, soupy oatmeal, and dry hash browns that Phainon douses in ketchup while Mydei looks on in horror. It’s also decidedly the fated Master Baiter shirt day, because it was still on the top of Phainon’s luggage and he’d grabbed it first. He’s paired it with khaki shorts, black socks that climb a third of the way up his shins, and slip on sneakers, and he looks like someone’s embarrassing uncle. Mydei has long since learned when to pick this battle and when to let it go. Phainon isn’t going to a job interview or a date, and as it stands, they’ll be in the car most of the day, so Mydei stays quiet. But he has thoughts. Many of them.

“I take it you love the outfit?” Phainon asks when he stares a little too long. Whether he’s making a face over Phainon’s clothing choice or the sheer amount of ketchup on his potatoes is up in the air.

“I hate you,” Mydei says, and could almost be convinced to mean it. He stabs his fork through his waffle, but the plastic prongs bend too much for it to be satisfying.

“Your sunglasses will really top it off,” Phainon tells him. 

“Do you do this on purpose?” Mydei asks. And he’d almost forgotten. They’ll probably see Cyrene today, and Phainon has chosen to dress like this.

“Well…”

Mydei flips him off, and he just smiles, laughs a little like he’s happy again, like whatever’s been wrong is okay right now, and Mydei bites his tongue and stirs brown sugar into his oatmeal.

“Are you excited to see your sister?” he asks.

“I…”  In an instant, the smile fades. Mydei looks at him, really looks. “Yeah. Super excited.”

“Is she okay, Phainon?” he finally decides to ask. He isn’t clueless. The same day Phainon decides he needs to see his sister, he starts acting weird. Always a little bit sad, like he’s guilty of something when he smiles. “Did she get hurt or sick, or… I don’t know, heartbroken?”

Phainon lets loose this shaky exhale. “Am I that bad at hiding my emotions?” he asks. 

“You are,” Mydei confirms. Phainon pushes the food around his plate. To their left, a family converses in Spanish. Everywhere else, people eating, talking, laughing. In the background, a song with too many synths plays. Phainon probably likes it. His knee bounces under the table.

“Sick,” he finally answers. “Acute Myeloid Leukemia, God knows how. It doesn’t run in our family. She’s always been perfectly healthy, she doesn’t have any risk factors, but—”

“Phainon.”

He stops. Exhales until his chest caves in. Helpless, his expression. He wets his lips. “Yeah.”

“It’s okay,” Mydei tells him. “I’m sorry.”

“I should’ve told you before,” Phainon offers, gaze falling to his plate, his fist around his fork. “But every time I open my mouth to say it, something stops me, like if I don’t say it out loud it doesn’t have to be real, and I know it doesn’t work that way but I— Fuck. Sorry. Are you upset with me?”

He’s all sad and teary eyed already. Much more of this and he’ll cry in public. Mydei’s chest squeezes tight, ties itself into knots. “Why would I be upset with you?”

“Because I didn’t tell you?” Phainon tries, blinking, sniffling, looking away. “She’s kind of your friend too, isn’t she?”

Mydei hasn’t spoken to her in years. Every now and then, he’ll pop in on Phainon’s calls to contribute when she’s bullying him, but that’s about it. “She could’ve told me herself if that were true,” he says. “It’s okay, Phainon. It’s not like you were trying to keep it a secret from me. I’m not the one that needs to be comforted right now.”

Phainon opens his mouth, closes it, swallows. Swiftly, he draws a knuckle beneath his eye and says, “Alright. Well. Can we just finish breakfast?”

△

Back in the room, Mydei lets Phainon pack his things in silence. A handful of minutes pass like that. Phainon putting his still wet toothbrush in a bag, collecting his shaving kit and deodorant from the bathroom counter. He unplugs his phone charger and plucks his keys from the nightstand. And when he’s finished shoving everything into his suitcase, zipping it up and setting it upright, wiping his hands on his shorts, Mydei pulls him into a hug.

“Really?” he says, voice wavering. Like muscle memory, his hands tangle in Mydei’s shirt, face hiding against his shoulder. Mydei can smell the hotel shampoo in his hair. “Right when I’ve pulled myself together?”

“You would have started sobbing if I hugged you downstairs,” Mydei tells him, rubbing his back, setting a hand on his head. Over the years, they’ve grown good at fitting together. Now, Phainon’s the tiniest bit taller but he folds into Mydei like he’s twice as small. Maybe the water here is softer, because his hair is too.

A fist hits his chest. Phainon shakes his head against him, hand smoothing out, winding around Mydei’s neck. “I’m gonna start sobbing now,” he protests, and probably means it from the way his voice wavers.

Mydei exhales, running his knuckles down Phainon’s spine, arm belting firm around his waist. White hair tickles his cheek. “Do you want me to cry with you?” he asks.

“Shut up,” Phainon says, close enough to crawl into his chest, warm enough to be the sun Mydei orbits. His body shakes with his breath, but he still holds the tears back. Mydei doesn't tell him to let them out, just lets him stay like this as long as he wants. “Don’t pity me.”
 “I don’t,” Mydei tells him. “But I’m not some asshole that’s going to act like this doesn’t fucking suck. Cancer has no business with her.” She’s too young. Mydei has never known anyone to get cancer that wasn’t already retired with a slew of other health problems. Cyrene barely drinks, doesn’t smoke, swims in races every other month and looks unreasonably photogenic in the photos Phainon shows him from her social media accounts. She’d been a healthy, energetic kid like the rest of them, so why her? Why anyone?

“Don’t pity her either,” Phainon mumbles into his shoulder. He squeezes tighter for a moment, so tight it hurts, and then relaxes in stages.

“Pity isn’t right,” Mydei says. “She’s not some kicked dog. But this fucking sucks, and I’m going to say so.”

Now, Phainon lets him go. One more breath in. He pinches the fabric of Mydei’s shirt and uses it to dab the tears from his eyes, sniffling once more. “God, I need a tissue,” he says, shoving Mydei back and turning away to find one in the bathroom. It’s liquid and disgusting when he blows his nose, loud even from a room over. Mydei waits a little longer. The faucet turns on, water runs, and then it’s silent. Phainon comes out with red rimmed eyes and the ends of his hair damp. He sets a hand on his suitcase, pressing the button on the handle to make it extend.

“Are you ready?” he asks, and his voice is mostly steady now. He looks high or allergic or miserable or all three, his hair a mess, dark circles still sitting like fingerprint stamps beneath his eyes. He makes more sense.

Mydei does a scan of the room to make sure he didn’t forget anything and zips up his hot pink duffle bag. “Yeah,” he says, and there’s a pit in his stomach now too, whatever sensation Phainon must’ve been learning to live with. What are they going to see, when they get there? What kind of fear is Phainon going to have to face? He hinges to get the bag off the floor. “Let’s go.”

△

“I can drive first today,” Phainon says after they check out of the hotel. The outside air is muggy and warm, the sky half cloudy and gray. It could rain. The air feels like it sticks in Mydei’s lungs.

He fishes his keys out of his pocket and tosses them over. Phainon catches them, drops them, and catches them again before they can hit the ground. “That was impressive,” Mydei tells him as he unlocks the car. They climb in. Their doors shut one after the other. It’s unreasonably hot for how little sun the car has been getting. When Mydei looks, Phainon has been waiting with his middle finger up. 

“Shut up,” he says, starting the engine. When Mydei grins, he offers the other middle finger too. “Direct me.”
