“Left out of the exit,” Mydei says, glancing at the directions on his phone. “Then right at the light.” He reaches to turn the air on, and while he’s thinking about it, takes the aux too. The volume is turned all the way down again. They keep listening until their ears are just about to bleed, and then give up with an hour to go. He picks a song without much thought. On cue, Phainon’s fingers start to tap.

“What’s the estimate for today?”

Mydei checks. “Eleven hours and thirteen minutes,” he says. “We’ll probably get there around midnight if we stop for lunch and dinner.” Phainon licks his teeth and makes a face. He slows to turn at the light, and Mydei checks the directions again. “The freeway entrance is on the left,” he says, so Phainon gets over.

“Do I have permission to speed?” he asks as he stops to wait for a turn light. The car in front of them has a custom license plate reading 404 GAS. Mydei is ninety percent sure it’s an electric model. He prays Phainon doesn’t notice it.

“Since when do you ask for permission? I caught you going over a hundred at least twice yesterday.”

Bug-eyed in those orange sunglasses, Phainon looks over. Earnestly, he says, “I’ll set cruise control to seventy-five if you say no.”

Mydei just barks a laugh. “Whatever,” he says, “just try to keep it under ninety. I don’t want to get pulled over.”

“Highway patrol is a myth,” Phainon says, and eases off the break. They merge onto the freeway, and Phainon is already going eighty. He slides his hands over the steering wheel, producing the sound of leather on skin, switching to tapping his free foot instead of his fingers.

“You know I watched you get a speeding ticket a few months ago, right?”

“Yes, well…” Phainon pauses, wetting his lips. “Maybe I’m a myth too.”

“That’s not a comeback,” Mydei tells him. “What is that even supposed to mean?”

Phainon doesn’t reply. “What’s he singing about?” he asks instead, because of course half his mind is on the music. The chorus of this song has a drumbeat like drowning, overpowering everything else. Mydei’s never really thought about the lyrics before. He hesitates.

“Nothing happy,” he decides on. Phainon just hums, listening to the bridge of the song. As it transitions into the last chorus, he says, “I feel like your music taste has changed a bit.”

“What do you mean?”

“Well,” Phainon says, lips curling up. “At least half the stuff you’ve played on this trip sounds like it was released after the year 1990.”

This time, it’s Mydei’s turn to flip him off. “Shut the fuck up,” he says. “If you have a problem, you can wear some fucking ear plugs.” But Phainon just laughs, and it sounds almost as real as his smile, and he seems like his normal self again for a moment until he guilts himself out of being happy and sighs.

“Thanks, Mydei,” he says after a moment.

Mydei looks at him. The line of his throat as he swallows. His eyes are on the road, as they should be. “...What for?”

“Coming with me,” Phainon answers. “I think I would have been pretty miserable on my own.”

“You would’ve been sleeping in your car; that’s a given.”

“Shut up, I’m serious,” Phainon says. “I’m glad you’re here.”

“I…” What is this? Three days of it, sentimental flashes. “...I guess I’m glad too.”

Half a smile. “You guess?”

“You’re so fucking weird lately.”

Phainon just laughs a little, rubs his neck with one hand, a finger slipping beneath his choker to pull it taut. They drive in silence. One song segues into the next. Mydei phases them away from rock and into gentler genres with a carefully picked queue. Phainon even hums a bit to this last song, something softer with a full band and lyrics that don’t make a lot of sense. And then he takes an audible breath.

“You know what I just realized?” he asks. Mydei only hums. “There was an electric car all the way back at the light with a license plate that said 404 GAS. Cause it doesn’t use gas, get it? Error 404 gas not found. That’s so fucking funny, how did I not get it until now?” He laughs, like saying he finds it funny isn’t enough, and Mydei sighs through his nose.

“I hate you,” he says, scrolling through his playlist for what to play next. “I really do.”

△

The sky steadily darkens. It starts raining about a couple of hours later. Phainon is still driving, but even he’s not dumb enough to speed like crazy in the rain. They’ve already shaved three minutes off their ETA, so he slows down a bit now. A little longer, the rain comes down harder, pattering on the windshield, drowning out the music, making the wipers work overtime. He gets out of the left lane, slows to crawl along the road with the rest of the cars. His knuckles are white on the steering wheel.

“Was it supposed to rain today?” he asks, and maybe it’s just because he’s used to his own car with brakes half as sensitive as these and a half inch less tread on the tires, but driving in the rain has always made him anxious. His molars dig sores into his cheek. Mydei turns the music off, so it’s just the low squeak of the windshield wipers, the sound of water on the roof of the car. Phainon quite likes rain, given the right circumstances. He’ll derail an entire schedule to go sit on the patio and listen to it. When he was a kid, he’d play in puddles just to come home soaked and dripping all over the floors. He never got sick, though. Cyrene didn’t either.

“You saw the sky,” Mydei says. “It’s hardly surprising.”

Sweat on the steering wheel. Phainon’s free leg bounces until he’s not sure if he’s doing it on purpose or if he’s just clenched it up so tight. Water gathers on the road. The rain comes down harder, deafening for a moment, little hailstones plunking against the windows. His hands slip. The car trudges along.

Mydei is looking at him. He can feel that much. Red light shines through the mist as the car in front of them brakes. Phainon taps theirs too hard; the car lurches. “You think I’d be used to your car by now,” he tries, chuckling. He’s torn up the inside of his cheek. He wipes one hand on his shorts, then the other.

“You can take the exit,” Mydei says.

The hail stops, but the rain continues just as violently as before. Phainon can smell it in the air the a/c pulls in. He resists the urge to tear up the inside of his mouth some more. “It’s fine.”

“HKS,” Mydei says. That old Kremnoan word again. He said it means hyena or something like that. The meaning is like scoundrel. His voice is always fond when he says it. “I’d be scared of driving in this too.”

Phainon’s driven in the rain plenty of times. Rain like this, even. He’s driven in worse in the winter. Snow and slush and black ice. But he’s never just… taken the next exit to wait it out. Does anyone do that? He doesn’t think so. He’s always just suffered through the stress. “Would you take the exit if you were the one driving?” he tries, more seriously than he intends.

“Yes,” Mydei tells him, and it’s awfully simple when he says it like that. He’s always been more cautious than Phainon, more careful. Safer. Steady, calm, stable.

“Alright,” Phainon says. Half a mile to go. He makes a conscious effort to relax. “We’ll wait it out, then.”

He takes the exit. Drives a little until he finds a supermarket to park at. It’s too early for lunch, or he’d suggest that to kill time, so for now he just pulls into a space and shuts the car off. Exhales. Wipes his hands on his shorts again, coming away covered in lint for how damp they are. The rain keeps coming, a gust of wind sending it spattering over the windows, shaking the tiny parking lot trees in their planters. New droplets make ripple upon ripple in the puddles. Phainon can still taste the humidity.

“Well,” he says. “This is fun.”

Mydei doesn’t reply, just reaches to pull the cover back from the sunroof. He leans his seat back and angles his head up so he can look through it. The rain falling from above, spilling down the sides of the car. The sky is all gray. Mydei’s eyes are lined in red.

“Look,” Mydei says, gesturing upward with his chin.

Phainon takes a breath in and undoes his seatbelt. “Right,” he says, fumbling with the seat. “Uh. How do you…?”

Mydei snorts. “There’s a lever under the seat on your left.”

Phainon finds it, moving the seat back, settling in with an arm behind his head. There’s not much to see through the sunroof. Just rain, more rain. A flash. Distantly, thunder crackles. He sighs. “We’re going to be so late.”

Mydei is quiet for a little while. “Were we going to see Cyrene today at all?”

Phainon opens his mouth. There’s no lump in his throat this time. “No,” he answers. “We’ll be staying at her place, but she’s in the hospital right now. She starts chemo today, actually. The first week is supposed to be really intense, so it might be days before she can go home.”

“Oh,” Mydei says.

“I…” Phainon sighs. “I should call her.”

“Do you want to?”

Another crack of thunder. He didn’t even see the flash this time. “Yes,” he says. “No. She sounds tired when I call, Mydei. It just makes it hard.” He can feel Mydei study him, turns to meet his gaze. Amber to ice. His expression doesn’t give away much.

“She still wants to hear from you,” Mydei says.

So Phainon lets out a shaky sigh and slips his phone out of his pocket. He puts it on speaker as he dials her. It rings, rings, rings. They wait in silence until the dial tone and Phainon hangs up. Three dull notes. He opens up their texts instead, types out good luck. “She might be in treatment already.”

“That’s alright,” Mydei says, still just looking at him. “We’ll try again later.” His gaze has always been so intense. Like he sees every goddamned thing. They’ve already established that Phainon is as clear as glass.

A thick feeling in his throat. He clears it. “It looks like the rain has let up a little,” he says, starting to sit up. Mydei’s gaze like a tangible thing. Why can’t he shake it off? “Should we go?”

It’s still pouring. Mydei stays leaned back, an arm under his head. “Wait a little longer,” he says. “Look at the sky.”

Tentatively, Phainon does. Storm clouds and water droplets. An edge of the sun peeking out. Half a rainbow, dim and mostly invisible, but there. Phainon traces its arc to the place it disappears, and then the whole thing fades as the sun hides away again. Another crack of thunder. He squeezes his phone tight, pressing imprints into his palm. “A little longer, then,” he says.

△

Lunch is an odd combination of spaghetti, chili, and cheese that turns out to be one of the best meals Phainon has ever tried. Mydei takes one look at the presentation and bursts out laughing in the middle of the restaurant because according to him it looks “so goddamned awful who cares how it fucking tastes.” He still tries it though, and admits that it tastes pretty good, even if he has to pause to chuckle a little between bites. With his reaction to the food and Phainon’s admittedly bad outfit, it’s unclear which of them is more embarrassing to be associated with.

After… that, they’re back on the road with mostly clear skies and Mydei at the wheel. Phainon plays the cutsiest, most high-pitched girl group songs he can find just to piss him off and make him complain about “vocal strain” and how “no way in hell can they sing this shit live.”

Phainon exists with half a smile for a bit, cheek in hand, propped on the base of the window. They’re cutting through civilization so there’s traffic, people on their lunch commute or heading who knows where. So many lives going by. Nothing stops for anything.

Seven and a half more hours of this. They’ve been on the road so long Phainon has forgotten what it’s like to do anything else. His ass has long since gone numb. He’ll hear the rumble of the road even after he gets out.

Mydei’s finished fuming. He just sits now, drives and digs his thumbnails into the steering wheel as Phainon continues to play music that does not align with his tastes. He’s remembered what he said earlier, about how Phainon likes the reaction. He wouldn’t put half as much effort into tormenting him if the result wasn’t rewarding. So Mydei just takes it in silence, and Phainon starts to feel a bit guilty. He picks a song where the singers don’t sound cute to the point of being slightly disturbing to play next.

“What.” Mydei says after a moment.

Phainon blinks, parrots it back, “What?”

They make eye contact briefly. Mydei’s red eyeliner. Phainon’s borrowed sunglasses reflecting him back. “It feels like you’ve been looking at me.”

And really, when is Phainon not? He’d grown up well. More than filled out his body, grew out his hair and cut it shaggy, covered himself all over in tattoos. It’s funny, looking at him and knowing him. He could be two different people.

Phainon’s still looking. God. His fingers itch. “I’m always looking at you.”

He watches the way Mydei’s lips part and close again, the way his eyes stay firmly on the road. He swallows, throat bobbing. “That’s a weird fucking thing to say.”

Phainon hums in agreement. “So is suggesting that your namesake’s lover might have had the same name as your best friend, even as a joke. But here we are.”

Silence. Mydei turns the volume on the music down. He’s still just watching the road. Not even a glance to Phainon’s side. He’s terribly good at being stubborn when he wants to be.

“Phainon,” he says. “Is this really a conversation you want to have now?”

It’s not the first time. Phainon raps his knuckles on the window, turns his attention outside to the billboards they pass. A memorial: Loved Beyond Words, Missed Beyond Measure. An ad for liposuction, a law firm, a community theatre. Something inside him twists into knots. “Probably not,” he says, and that’s that.

△

He’s not stupid, is the thing. Neither of them is. Phainon has carried this torch for a couple of years now. Mydei… At least four months, five. He doesn’t actually know, because they don’t talk about it. They’re a little closer than friends often are, and every now and then they say weird fucking things, but they don’t talk about it. Phainon just doesn’t know what they’d be like as more than friends. He can’t really see himself holding Mydei’s hand.

The conversation dies for a bit after that. Mydei turns the volume back up. Phainon plays music both of them can tolerate. The miles blur by. Cyrene texts back.

The soup they gave me tastes like nothing. Attached is a picture of a bowl of sad, milky broth. Her left hand in the corner of the screen making a peace sign. It makes Phainon laugh, kind of wetly, kind of startled. Mydei looks over. He presses call. She picks up in two rings.

“It really does,” she says, rather than greeting him. And oh, she sounds exhausted, but there’s the hint of a smile in her voice. Phainon puts her on speaker, and Mydei reaches to mute the volume again. “They said I shouldn’t have too much salt, so they basically gave me water.”

“How’d it go?” Phainon asks, terribly breathy, chest flipping over and over and over.

“I’m fine, Phainon,” she says, hearing that in him. She laughs a little. “They gave me a port, which still hurts a bit, but allegedly it’ll make treatment way easier in the future.”

“But… How do you feel?” he asks her.

“Tired,” she says. “Kind of high. In pain. Not too fond of the food.”

“Cyrene.” She laughs, almost sounds like herself. “Mydei is here. We’re seven hours out.”

“Hi,” Mydei says, a bit awkward.

“Hi, Mydei,” Cyrene greets him. “Phainon didn’t tell me you were coming. It’ll be nice to see you.” She pauses. Ceramic clinks on her end as she drinks her flavorless soup. “Seven hours… It’ll be like one in the morning!”

“We got delayed by a storm,” Phainon tells her. “It’s alright though; we’ll still come see you tomorrow. We just probably won’t wake up all that early.”

“Just drive safe, both of you,” she says.

“We will,” Phainon assures her. He opens the picture she sent again. “What’s in your soup?”

“Beans,” she answers. The sound of her spoon clinking. “Water. That’s about it. I feel a little sick, though. I don’t know if I’d be able to get much else down.”

“Mydei can cook for you.”

“I…” He glances over again. Phainon, his raised eyebrows, the phone. He sighs through his nose, shakes his head. “I can, if you want. Soup that actually has flavor, or something. Is there anything you’re supposed to avoid during treatment?”

“You’re sweet,” she says, and Phainon can hear her smiling again. “They gave me a whole pamphlet, but I don’t think it said anything about not being able to eat certain things. Just like… no raw meat and avoid acidic and spicy things in case I get mouth sores. I would be happy with anything you want to make.”

“She got the soap gene,” Phainon says. “Don’t give her cilantro.”

It makes her chuckle, kind of weak but still sincere. She yawns after, clinks her spoon in her soup some more. “I’m glad you called,” she says after a moment, a little softer now. “It’s been lonely.”

Sometimes Phainon forgets that she’s just as alone as he is. That she lost her family in the fire too. That her only sibling lives across the country from her. She has friends, just like he does, but there’s a separate, empty box in the equation for family. He can’t imagine what it would be like to go through this alone. A glance at Mydei. Phainon watches the corners of his mouth tick down, watches a line of three silver cars in a row that they pass. “We’ll be there soon,” he says.

“I know,” she tells him. He can see her smile. Her hair, dyed pink over the white they got from their mother. He hadn’t— She’ll lose it with the treatment. “I’m just grateful. To you too, Mydei. Thanks for tagging along with him. He worried me a lot when he said he’d come out by himself. I’m glad you’re with him.”

Mydei chuckles. “You think I’d let this idiot drive thirty hours by himself? He was planning on sleeping in the car for the night. He wouldn’t have made it.”

“Don’t doubt me, Mydeimos, I would have—”

Cyrene laughs, high and tinkling. “You’re too good to my idiot of a brother, Mydei,” she says. “Thank you for keeping him alive all these years.”

△

The hours crawl by. The sun goes down. They reach another point that’s just the middle of nowhere, passing another car once every ten minutes or so. Mydei turns on his brights, lighting further along their path, reflecting off signs and the paint on the road, tinted slightly blue. There aren’t any streetlights. Just them and the dark.

Phainon pulls the cover on the sunroof open and looks up, trying to see the stars. It’s dirty, covered in water spots from the rain, but the sky is there. No moon, but so many stars, brighter here in the dark, blinking softly. He wishes he knew more constellations, but the only ones he’d ever been able to find are the Dippers, and he even gets those confused when he can’t see them both at once.

“When you get sick of driving,” he says to a car filled with silence. They’ve turned off the music again, sick and out of things to play hours early this time. “Pull over so we can look at the stars for a bit.”

“We’re already going to be late,” Mydei reminds him. He’s a map of shadows in the dark, details blurred out, tattoos turned black. Phainon’s leg bounces. He traces patterns into the back of his phone, swirls and stars and zig zags.

“I know. What’s a little later?” he asks. They still haven’t stopped for dinner, but at this point it’s ten at night and they probably won’t. There are snacks in the back. Phainon has had three pieces of fruit leather and half a bag of chips. Maybe they’ll steal something out of Cyrene’s pantry when they get there. “I don’t mean for a long time, anyway. Just for a bit since there’s hardly any light pollution.”

Mydei hums, reaches for his water bottle to take a sip. Barely a minute passes before he pulls the car onto the shoulder and slows to a stop. The sound of gravel under tires. The roar of the road still lingers in Phainon’s ears. “As it turns out,” Mydei says, unbuckling his seatbelt. “I’m sick of driving.”

And all Phainon can do is laugh as he opens the car door and steps out, fumbling to follow suit, and as he comes out he’s struck by cool air on his sweat-soaked back and a sweet, fresh smell from the trees. Mydei climbs onto the hood of the car, and when Phainon joins him, the metal seems to shift in protest. “I feel like we’re going to dent this,” he says, a bit hesitant.

Mydei looks over. “Maybe,” he says. “It’s never had to support two people at once.”

“And is that… okay?” A shrug. Helpless, Phainon laughs. “Mydei, it’s your car. I can get off.”

“It’s pretty sturdy,” is all Mydei says.

“Are you going to get mad if there’s an imprint of my ass on here later?”

Again, Mydei looks at him. What scant light there is reflects off his eyes. “Sit further on the side so it’s not in the middle,” he says. Phainon scoots a bit. The metal seems to protest a little less, so he turns to look at the sky, clear and unobstructed without the dirty window in the way. The blue-black of it, the soft gray of a handful of small clouds, the twinkle of a myriad of stars.

“It’s pretty,” he says. A grunt from Mydei’s side. Phainon chuckles. “Are you agreeing with me or do you think this is totally lame?”

“Just tired,” Mydei says. “I like it.”

Again, Phainon looks at his blur in the dark. He’s leaning back now, the upper half of his body against the windshield, though Phainon is a bit too afraid of breaking it to join him. Instead, he sits and looks at him instead of the stars, and thinks this would be a painfully good time to be honest. His chest aches. A lump forms in his throat, so he turns back to the sky. Distantly, there’s the rumble of another car. It’s a handful of seconds before they pass and disappear in the distance.

“Are you worried?” Mydei asks. He doesn’t specify about what.

“Yes,” Phainon answers anyway. He’s tangling his fingers in his lap, pulling on each until the knuckle pops. “You heard her. She’s so good at pretending to be fine.”

“She just doesn’t want to worry you.”

“Of course I’m going to worry,” Phainon protests. “She’s my sister. She’s… she could be dying from this.”

“You can’t make that judgement until we see how the treatment goes,” is all Mydei says. He’s quiet for a little while, maybe waiting for Phainon to say something, but he has nothing. “She’s young and healthy, Phainon. Her odds are good.”

Phainon sniffs. He’s frustrated with himself. “I know,” he says. Again, “I know. I just can’t lose her too.”

A pause that seems to stretch for eternity. Mydei isn’t particularly adept at comfort. “Should I hug you again?” he offers, a bit stilted, and oh, Phainon could laugh.

“Fuck off,” he says, wiping his nose on the back of his hand. “Why would you make me ask for it?”

Here, a soft, rumbling laugh. Mydei slips off the hood of the car and comes around, shoes crunching in the gravel, just a body shaped blur in the night. He stands there with his arms open, and Phainon curses him again, just once, just softly, before he joins him on the ground, punching him in the chest first, then walking into him until they figure out how to fit. His face against Mydei’s neck. Mydei’s arms tight around his shoulders. He doesn’t realize he’s cold until right this moment.

“You’re terrible at this,” he says. The vibration of Mydei’s laugh. His fingers playing with the ends of Phainon’s hair.

“I know,” he says. “But you feel a little better, don’t you?”

“...Shut up.”

△

They get to Cyrene’s place late. So late, abysmally late. Two thirty-six in the morning, they lug their stuff up three flights of stairs and down the hall for Phainon to punch in the code to open the door. The lock buzzes and clicks. He pushes the door open, fumbles for a light switch. The air he’s met with smells like lavender.

Cyrene’s apartment is small and neat. The kitchen immediately to their left, nothing but a toaster, a microwave, and a knife rack left on the counter. Spices along the top of the stove. A sink, empty but for a single spoon, a humming refrigerator. Straight ahead is the living room, sparsely furnished, just a loveseat, coffee table, and TV stand. Phainon leads the way to the bedroom, where there’s a desk, a made bed, a bookshelf lined with a hundred novels arranged by color. They leave their stuff in one corner, Phainon digging for his toiletries so he can brush his teeth and be done with the day.

Mydei follows him into the bathroom, wordless as he wets his toothbrush and squeezes toothpaste onto the bristles. Their shoulders brush. They’re side by side in the mirror, brushing their teeth, tired-eyed and worn out from the drive. Mydei’s eyeliner smudged somewhere down the road. The sound of Phainon’s electric toothbrush buzzing fills the room. A couple of minutes pass; the timer goes off. He brushes his tongue, makes himself gag, and spits in the sink. When he’s done rinsing and steps back, Mydei takes over.

Phainon should shower. He’s sweaty and gross from sitting in the car all day and the sheets are fresh, but he’s so tired it’s all he can do to change into his pajamas. The same ones he’s been wearing this whole trip, blue shirt and shorts, worn soft.

He found the source of the lavender smell: plug in air fresheners, one in the living room, another in the bedroom. The walls are painted soft green. He doesn’t think he’ll have a hard time falling asleep tonight.

Cyrene’s bed is a full, not a queen, so it’s a bit of a squeeze, but he slips into the side closest to the bathroom, not the window, and feels the way his body weighs heavily into it. The light burns red behind his eyelids. A little longer, Mydei comes out of the bathroom with his hair tied back and his face washed clean. His eyes are softer unlined. Phainon doesn’t have the presence of mind to look at him without saying something stupid, so he shuts his eyes again. Listens to the shuffle of fabric as he strips off his shirt and changes into pajama pants, feels the dip in the mattress as he sits.

“Tight squeeze,” he murmurs, and Phainon hums in response. The mattress shifts again as Mydei gets up to turn off the light. Phainon finally relaxes in the dark.

Weight behind him as Mydei slips under the covers. He bumps Phainon a couple of times with the way they’re packed in tight, murmurs an apology. “Goodnight,” he says after a bit. Phainon can barely even say it back.

Chapter End Notes

more characterization tidbits just for fun: Mydei is actually a very light sleeper but struggles profusely with sleep inertia. He is doomed to be perpetually eepy and disturbed when he wakes up. Phainon tends to sleep okay, but it takes him a long time to get there. He's a frequent dreamer and serial dream-forgetter, but he occasionally gets nightmares that wake him up and screw over any chance of a good night's sleep. He also has ADHD!

Chapter Notes

Just a note: I've been doing my best with the research but I am neither a doctor nor an AML patient. pls suspend your disbelief if anything is inaccurate!

Also... why did no one tell me there was a typo in the summary... 3 weeks it sat there while I was oblivious... top 5 most embarrassing things of my ao3 career...

In the morning, Mydei wakes to too much warmth. A blanket tangled around his legs. Sweat under his arms. Someone else’s body against his back. He’s too tired to move much. The most he can do is kick the comforter off. There’s a puff of breath against his neck, something like a laugh.

“You’re awake?” Phainon asks, and the sound is so close that it gives Mydei a chill. But his body is still so heavy, and there’s no strength in him yet to speak, so he doesn’t, just turns his face into the pillow. Phainon’s arm slips off his waist. His heat at Mydei’s back disappears when he rolls over and they aren’t touching anymore. Without him, it’s almost cold. Mydei shoves his feet back under the covers.

“Seems like a no,” Phainon muses, too awake for the hour, whatever the hour is. His voice is soft, but there’s no rasp from the morning in it, none of the last dregs of sleep. Mydei can’t even open his eyes. He’s half convinced this must be a dream, but there’s the shake of the mattress as Phainon moves, the hand that brushes his mess of hair neatly behind his ear. And it’s cold, suddenly it’s cold, goosebumps prickling over his arms and neck.

Mydei rolls onto his back and forces one eye open. Phainon looks down at him, blue-eyed and bed-headed. His expression is gentle. “Maybe a yes?” he says, but Mydei has forgotten what he was asking.

Sleep slips further and further away. Mydei is still so tired. He grunts, tries shutting his eyes again, but he’s cold now, and the blankets are tangled at the foot of the bed. He makes an unhappy sound, and the mattress shifts again.

“I’m going to figure out breakfast,” Phainon tells him. “Go back to bed. Or join me if you want.”

And then he’s gone, and Mydei breathes with his eyes shut for a while. Maybe he dozes. It’s still cold. After a while, a handful of minutes at best, he cracks his eyes open. Nothing but ceiling. The sprawl of daylight. He rolls onto his side and his eyes slip shut again. His mind is starting to wake, but his body refuses. He curls in on himself because he can’t find the strength to get the blankets back.

Time passes. There’s an infernal racket from the other room, and the sound of it is almost enough to shock him into wakefulness. As it stands, there’s no screaming, so he rubs a crust from his eye and lays a little longer. Just… to the count of ten. Just…

He thinks he dreamt last night. Something about a dinner party. Yes, he’d been cooking, and Phainon had stolen his sauce. He was dipping carrots in it, and one of the guests was crying, and the sun was shining straight into his face. Red behind his eyelids, the scrape of metal eyelets on the curtain rod. The room shaking. Pressure on his shoulder, something poking his cheek. He peels his eyes open to too much sunlight and Phainon’s index finger prodding his face, his thigh against Mydei’s shoulder as he sits cross-legged at the top of the bed.

“It’s almost noon, Mydeimos,” he says. “You’ve really got to get up now.”

“Mmph.” Mydei grabs his hand to stop the poking and forgets to let go. “Fuck off. Fuck… that light.”

A laugh. Phainon tries to pull his hand free, but Mydei tightens his grip. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen you this tired,” Phainon says. Mydei cracks an eye open to look at him. Blue-eyed and… he combed his hair. Mydei’s eyes slip shut again.

“None of that.” Phainon prods his cheek again. “Wake up.”

Mydei grabs his other hand too, managing to glare. Phainon only raises his eyebrows and stretches out one leg to lightly kick his hip. Mydei doesn’t have a third hand to catch his leg too, so he grumbles and pushes himself upright, closing his eyes and breathing here for a moment. Now, Phainon pokes the place where his back tattoos converge in the dip of his spine.

“Quit,” Mydei mumbles. “I’m getting up.”

“Doesn’t really seem like it,” Phainon points out.

A couple more breaths. “...Fuck off.”

And again, Phainon just laughs and slips off the bed. “I made pancakes,” he says. “I even saved the better ones for you. They’re probably cold by now, though.”

That explains the racket. Phainon isn’t exactly hopeless in the kitchen—despite how they like to joke—but he only has about a half dozen things he knows how to make and none of them are particularly exciting. Pancakes, grilled cheese, eggs, pasta… The most basic foods known to man. Ask Phainon to cut a vegetable and he might fuck the whole kitchen up. Ask him not to and, well, he’s still rather clumsy. The pancakes should be edible, though.

Mydei yawns and stretches, first overhead, then forward, hands sliding over the sheets, head down. He has to resist the urge to stay here, reluctantly dropping his feet over the edge of the bed and standing up. God, he’s so tired. Sleep clings to him like an upset child, latching onto his legs and refusing to let go. He usually struggles to wake, but this is a new level. The drive last night must’ve done him in. He finds his shirt from last night on the ground and pulls it back on.

Phainon’s pancakes are passable. Shaped a little odd and a little browner than Mydei likes, but good enough with some syrup and a banana almost old enough for banana bread cut into slices. As he eats, seated at a chair pulled up to the counter, Phainon disappears to do who knows what. Mydei is still far too tired to care, chewing slow, trying to wake himself up with a glass of cold water. He could almost be persuaded to suffer through a cup of coffee.

When he’s done, he goes for a shower, keeping the temperature far colder than he’d like to shock himself awake. This helps a bit, but still, as he digs through his bag for a fresh change of clothes, he’s stuck yawning again.

Phainon comes in when he’s done dressing, wearing one of the few outfit combinations he’s had confirmed to be acceptable by Aglaea, which is how Mydei knows he’s taking today seriously. Black jeans and a button up with the top two buttons undone, no Master Baiter shirt in sight. He isn’t wearing shoes yet, but his socks are plain black and it’s unlikely he can mess this up with any of the footwear options he’s packed.

“I want to buy flowers before we go,” he says, and Mydei is so tired that he must glare by accident, because Phainon’s demeanor turns unsure and awkward. “Um. If that’s not…?”

“That’s fine,” Mydei says, fixing the band of his sock and standing up off the bed. He slips into the bathroom, and Phainon continues to hover as he gets his comb and starts unpicking the knots in his hair from the bottom up.

“You just…” Phainon comes to stand in the doorway, still frowning a little. “...Had this face.”

“I always have a face,” Mydei says drily.

“You do!” Phainon agrees. “And usually it’s a very nice one. But, well, the things you were doing with it just now...”

Mydei meets his eyes in the mirror. He still looks a little uncertain. Phainon’s so easy to rile up, to tease, but the moment he thinks it’s even the slightest bit serious he gets all pouty and insecure like this. Mydei sighs. “...Sorry,” he says. “I didn’t mean anything by it. I’m just tired.”

“Oh,” Phainon says, and his face brightens like he has a lightswitch and Mydei just flicked it. “Well then. I found a florist that’s kind of on the way to the hospital. Like… an extra seven minutes of driving or something like that. But if you don’t want to, we could also just stop by a grocery store and pick some up there, even if they won’t be as nice…”

Mydei sighs, snags the comb on a tangle. “Phainon,” he says. Phainon closes his mouth, makes a small sound in answer. “The florist is fine. Quit acting like a kicked dog; I already told you I didn’t mean to glare.”

“Well, I—” Phainon chooses not to continue, pressing his lips together. “Okay. We’ll get flowers, then.”

“And Cyrene will like them,” Mydei agrees, because he knows Phainon is already stressed and nervous and as uncomfortable as it is, it can’t hurt to reassure him a little more. Not when he so clearly needs it. Even if it brings an unwelcome squirming sensation to Mydei’s stomach. He grumbles the next bit, “It’s a good idea.”

“Oh,” Phainon says. Oh, oh, oh. That fucking lightswitch again. His smile is blinding, and it’s terrible because Mydei wants him smiling all the time, but hates to be the cause of it. He’d look away, but his gaze is stuck like his comb on a knot. “I was thinking of sunflowers or something. I looked it up and those are the best get-well-soon flowers, and I know she likes them.”

This much, even Mydei remembers. High school, they’d been driving somewhere, sometime. It was summer, he remembers that much. She’d said it always made her happy, seeing them grow on the side of the road. They’re like hope, she’d said, or something like it. Toss the seeds anywhere and they’ll find a way to grow. She was always kind of poetic like that. A romantic at heart. Phainon too, but he’s less obvious about it.

“Sunflowers, then,” he agrees.

“Alright,” Phainon says. He leans against the doorframe, keeps smiling. “Whenever you’re ready, we’ll head out.”

△

They head out pretty soon after that. Mydei drives by default because it’s his car, but Phainon doesn’t choose to put on any obnoxious music. He leaves the stereo muted like it was last night, and steals Mydei’s sunglasses again because the midday sun is blindingly bright. Mydei’s left arm burns to a crisp from the light coming in the window, but Phainon just sits like a happily photosynthesizing plant.

“I’m optimistic,” he says when Mydei doesn’t ask. “Or. Trying to be.”

Mydei spares him a glance. “Seems like you’re doing a good job of it.” He’s still exhausted himself. Maybe he’d just been stirred awake at a bad time in his sleep cycle. Maybe Phainon’s stupid pancakes were poisoned.

“Thank you,” Phainon says, though it wasn’t exactly a compliment. “I just don’t want her to see me sad, you know? I think it would just make her feel worse. She’s already going through way too much.”

Another glance. The glasses hide his eyes, but it’s a front, so obviously a front that he’s putting up because he doesn’t want to make everyone around him miserable. Mydei should take notes from him and stop being an asshole right now. “She’ll be happy to see you,” he offers.

“Sure,” Phainon says. Again, more subdued, “Sure.”

Mydei sighs as the car in front of him slows for a turn without signalling. His thumbnails dig dents into the steering wheel. Phainon is back to being weird. “Do you want to get her a gift?” Mydei offers. He thinks of her color coded shelf in the bedroom “A book or something. She still likes reading, doesn’t she?”

“Yes,” Phainon says, nodding, thinking about it. “Yes, but… maybe tomorrow. We can take a picture of her bookshelf to make sure we don’t get her something she already has. Besides, she’ll get mad if I bring her a ton of stuff all at once.”

“Alright,” Mydei says, stopping at a red light. Without the sound of the road, he can hear the way Phainon’s leg bounces, the fabric of his pants hissing against the seat. “So think about that instead of making yourself sad.”

“Ah.” A laugh. “Optimistic, right.” A forced smile. Phainon adds, “I must be a pretty shitty friend to be stuck with for days on end right now.”

“Your sister has cancer,” Mydei reminds him. “I’m really not being the one put out right now. Quit worrying about it.”

The light goes green. Phainon’s leg bounces a little more aggressively. “That’s the second time you’ve had to tell me that today,” he says. “Sorry. I’m just. I don’t know, my mind is going a mile a minute and nothing it lands on is good today. I’ll try to stop.”

Mydei hums, checks the directions he’d set up on his phone. Left in half a mile; he gets over into the next lane. “And I still won’t be upset even if you don’t. Just in case that wasn’t clear.”

“Fuck,” Phainon whispers. He goes still for all of ten seconds before he’s bouncing his leg again, rapping his knuckles on his thigh.

“Something wrong?”

“I’m in love with you,” Phainon tells him. “God fucking damnit.”

He’s got a hand over his mouth. A furrow between his brows. He looks sick of himself. Mydei laughs lightly. “Sure,” he says, only because Phainon doesn’t say it like he’s serious, even though he probably is. “You’re so fucking in love with me.”

Phainon laughs too, helplessly. “Asshole move not to say it back,” he tells Mydei.

And Mydei just hums. “Maybe next time,” he says, and Phainon just leans against the window and offers him a thumbs up.

△

The get-well-soon flowers Phainon settles on—after much unneeded stress and discussion of flower language with the florist—are arranged in a neat bouquet, wrapped in yellow paper and white ribbon. Big golden sunflowers interspersed with orange tulips and white daisies. There’s even a card stuck in the middle that has get well soon written on it in the florist’s neat hand. They’re beautiful flowers, and Phainon forks over a pretty penny for them and won’t let Mydei contribute.

On the drive to the hospital, he holds them carefully in his lap, not even moving much for fear of jostling them. It could almost be funny if it weren’t obvious how hard he’s trying. Mydei doesn’t end up commenting, just sets up his directions and drives.

The hospital parking lot is a whole challenge, with a dozen different signs for a dozen different care units pointing in a dozen different directions, but they eventually find the right place and park. Inside, they’re told Cyrene is in treatment and asked to wait, and there’s Phainon in a blue plastic chair, wiping the sweat from his hands on his pants and tensing up his leg so he won’t shake the flowers.

“You could put those on another chair,” Mydei points out. 

Phainon takes this deep breath. “You’re right,” he says, and does so with terribly gentle hands. Only then does he exhale, hands balling to fists on his thighs. “Holy fuck, what am I so nervous for?”

“She’s not going to look like she’s aged a hundred years,” Mydei says. “You’re not seeing her on her deathbed. She’s just in treatment.”

“I know,” Phainon says, exhales again. “I know that. She’s just… My sister. I have this image of her in my head, swinging in the backyard, running around and smiling, you know? Even when she got sick, she stuck it out, she was never…”

“And what makes you think this won’t be the same?” Mydei asks. He bumps his knee into Phainon’s, feels his lips twitch when Phainon bumps him back.

“You’re right,” Phainon says. “I know you are, but something in me just won’t listen. I… I’m sure I’ll get over it when I see her, but right now…”

“That’s normal,” Mydei tells him. He bumps Phainon’s leg again. “Do you want to hear another legend?”

“Yeah,” Phainon decides. “Yes, that… I think that would be good. You never told me why King Eurypon was so shitty anyway. Well, aside from throwing his kid in the sea, but, you know.”

The chair isn’t exactly comfortable no matter how Mydei sits on it. He shifts, leaning back a little further and folding his arms. “Eurypon,” he considers, trying to remember the details of this particular story the way his mother told it. “He was a good king at first. He fell in love with his queen, Gorgo, after they fought a duel and tied. After Mydeimos was born, there was a prophecy that said he would kill Eurypon and lead to the end of the Kremnoan Dynasty, and that’s when Eurypon went crazy.”

“So he was scared,” Phainon says.

Mydei turns to look at him, nods. “It’s a given, though. Every Kremnoan king is crowned in the blood of his own father. Eurypon too, and his father before him for a dozen generations. Of course Mydeimos was going to kill him.”

“Well…” Phainon purses his lips, smiles awkwardly. “Yeah, that’s not really an excuse to throw your kid in the sea.”

“It gets worse,” Mydei tells him. “Gorgo was the only one brave enough to oppose him, and since they were equals in everything, he poisoned her so she would lose their duel. He killed her and threw Mydeimos into the sea.”

Phainon frowns at this, brows pinching together. “But he loved them, didn’t he? Or, at least Gorgo, how could he just…?”

“He went crazy over that prophecy,” Mydei offers, shrugging. He doesn’t know why Phainon gets so into these stories, but he’s always been like that. No one else would give two shits if Mydei tells these stories or not. No one else would bother analyzing the characters’ motivations. “For the record, it doesn’t make a lot of sense to me either. I don’t know how he could just wake up one day and plot to kill his wife and child. Not to mention the cowardice of poisoning someone he thought of as his equal. He’s… my least favorite Kremnoan king for that reason.”

“You mentioned that equals were important to Kremnoans,” Phainon notes. He always remembers the most random things that Mydei says, completely forgets the most random things too.

“Yeah,” Mydei agrees. “It was bigger than love, to them. What Eurypon did was disgusting, and everyone agreed, but no one did shit.”

“You said he brought more bloodshed than any other king?”

“He’s where the bloodthirsty Kremnoan stereotype came from, at least after he went crazy,” Mydei explains, shifting again in this stupid uncomfortable chair. “He loved killing for sport, watching other people kill for sport. He started three separate wars and made death the penalty for most crimes.”

“That’s… fucked up.”

“Yeah,” Mydei agrees. “It is.” A bit of silence. Just as he’s about to ask if Phainon wants to hear another story, the receptionist calls them back up.

“She’s just finished her infusion,” they say. “She’ll be a bit tired, but she’s ready to see you. Room 216, to your left and up the stairs. There are elevators at the end of the hall.”

“Awesome,” Phainon says, all breathy. He smiles, the paper wrapping on the flowers crinkling as he passes it to his other hand so he can wipe the first on his pants again. “Thank you.”

The receptionist nods politely. “Of course,” they say. “Head on up.”

△

“Cyrene?” The door rolls open after she answers his knock, but he just hovers in the entryway. The smell inside is odd and sterile. The room itself is bathed in light from the window, with cold linoleum floors and pale blue walls. Cyrene sits up in her hospital bed, a blanket spread over her, a tray table over her lap with her lunch.

She does look tired. She does look sick, her skin paler than usual, her eyes heavier, but she still smiles when she sees him. She still looks like herself. “Hi,” she says, and there’s relief in her expression too. “Come in! Quit hovering.”

So Phainon comes in, sees her dressed in her own clothes, a soft purple shirt that’s loose in the collar. He can see the deep red scabbing of an incision below her collarbone, her chemo port hooked up to an IV. She fixes her shirt before he can get a good look, and he holds out the flowers rather stiffly. “We got these for you,” he says.

“Sunflowers.” She smiles a little, a rasp to her quiet voice, and winces as she reaches to take them. Her head cranes to smell them, pink hair falling into her face, and Phainon can’t imagine what she’ll look like without it.

“He wasted a ton of money on these, didn’t he?” Cyrene addresses Mydei now, standing with his arms crossed a few paces behind Phainon, looking approachable as ever.

“For sure,” Mydei confirms. “You wouldn’t even let me contribute, and here he is saying we got you those.”

“It’s not like I wasted anything,” Phainon protests, frowning. “It’s not like you hate them, right, Cyrene? It was money well spent.”

And now she laughs, a small thing since she doesn’t have the strength for more, but she laughs. It’s a contagious sound. Phainon can’t remember a time when she’s laughed and he hasn’t. “Sure, you big baby,” she says. “They’re beautiful, thank you.”

Paper crinkles as she shifts, slow and lethargic, to set the flowers on her bedside table. There are a couple of cards propped up there already. Some of her favorite candy, a potted plant. Phainon wants to help, but he doesn’t want her to feel helpless, so he lets her do it herself. “How are you feeling?” he asks.

“Exhausted,” she answers, settling back into her spot. She lifts her spoon and stirs her food around. It seems she has mashed potatoes and veggies today. A cup of fruit juice, chocolate pudding for dessert. “The fatigue is the worst of it. I’m sick of staring at the wall, but I’m too weak and it’s not like I can do anything hooked up to all this anyway.” She gestures to the IV with her spoon, takes a bite.

Phainon sits in one of the chairs by her bedside, gestures for Mydei to stop looking so imposing and sit down too. He comes and sits in the other chair, and these are a bit more comfortable than the ones in the waiting room, brown and cushioned instead of pure plastic. “Is the treatment not done for the day?” he asks.

She purses her lips, gives him a tight smile. “It’s a twenty-four hour infusion,” she says. “Seven days of it. That’s why I have to be in the hospital instead of just coming in for chemo appointments. They’re also giving me another drug the first three days; that’s what they were doing before you came up, actually.”

“Well that fucking sucks,” Mydei says.

Cyrene lets out a startled laugh. “Yeah,” she agrees. “It does, doesn’t it? I have to drag this thing around if I want to get up. And the food totally sucks.” She punctuates it with a stab to her mashed potatoes.

“I’ll make you something tomorrow,” Mydei tells her, propping his elbows on his knees.

Her eyes crinkle at the corners. “I was joking about that, you know,” she says. “You don’t actually have to go out of your way to do that. I’ll survive on this.”

“I have to cook to keep this one alive anyway.” He juts his thumb at Phainon, who makes a face at him. “I’ll just make a bit extra; I wouldn’t be going out of my way at all. Any requests?”

“Whatever you can find ingredients for. I’m not picky, but there's barely anything in my fridge,” she replies. She takes another bite, swallows. She’s always been a slow eater, but it’s clear she’s having difficulty eating now. Perhaps she’s nauseous, or lost her appetite from the medication. But she’s always been like this. She complains in small doses when really she has enough to gripe about for hours.

“We’ll get some groceries too,” Mydei says. “I can just go for soup, to make sure you can keep it down.”

“Thank you, Mydei,” Cyrene says. “I appreciate it a lot, even if it’s not a bother. And it’s nice to see you again after who knows how long.”

“Of course,” Mydei says, and his expression softens too. He’s always been kind, on his best behavior around her. Like he wants her to like him, to approve of him. Phainon’s always felt… some kind of way about that. “It’s good to see you too, though I wish the circumstances were better.”

“Agreed.” She stirs her food some more, sets her spoon down to take a sip of the juice instead. “But I’ve just got to survive this week, and then the worst of it is over. Allegedly.”

“If you want us to bring you anything to make your stay slightly less miserable, just say the word,” Phainon tells her. “One of your books, or something else at home. Let us know.”

She smiles a bit. “That would be nice, actually,” she says. “Thank you, Phainon.”

△

They pass the time catching up. They call often, but not often enough that they don’t have random stories and things leftover to share. Cyrene tells them about swimming, about her friends and their shenanigans, about her work. Phainon tells her about living with Mydei, about the movies he’s watched, about the things they’d seen on the drive. Mydei contributes bits about himself when prompted, but mostly hangs back and offers commentary when Phainon voices an opinion he finds particularly offensive.

Cyrene sinks into her bed as time goes on. She finishes most of her food and pushes the tray table away, though Phainon is sure it goes cold for how long it takes her to get it down. She laughs a lot, tag-teams with Mydei to tease Phainon on more than one occasion, and seems… happy. It’s still her. She hasn’t been replaced by some sad, sickly creature. It’s still her, even if this version of her is a bit low energy and less mobile.

Eventually, she’s basically flat. Her eyes have slipped shut and Mydei and Phainon are the ones talking now—arguing, more like—though she still interjects every now and then. Her mouth stays curled up at the corners until she brings hand to cover it as she yawns after a while.

Phainon quiets instead of responding to whatever Mydei had been spouting at him to look at her. One of her eyes cracks open, clear blue like their dad’s had been, like his are. Phainon holds a finger up in front of Mydei’s face, ignoring the way he scoffs and bats it away because it still makes him shut up.

“Did we tire you out?” Phainon asks Cyrene.

“Oh, yeah,” she says, yawning again, a little sarcastic. “It was totally you, not all of the highly toxic drugs in my system, no sir…” A little hum. She rolls onto her side to face them better, the IV tube stretching over her shoulder.

“Should we let you rest?” Mydei asks her, and his voice goes so much softer for her. “It’s about time we got something to eat anyway.”

“I wish I had a bit more energy,” Cyrene admits. “I’m just…” Again, she yawns. “Sorry. So out of it.”

“Don’t worry about it,” Phainon tells her. With her eyes closed, still smiling a bit, she’s peaceful, she’s okay. She’s eased a bit of that sick, twisting feeling in the pit of his stomach. Tonight, at least, he doesn’t think he’ll have to worry about her too much. Not if she’s just resting like this, not when he’s heard her voice and seen her up close. “We’ll be back, alright? Get some good rest.”

“Yeah, yeah,” she says, shifting a little. Her cheek squishes against the pillow, and her tired eyes crack open again. “I’m already asleep, get out of here.”

“Yeah, yeah,” Phainon echoes right back, a laugh on his lips, something a little bittersweet in his chest. He stands up, pats his pockets to make sure he hasn’t left anything behind. “We’re going, we’re going.”

“See you, Cyrene,” Mydei tells her, hiking his pants up as he stands, lightly kicking the backs of Phainon’s knees as he makes his way to the door.

“See you,” she says back with a laugh, and as Phainon turns to follow, scowling as he recovers his balance, she calls, “And Phainon?”

“Yeah?” he says, stopping to look at her again.

“Thanks,” she tells him. “I’m glad you guys came out. I feel a little better now than I have in a week, just for that.”

“Yeah,” he says, but it comes out all weird. “Of course.”

“The books on the bottom shelf are the ones I haven’t read yet,” she adds. “I trust you to pick a good one.”

△

“So?” Mydei asks as they head out the double doors to the hospital and into the heat of the parking lot. It isn’t boiling today, at least, just a bit humid. Phainon almost trips over nothing, but swiftly rights himself.

“So?” he repeats, raising an eyebrow at Mydei, who raises one back and pointedly glances at his feet.”Shut up,” Phainon tells him before Mydei can comment on his miraculous ability to trip on air. “What do you mean?”

“You saw her,” Mydei says.

“Yes,” Phainon agrees. The sun slips out from behind a cloud, so he shields his eyes.

They’re both quiet for a moment. Asphalt beneath their shoes, the jingle as Mydei digs his keys out of his pocket. He unlocks the car, and Phainon slips in the passenger side. Twin thunks; the doors close. “We don’t have to talk about it,” Mydei says.

“Don’t say it like that,” Phainon tries, but Mydei doesn’t even look at him as he pulls out of their parking space, and that’s… He’s driving, God, of course he isn’t looking, he shouldn’t be looking. Phainon was feeling okay, he was optimistic, and Cyrene seems okay, so what is this? 

“Like what?” Mydei asks. “And get your directions up; I don’t know where I’m going.”

“Like…” Phainon digs out his phone, typing in the first bit of Cyrene’s address before the GPS fills it in for him. He taps on it, and watches the map load as it routes them. “Like I have trauma, or some shit. I’m fine. I’m not the one we need to be worrying about right now.”

“At the stop sign, turn right,” the robotic voice of Phainon’s maps app intones. Mydei slows, stops. Checks left and right. Checks Phainon too.

“I don’t know why I have to keep saying it, but your sister having cancer isn’t just another average day,” he says, turning the car when it’s clear. The bumper scrapes as they pull off the curb. “You know that’s the kind of thing you give condolences to the family for too.”

“You saw her,” Phainon says, thinking of her smile, her voice. The way she seemed so pale, so tired. “She’s doing fine.”

The rumble of the road. The GPS, “Go past this light, and then turn left.” The sound of Mydei’s blinker as he gets over.

“She has cancer,” Mydei reminds him. “And she’s doing a great job of sticking it out, considering, but she’s still sick, and she’s still your sister.”

“You think I don’t know that?”

“I know you know that,” Mydei retorts. “Which is exactly why I don’t get why you’re being so goddamn stubborn.”

“I’m not being stubborn,” Phainon protests. His hands ball to fists. His leg bounces hard enough that his phone falls off his leg and the directions are lost under the seat. “Turn left,” they say, and Phainon jams his knuckles into his thigh as he bends to find his phone. “What even is there to be stubborn about?”

“I don’t know,” Mydei says, pulling into the left turn lane. “All of this? The fact that instead of just admitting that you’re sad, you just… do whatever this is half the time. You act super fucking weird and don’t tell me shit. It’s so obvious that you’re miserable, and there’s a damn good reason to be right there, but you’re still trying to insist that you’re fine. I don’t get it.” The blinker ticks, unusually fast or unusually grating. Phainon is shaking the car with his leg, now that they’re stopped.

“Fine!” Phainon admits, and his fists squeeze so tight his fingernails dig into his palms a little. “I’m sad, I’m upset! Is that really what you wanted to hear? Did you want to spend all day listening to me mope?”

Mydei inhales, sighs it back out. The light goes green, and he inches forward, waits for a couple of cars going straight before he turns. “I’m here for you, you know,” he says. “I’m here because I saw your fake-ass smile that morning and cared enough to come with you when I didn’t even know what was wrong.”

“I didn’t ask—”

“—No, you didn’t,” Mydei interrupts. “But I’m here anyway! You know what that’s called?”

Phainon opens his fists when his nails start to hurt. White crescents in his palm. They’re all sweaty, so he wipes them and wipes them and wipes them on his pants until his hands are tingling with weird sensation. And he could cry again, pushed over the edge by this, whatever this is, this hostility, this frustration, this annoyance directed at him. And he knows he’s a goddamned nuisance. He knows he’s been dragging Mydei around by the hair for the better part of their lives, wasting his time, his attention, putting him out again and again, but he’s the only person who’s ever stuck around for all of Phainon’s shit.

“You’re a liar, you know that?” And there, those are the tears that Phainon just isn’t good enough at holding in. He tries, and then a handful of words are enough to crush him to pieces. Mydei isn’t even being mean. How can he shoulder the weight of his own emotions, Cyrene’s cancer, anything, when he can’t even shoulder this?

“When did I fucking lie?” Mydei asks, and he sounds affronted now, upset about this enough to look Phainon in the eye, and his gaze is furious. Furious at him, at whatever this is, at whatever Phainon is doing.

He wipes a tear with the side of his hand before Mydei can see it, because he’s still driving and still has to look at the road more than he can look at Phainon, but a moment is enough to pull himself together and say, “you said you wouldn’t get upset!”

“And I’m fucking not!” Mydei says, but his voice is raised and his knuckles are white on the wheel.

“In five hundred feet, turn right,” the directions say, and Phainon squeezes his phone so tight he holds the power button and shuts it off. 

“Then what is that?” Phainon laughs, but nothing is funny, and the way he’s digging the hard edge of his phone into his leg doesn’t hurt enough. “Why are you yelling, if you’re not upset? You think I don’t know I’m stupid and miserable and wasting your time? You think I don’t—!”

“I’m trying,” Mydei says over him, wrenching the car into a right turn that sends Phainon bumping into the car door. And then he slows and finds a place to pull over, because he’s the type to wait out a rainstorm rather than drive through it, because he’s the type that won’t risk driving angry. He’s so fucking safe like that. The look on his face is nothing but danger. “To have a conversation. I’m not upset.”

All Phainon can do is laugh, nervous enough that it bubbles right out of him with another tear down his cheek. “You totally are,” he says. “And— And I get it, I would be too, I—”

“Phainon,” Mydei says, tiredly now. He knocks his fist into the side of Phainon’s seat, leaning toward him. “I’m sorry, okay?”

“You’re…” He stops short, throat dry. “Sorry?”

Now, Mydei speaks slowly, carefully, studying Phainon to make sure that whatever he has to say lands correctly. “I am aware that sometimes the things that I say come out… more aggressive than I mean for them to.” His expression pinches at this, and it’s clear he’s discomfited having to say all this. He inhales through his nose. “I get… frustrated easily, but I am not upset with you.”

Phainon breathes out a laugh, a lump in his throat. “The way you’re glaring, I’m worried you’ll punch me in the face if I so much as look at you wrong.”

Mydei grits his teeth, blinks hard. His hand falls off the seat and he backs off, and suddenly Phainon can breathe again. “Not in the car,” he says, pinched.

“‘Not in the car?’” Phainon repeats, incredulous. “So if we were outside of it, you’d—”

A fist to the cheek. Not a punch, really, because Mydei is much too gentle for that, but there is a fist against Phainon’s cheek, shutting him up. “Don’t think I won’t,” Mydei says. “It’s not like I haven’t done it before.” And he has, during the bigger of their fights throughout the time they’ve known each other and during spars. He once chipped one of Phainon’s teeth.

As his hand falls away, Phainon laughs, helpless. His throat goes tight. His sinuses start to hurt as his eyes water, and god fucking damnit, he doesn’t want to cry now. 

Mydei sighs through his nose and starts the car again. “Do you have your directions?” he asks as he pulls back onto the road. Phainon fumbles for his phone.

“Sorry,” he says, all watery, pressing the power button. “I turned my phone off by accident. Just— Just a second.”

A laugh. “For the record,” Mydei says, just driving. His expression pinches, a bit. “I care about you. That’s why I want to talk, not because I’m the one that’s upset, but because you are. And then I get frustrated because you’re so insistent upon suffering alone, even now that I know what’s wrong, even when I…” He grunts. “Nevermind. Sorry I blew up on you.”

Phainon clears his throat as quietly as he can, opening his directions as his phone boots up so slowly. “I’m sorry too,” he offers. “I just… don’t want to talk about this right now.” His throat is still choked. His sinuses are still stinging.

“That’s fine,” Mydei says. “Sorry I pushed.”

“In five hundred feet, make a U-turn.”

Mydei laughs. “Guess I went too far, didn’t I?”

△

They go grocery shopping, both for themselves, and for ingredients to make something for Cyrene. Phainon kind of just tails Mydei around the store like a lost dog, keeping quiet though his head is so loud. Various iterations of he’s tired of your shit play alongside various iterations of your sister is going to die. Neither is true. Neither is true, right? Mydei isn’t upset with him, he said so himself. And he’s always like this, a little bit gruff and grumpy, long-suffering over Phainon’s antics but ultimately fond of him, caring for him, happy when he’s around. Otherwise he wouldn’t stay, right? Otherwise he’d have left a long time ago like everyone else in Phainon’s life.

And Cyrene… She’s young and otherwise healthy. He’d spent a night drowning himself in statistics, and depending on the source, anywhere from seventy-one to fifty-two percent of her age group survives AML for at least another five years. More than half. She’s always been lucky, and she eats well and exercises, so that has to tip the odds in her favor, doesn’t it? And yet Phainon looks at those numbers, looks at her and her tired eyes, and he thinks what about the twenty-nine percent that’s left? What if, he thinks. What if, what if, what if.

What if he loses her too, just like he loses everyone else?

His parents in the fire that took his home away from him as a youth. One childhood friend to suicide, another to a car crash, all the rest to future plans that don’t involve him. He isn’t ready to grieve again, because he never really finished. He’s still grieving, he’s still stuck, and now his sister is sick and his most important friend in the world is a little bit upset with him, and his brain won’t shut up. 

What if Cyrene dies, and Mydei finally gets tired of him? What then? Where does that leave him? What does that leave him with? Nothing, really, because Phainon is the type with a hundred friends but only one who really knows him, and deep down, more than anything, he’s terrified of being the only one left.

So here he is, following his best friend like a dog in the grocery store, keeping quiet because he’s afraid to say the wrong thing and start another fight, the fight that ends it all. Keeping quiet because somehow he’s grieving someone who’s still alive, grieving the twenty-nine percent, because what if she falls in with the rest of them? What if she becomes one of those numbers? What if, what if, what if?

“You like these, don’t you?” Mydei asks. He’s holding up a box of those fluorescent orange cheese sandwich crackers. He likes to call them radioactive, likes to sneak them out of the shopping cart, likes to scold Phainon for poisoning himself when he eats them, but here he is, holding them up with his eyes averted.

He feels guilty, doesn’t he? He’s worried Phainon is upset the same way Phainon is worried he’s upset.

Because… it’s mutual, whatever this is. Otherwise they wouldn’t have stuck together for so long.

“Yeah,” Phainon says, though it comes out a bit weird. “I love them.”

So Mydei just grumbles something about how he can’t believe he’s enabling Phainon’s terrible eating habits and tosses the package in the cart.

Chapter End Notes

More characterization tidbits: I am a boyfailure Phainon enjoyer just as much as the next guy, but he's actually quite competent in this universe! He's a mediocre chef! The toilet sparkles when he cleans it! He can fold hella fitted sheets! He's just a bit clumsy (and plays it up because he knows it's charming) and tends to be rather impulsive. He does things without thinking and faces the consequences after, but he's a good enough problem solver that he never Really needs to be saved. Mydei just saves him anyway. He's an acts of service guy like that.

chapters.title: Chapter 5
chapters.html:
The hospital staff are kind and sympathetic in a way that doesn’t make her skin crawl. They’re used to this. They’ve seen hundreds of patients with cancer, with worse, enough that each case isn’t some brand new, aching tragedy. Cyrene appreciates that, appreciates that they give her the facts and deliver her medication compassionately but without pity. She’s spent more than enough time crying and pitying herself. She doesn’t need it from the doctors too.

One the third day of treatment, Cyrene’s red blood cell count gets low enough that she needs a blood transfusion. Everything makes her lightheaded and exhausted. Her muscles and joints ache, she’s always a little bit nauseous, and she’s plagued with diarrhea. Her mouth feels sore. She bumps her hip on the way out of the bathroom and later finds it bruised like a peach.

She’s given a handful of medications to help the side effects: painkillers and pills for nausea, a mouth rinse for the sores. She takes them, but she hates how many drugs she’s on, hates the way she feels, hates the way she can barely barely get out of bed.

All this, but on that third day before her last anthracycline infusion, the doctors test her blood and find that the percentage of abnormal blood cells is going down as planned. All this, and they tell her the treatment is working.

It’s still early enough that things could change and go south, but as soon as she’s alone, Cyrene cries with something like relief. The suffering isn’t for nothing. The chances are that she isn’t going to die. It’s more likely than not that she’ll recover and go back to living a normal life someday, however many months from now. She’ll be able to go on walks and start swimming again, go back to work, go out and do things with her friends and her brother. She just needs to survive this first.

For now, she struggles through a meal of tasteless hospital food and tries her best not to throw it back up. It always feels like she will, even if she hasn’t yet. She just has to eat slow, excruciatingly slow, because the faster she eats the more her stomach struggles to settle. It doesn’t help that she has no appetite. The only thing motivating her to eat is the fact that she knows she has to.

Phainon and Mydei are coming again today, a bit later because she’d asked them to wait after the blood transfusion. Allegedly, they’re going to bring soup. Part of her is afraid she won’t be able to eat it, and all that effort will have gone to waste.

She hates that they’ll have to see her like this. Tired, bed-ridden, broken to only her most essential parts. She’s seen the way she looks in the mirror. Too pale, hair limp, so obviously exhausted.

The flowers Phainon gave her sit in a jar on her bedside table. The nurse helped her cut the stems and arrange them nicely, but they hadn’t gotten to them in time to keep them from wilting a bit. They’re still pretty, though. Big golden sunflowers, sweet white daisies, soft orange tulips. Sunflowers have always been her favorite. She’s never met a flower so persistent. She’s never seen a nicer shade of yellow. Spread the seeds and they’ll grow anywhere. They remind her of her brother, a bit.

Oh, how she’s missed his stupid smile. It’s been a while since they both left their tiny hometown, but she still thinks of him, still misses him. They’d always been close, but the fire made them closer. And now, there’s this.

When she’s feeling a little better and one of the nurses comes to check on her, she pushes herself upright, legs folding, hiding a wince as the IV tube tugs at her port, still sore as the incision heals. “I’d like to ask something,” she says.

“Of course.” The nurse smiles. “How can I help?”

Knots in her stomach, nausea. She’d spent a long time looking at herself in the mirror before this. Working up the courage. “I was wondering if it would be possible to get someone to come and cut my hair?”

She doesn’t want to lose it slowly, doesn’t want to prolong the grief like that. There’s understanding in the nurse’s smile. “Of course,” they say. “Haircuts are a free amenity for all cancer patients.”

△

Phainon and Mydei come in time for dinner. She hears them arguing in the hallway before they even reach her door, and the sound of it makes her smile, makes her ache with this sweet, long-suffering nostalgia. She calls for them to enter when they knock.

Mydei comes in first this time, rolling the door open with one hand, the other holding a thermos by the base. He’s calling Phainon stupid for some reason or another, and there’s a smile tugging at Cyrene’s lips before she realizes it.

Phainon comes in after, a book under his arm that she’s fairly certain did not come from her shelf, shooting something back about how at least he’s considerately stupid, and then he and Mydei take the seats at Cyrene’s bedside and promptly stop arguing. Mydei looks calm and unruffled, expression smooth, eyes lined in red more symmetrically than Cyrene could ever hope to do on herself. Phainon is looking at her like he’s expecting her to tell him he’s won the lottery, dressed in a few too many of his favorite colors, hair doing anything but lying flat on his head.

“Hi,” he says, hands on his closed knees, shoulders hiked up. Mydei lounges next to him, leaning back, legs spread wide, clad in all black, and something about it has Cyrene laughing hard enough that it hurts the incision in her chest and makes her nauseous all over again.

“Ha ha…?” Phainon laughs with her, clearly confused. “As much as I love to see you laughing, Cyrene, would you mind sharing what you find so funny?”

“Just…” She presses a hand to her chest, feels like her eyes are watering. “The two of you.”

“Soup?” Mydei offers, lifting the thermos, and it just makes her laugh again, softer this time because it still hurts and she’s still tired, but she reaches a hand out.

“Please,” she says, so he stands and rolls the tray table over her bed, unscrewing the lid of the thermos and offering her a spoon. After he does that, he waits for a bit so see if there’s anything she needs help with before he sits back down. He isn’t fretful in the way he helps, just quietly attentive, the same he is to Phainon whenever he isn’t looking. She likes it the way she likes how used to illness the nurses are.

“Improvised chicken noodle,” Mydei tells her, kicking Phainon’s ankle as they sit, hiking one arm over the back of his seat.

“Improvised?” Cyrene repeats.

“I forgot to buy eggs to make the noodles, so I just used the macaroni in your pantry,” Mydei explains. “I also added the mushrooms you had in the fridge; they were about to go bad.”

“It’s really good anyway,” Phainon adds.

Cyrene dips the spoon in the thermos, stirring the contents around. Sure enough, macaroni noodles surface. Carrots, celery, mushrooms, pieces of chicken all cut neatly. The smell of it is warm and hearty, the broth gold and shimmering, speckled with herbs. No one in her family has much of a history with cooking. Her mom liked baking, and her dad could make simple dishes every now and then, but that’s about it. She keeps herself alive by meal prepping twice a week and microwaving frozen or canned foods, but she never really makes anything like this for herself. Nothing that smells this good, certainly, though the macaroni is quite silly.

“It looks delicious,” she says, a bit hungry and still nauseous at once. Medicine has eased the worst of it, but she’s still nervous, almost. Hopeful. “Thank you.”

“It’s nothing,” Mydei says, and he’s been like that since she saw him last when they were kids. He’ll do a nice thing and do everything in his power to make it seem like nothing at all. Maybe that’s why he and Phainon get on so well. Phainon struggles to accept being cared for, and Mydei likes to pretend he isn’t caring for him. And now Cyrene by extension. “I had to cook dinner for myself anyway.”

“Sure,” she says, smiling slightly, stirring the soup for a moment longer before she lifts the spoon out to taste it. A breath, she takes a bite, chewing slowly, tasting it. Warm, savory, though light on the salt. The vegetables are cooked to perfection, and while the noodles are a bit of an odd texture, it still works. It’s good. Maybe the best soup she’s ever had, since she’s not in the habit of eating soup often, but it makes her realize she might be losing her sense of taste. Something is just a little bit off, but she knows that it’s her and not the soup. It was on her list of possible symptoms. Loss of taste, right alongside nausea and vomiting and diarrhea.

“What do you think?” Phainon asks as she swallows. He wasn’t even the one who made it. Mydei just sits there coolly.

“It’s delicious,” Cyrene tells them, stirring the soup some more so she has something to do with herself while her stomach settles from the upset of a single bite. Another bite, and the feeling isn’t quite so bad. It warms her from the inside. Her stomach calms faster and faster as she gets used to it, though most of that is the medication. Even if she can’t taste it all the way, it still feels like comfort. “You’re a wonderful chef, Mydei.”

Mydei just grunts in acknowledgment until Phainon kicks him in the foot and he replies, “Thanks,” after kicking him back. She has to laugh again, just softly. She’s always found them to be an odd pair. Good for each other, but odd. They’re so different and yet the same. They’re so mean to each other but so kind. At first glance, they’re terrible friends, at third, they might be halfway in love with each other.

“I brought this for you too,” Phainon says, holding out the book he’s been carrying. She doesn’t even recognize the cover, but the name of the author printed on it is one of her favorites. She reaches to accept it with her left arm, the side with the port, and winces at the soreness.

“I don’t own this,” she says.

“You do now,” Phainon tells her, this bright, awkward smile on his face. He’s never been much of a gift giver, but here he is. “You like this author, don’t you? I checked your Goodreads, and you rated three of their other books five stars, so I thought…”

“You stalked my Goodreads?” Cyrene laughs, turning the book over so she can read the summary on the back, keeping it clear of the soup.

“In my defense,” Phainon starts. He pauses, Cyrene glances up from the book to see him open his mouth and close it again. “It was Mydei’s idea to get you a book.”

“Shut the fuck up,” Mydei says, and then they’re kicking each other again. “You paid for it, and I didn’t tell you to stalk her.”

Cyrene just shakes her head and ignores them, finishing the summary. A girl inheriting the power of the God of Time and her journey to save the world with her childhood friend. It sounds interesting enough. Another bite of soup, she flips the back cover open to see the page count. Four hundred thirty-six. If the fatigue doesn’t make it hard to keep her eyes open, it should keep her occupied for a few days.

“Thank you,” she says, interrupting their squabbling. Both shut up, turning to her immediately, and that’s funny too. The way they’re so ridiculous for each other but on their best behavior for her. It feels like high school again.

“Does it look like something you’ll like?” Phainon asks.

“Yeah,” she says. “I do love this author. I’ll let you know if it’s any good once I read it.”

“Cool,” Phainon says. “Good. Nice. Yeah.”

She laughs through her nose and tells him, “Now stop buying me stuff. I have like a dozen unread books at home, and the flowers will be dead in two days.”

Phainon just makes a face at her. “So ungrateful,” he says. “Next time I’ll buy you two books.”

Mydei scowls at him. “That doesn’t even make sense; why would you buy her more stuff if she’s ungrateful?”

△

Later, Cyrene is working her way through the last dregs of the soup—cold now—and Phainon steps out to use the restroom. It’s just her and Mydei, who’s terribly polite to her, but also awfully quiet. She guesses she’d never really considered him one of her friends, even growing up, but they’d been friendly. They could joke and laugh together so long as Phainon was around. Now, they’re a little awkward.

He’s grown up now. As much as Phainon talks about him and shows her pictures, she’s still been imagining him as the teenager he’d once been. Still growing into his limbs, still learning to scowl, still swearing far too much. Well, that last one stands true even now, but he’s all tall and muscular and tattooed now. He has the scowl perfected—though it seems to be exclusively for Phainon so far—and if she didn’t know about how much he loves small animals and cute things from Phainon, and hadn’t tasted his improvised chicken noodle soup, she might even find him a little bit scary.

What a pair they make, Mydei and Phainon. It’s reassuring knowing that they have each other.

“I’m glad you two are still friends,” she says after a brief moment of silence, because Mydei may be terrible at small talk but she isn’t. The last bit of broth doesn't collect in her spoon, so she tips the contents of the thermos into her mouth. Just broth, a noodle and a single piece of celery. She sets the thermos back down with a soft clack, spoon jingling against the sides.

“Yeah,” Mydei agrees. His gaze drifts to the door, like Phainon is going to appear through it saying, sike! You actually believed I needed to pee? He doesn’t, and Mydei adds. “He’s like a fungus. I couldn’t get rid of him if I wanted to.”
