She laughs at this, finds it funny because it looks like that, doesn’t it? Every friend Cyrene has ever had has casted Phainon as a golden retriever when asked what kind of animal he’d be. He’s very eager to please, very smiley, not quite clingy but open in his affection. Dog like, certainly. She wouldn’t be surprised if it were Phainon following Mydei around, but how many times has she listened to him on the phone talking about some adventure or another, saying I wanted to do this and Mydei decided to tag along, I was going to do that but Mydei made me wait until his day off so he could join, I’m driving across the country to see you in the hospital and by the way Mydei’s coming too.

So really, which one of them is the fungus? But she knows well enough not to say something like that out loud.

“Sure,” she says instead, stretching her legs out under her blankets, muscles aching a bit, “but he’s sweet about it. How’s he doing, by the way? I don’t think he’d tell me if he was having a hard time, not when I’m like this.”

Mydei hums, closing his legs when he seems to realize how he’s sitting. “He’s trying very hard to pretend he isn’t sad,” he answers. “But I think he’s more okay than not. He’s doing a pretty good job of staying optimistic.”

“Ah,” she says. She’d been worried. Phainon is very good at putting on a smile when he feels like he needs to. Sometimes it crumbles around the people he’s close to, but he’s good at it. She kind of wondered if he might be more afraid of this than she is. He’s lost too many people; he’s probably come to expect it left and right. She hates the thought. “The meds seem to be working, you know. I’m sure I look as terrible as I’ve felt the past few days, but they’re working. I’ve been trying to keep up a smile for him.”

“And he’s been trying to keep one up for you.”

She laughs softly, sighs, slides down in her bed so she can lay down. Sitting up so long makes her tired, and her stomach seems to have calmed after eating. A weak push to the tray table; it rolls away a few inches until Mydei stands and helps tuck it away, taking the thermos to bring home later. Oh, how she misses home. She just hates the way the hospital smells. The way there’s nothing for her to do but lay here and be uncomfortable and tired all the time.

“We would both do that,” she says. “We got lucky being so close in age; it meant we were close too. But now it just means we both see ourselves as responsible for the other. So we do things like this.”

“I don’t think he sees himself as responsible for you,” Mydei says, settling back into his spot. “He just wants to see you happy, and he’s scared of making things worse.”

Cyrene hums softly, watching the ceiling, the door that rolls open now. “I guess so,” she replies, but Mydei’s attention is back on Phainon, and they both know this conversation is over.

“I hope you didn’t miss me too much,” Phainon says, coming back in. “I may or may not have gotten lost on the way back.”

△

“I’m going to shave my hair,” Cyrene tells Stelle and Dan Heng when they visit the next day. They’re the two best friends she’s had here since moving away. Stelle is a friend from her old internship at a publishing house. They bonded over mischief and things they weren’t supposed to have access to. Dan Heng is a friend from college, initially a transfer student from China before he decided to settle for a more permanent stay. They bonded over a shared love of books. She’s still not a hundred percent sure how these two know each other.

“I think,” Stelle starts, “you’re going to look really badass with a shaved head.”

Dan Heng gives her a withering look. “That’s a hard decision,” is his reply, slightly more sympathetic.

They’d given her candy this visit, as they had the last, but Cyrene doesn’t have the heart to tell them it doesn’t taste right to her anymore. She nibbles on it just for their sake, tries to offer a smile. They both want her happy, they just have different ways of going about it.

“Yeah,” she says. “I just don’t want to sit around and watch it fall out, so…”

“Badass,” Stelle says again, and Dan Heng gives her that exact same look.

“Maybe,” Cyrene chuckles. Plenty of women look good with shaved heads, she knows that. It’s just… a choice, for them. It’s bold, empowering. For Cyrene the thought just makes her feel terribly small. “And it’ll grow back after treatment, anyway, so…”

“It’s still a hard choice,” Dan Heng repeats. “You’re very strong, Cyrene.”

This makes her laugh. Just a little, because she doesn’t want to be mean. This is the weakest she’s ever felt in her life. She can barely move, can barely eat, can barely do anything but sit here or sleep. Her emotions are all being trampled in the dirt, and here Dan Heng is, calling her strong. Here Stelle is, calling her badass. She feels like the opposite.

They’re just trying to cheer her up, she knows. They need to offer some kind of response or they look like total jerks, but these aren’t the words she needs to hear. She doesn’t know what those words are; maybe they don’t exist, but she doesn’t want to be told that she’s strong or badass. Not when she feels like this. It just sounds like something on a motivational poster. Like words for someone else, but not for her.

Having the right ones is so hard, she knows. What do you say to someone losing their hair if not those kinds of things? She doesn’t know. She’s too tired to think about it.

“Thanks,” she says instead. Tries for a joke, “I think I’ll look like an egg, the next time you see me.”

But it doesn’t earn the laughs that she means for it to. Stelle and Dan Heng just exchange a glance, and then Stelle asks, “Do you have a hat? Or a scarf or something if you want one?”

And oh, her throat tightens. Maybe those are the words. Maybe this is what it feels like to be cared about. “I have one,” she says. “Thank you, though.”

△

Phainon visits by himself today, though he brings a rice and veggie dish from Mydei in a plastic grocery bag.

“He said, and I quote ‘you can go by yourself today in case you want to cry or some shit without me there.’ He’s very considerate like that,” Phainon explains, helping to set up the tray table so Cyrene can try to eat. Her appetite has been particularly bad today. Her mouth is starting to grow sores. “But if you miss him I can call him up.”

She smiles. “I don’t mind much either way,” she tries, taking the lid off the container of food. It’s quite pretty; not too greasy-looking, colorful from all the different vegetables. “He’s here for you more than he’s here for me anyway.”

“He’s here for you too,” Phainon protests. He’s always so weird when it comes to Mydei. Unable to shut up about him but defensive the moment someone comments on it.

“To some extent, sure,” Cyrene concedes, trying a small bite of the rice. The texture is perfect, but her tastebuds are still dull. “But he’s your friend, Phainon. If you weren’t here, there’s no way he’d drive thirty hours to see me.”

“It would be pretty weird of him to visit my sister without me,” Phainon admits, chair scraping the floor as he scoots it closer. He nods at the food. “How is it?”

“Good,” Cyrene says. If only she could just taste it, but she doesn’t say that. They put up smiles for each other. She doesn’t want Phainon to have to worry about this too, so she just takes another bite and smiles a bit. Taste is just another thing that she’ll have to wait to get back after treatment. Like her strength. Like her hair after she cuts it. “Thank him for me.”

“I will,” Phainon says, and hesitates for a moment. He reaches for the bag he’d had the food in, and it crinkles as he digs something else out. “I brought your hat, like you asked. This is the one, right?”

Soft, gray knit; he holds the beanie out and she takes it, feeling the fabric between her fingers. “This is the one,” she confirms, setting it in her lap. “Thanks.”

“Of course,” Phainon says, balling up the plastic bag now that it’s empty. His knee bounces as he sits. “Are you… cutting your hair?”

He’s more perceptive than most people give him credit for. This, though, must be obvious. Why else would a cancer patient be asking for a beanie in the middle of summer? “Yeah,” Cyrene answers, waiting for her stomach to settle. Nerves and nausea both, every time she thinks about it. “Figured it would be better than waiting.”

“Pythias would be glad you can’t break dress code anymore,” Phainon says with this sad attempt at a smile. And maybe he gets it. Hiding compassion behind humor. He’s grieving the same Cyrene is.

She laughs, softly. Her mouth hurts, muscles ache. “I miss being a kid,” she says. “Having teachers and rules to break. That was fun.”

“Mom always loved your hair.”

Her exhale comes out shaky. “It’ll grow back.” Now she’s the one saying useless things to fill the silence. “After treatment is over, it’ll…” She trails off, because it doesn’t matter. Sure, it’ll grow back, but it’ll be months before it even starts, years after that to get it back to the length it is now.

“Have you thought about getting a wig?” Phainon asks gently. Her sweet, earnest brother. Always trying to fix things.

“Not much,” Cyrene admits. “But… you’re right. That would probably make me feel a lot better.” She rubs the soft fabric of her beanie between her fingers. Knit with thin cables, old enough that it’s starting to pill. “The hat will do for now. Everyone here knows I’m sick anyway.” A bite. Her stomach turns against it when she forces herself to swallow.

“Maybe,” Phainon says. He hesitates, his expression obvious and troubled. “Just think about it, would you? I can help pay if they’re expensive, I—”

“No, Phainon,” she interrupts him before he can continue down that path. This burden is hers; he carries more than enough of it anyway, just by being her earnest, caring, terrified of being left brother. She knows he’s broke anyway. She hasn’t questioned him coming here, but she does wonder if he can afford it. So much time off work, the cost of hotels and gas and whatever else they need out here. It helps knowing that Mydei is splitting the costs, but she worries. She doesn’t want him to go, and can’t bring herself to ask him to, but she hopes he heads home before the costs can amount to too much. “I don’t want you paying a cent for any of this.”

Now, his expression pinches. Brows furrowing, the corners of his mouth turning down. “Cyrene,” he says. “How are you paying your medical bills?”

“Hah.” What a thing to ask. He knows she’s on medical leave and unpaid for it. Her insurance is good but cancer is a bankrupting affair even then. She has savings, but not that much, and he knows it.

“Take it out of the trust, however much it is,” Phainon tells her. “Mom and Dad would have wanted it.”

“That money is yours too, you know,” Cyrene murmurs. In truth, she doesn’t have many other options. In there is everything their parents left behind. They each used it to pay for their schooling and haven’t touched it since. The plan was to save it to buy a house when the time came.

“I’ll sign off on it,” Phainon says without a beat.

Cyrene can’t help a tired laugh. “That isn’t what I meant.”

“It’s not like you’d need all of it, would you?”

“No.” She shakes her head. “Not unless I’m stuck in treatment for years, I’d imagine. But… it would still be a pretty hefty chunk of it.”

“That’s fine,” Phainon tells her. “Mail me any paperwork, if you need it.”

She might take it for granted that she doesn’t have a greedy bastard for a brother. She’d been planning to have this conversation anyway, but had no idea how to bring it up, and every other time they’ve been face to face Mydei has been there as well. This would’ve been an awkward conversation to have with him in the room. Maybe she’s taken that for granted too, the fact that her brother’s best friend is a far more empathetic creature than he tries to pass himself off as.

“Thank you,” she says. One weight off her chest, though another, smaller but heavy with guilt and shame, settles in its place.

“That’s what the money is for, anyway,” Phainon says. “We’d be having this exact same conversation if it were me in your place.”

She makes a face at him and nudges the tray table away, opening her arms in his direction. He laughs, stands up, and bends to hug her. It hurts a little, with the soreness of her port, but she presses her face against him as he rubs her shoulder. They don’t get to hug all that often, but he’s so warm. She’ll never say it to his face, but he’s probably the best brother she could ever hope for.

He smells familiar, and she laughs weakly, fighting the wave of nausea that hits her. “...You’ve been stealing my shampoo, haven’t you?” she asks.

“No idea what you’re talking about,” he says as he pulls back, and they both smile as he rolls the tray table back over and falls into his seat. Quiet, just for a moment. “You should try to eat more.”

She wrinkles her nose at him. “I’m trying my best, dude,” she says, stabbing her fork into the rice and scooping up a bite. It’s soft and probably delicious, but it goes down like gravel. “Distract me from the battle within my stomach, O Great Deliverer.”

“It’s been years since we brought that back,” Phainon laughs. His tone shifts as he plays along. “Very well, Holy Priestess. What tale do you wish to be told?”

She laughs too, enough that it hurts a little, enough that her chest gives this warm, aching squeeze. “I don’t know,” she says, breaking character. She clears her throat. “What have you and Mydei been up to between visits?” she tries, because all they’ve been talking about is her. Her illness, her symptoms, her suffering. She wants to hear about something else for once.

“Some dumb touristy stuff,” Phainon answers, toying with his choker as he reaches up to rub at his neck. His gaze shifts around the room like he’s embarrassed, leg bouncing furiously. “We, um… We went and made candles, actually.”

“Candles,” Cyrene repeats, stirring the rice some more but unable to coax herself into taking another bite. Her insides still fight her. All she’s doing is trying to keep them alive. “That sounds fun.”

“They were way too expensive, but yeah,” Phainon agrees. “Mine is almond and cherry scented. Mydei’s was something fruity; pomegranate and pear, I think. We also went to the beach and the natural history museum and walked around town a bit. It’s been… good.”

“I’m glad,” Cyrene says. Glad Phainon is doing things, glad Mydei is keeping him out of his head, glad they’re… good. Not miserable like she is. Good. Together, like they always are. “Would you humor your dying sister for a second?”

Phainon’s mouth twitches downward. “You’re not dying, Cyrene.”

She’s not. She hopes she’s not. “Do you like him?”

Phainon’s gaze flicks about the room. “He’s my best friend. Of course I like him.”

“You know what I mean.”

A sigh. Phainon sucks on his teeth. “If you’re asking it must be pretty obvious how I feel about him.”

It is. So painfully obvious. They’ve probably liked each other for years now. “So why don’t you do anything about it?”

Phainon just laughs. “That’s a loaded question.”

Cyrene rolls her eyes. “It’s not like I’m going anywhere.”

△

They bring a hairdresser in the next day, a kind woman who offers a hand to help Cyrene sit like she only does it as courtesy, not because she thinks Cyrene needs it. She’s older; somewhere between fifty and sixty, and there are smile lines around her eyes. Her head, curiously, is wrapped in a peach colored scarf. The kind Cyrene has seen other cancer patients wear. She’d been considering finding one for herself, but for now she just has that old gray beanie she wears in the winter.

When the hairdresser notices Cyrene looking, she just smiles and says, “Alopecia areata. Most of the time hair grows back from that. Mine didn’t, so I started doing this because I know how it feels.”

“Oh,” Cyrene says, and there’s an odd, tight feeling in her throat. She settles into the chair, sick with nerves and nausea both. “That’s kind of you.”

“A little bit of compassion goes a long way,” she answers, wrapping a cape around Cyrene’s shoulders and buttoning it up in the back. “I’m Eleni, and I’ll be cutting your hair.”

“Cyrene,” she introduces herself in turn. “And I appreciate it. A lot, really. I don’t think I’d be able to stand watching it all fall out, so thank you.”

Gentle fingers in her hair, brushing it behind her. “Don’t worry about thanking me,” Eleni says. “Now tell me, are we cutting it all off today, or do you want to try something like a pixie cut?”

“All of it,” Cyrene answers. She tries to laugh a little, but it doesn’t come out right. “I just want to get it over with. Like ripping off a bandaid.”

“I get that.” Eleni pulls a comb from her apron and starts untangling the knots in Cyrene’s hair. “Do you want to donate it?”

An exhale, oddly shaky. Cyrene wrings her fingers in her lap. “Can I, even?” she asks. “It’s dyed.”

“Well, that depends on the charity, but yes. Plenty are happy to accept colored hair.” Eleni’s fingers skim her temples before she resumes her brushing. “It’s up to you, of course.”

“Yes, then,” Cyrene answers. “I want to donate it if I can.”

“Lovely,” Eleni tells her, and exchanges the comb for a couple of hair ties. She sections Cyrene’s hair into three, tying off each spot. “Anything you want to do before I cut?”

She’ll cry if she tries to wait much longer, and she really doesn’t want to do that. Not right now, in front of this kind stranger. “No,” Cyrene replies, and takes a breath big enough to make her lungs hurt. Her hands are weak where they tangle together and squeeze under the cape. “I’m ready.”

There’s the soft, metallic snip of Eleni’s hair cutting scissors. It’s a strange sensation, the way she can feel each strand break under them. It tickles, a bit. Eleni cuts above each hair tie, and when she’s done with the first spot, the short strands left over fall into Cyrene’s face. She exhales, rolling her eyes back to watch them sway with her breath. The second section gone. The third. Her head feels lighter. Her heart beats, beats, beats.

Next, Eleni prepares her clippers. Cyrene catches sight of her lost hair. Three pink ponytails lined up neatly. She hopes they’ll make someone a nice wig. Maybe someone like her. A kid with cancer. The thought comforts her more than expected.

“Ready for this too?” Eleni asks. Cyrene nods, wills away the tremble in her chest. The clippers buzz none too softly as they turn on. Eleni sets them to her head and starts to work, gently but efficiently. Cyrene closes her eyes. It tickles when the hair falls onto her neck or her cheeks. Soft like feathers. Soft like tears.

It takes no more than a handful of minutes, and then Eleni is cleaning her up and putting away her tools. The strangest part is how cold her head feels, how light. When Eleni passes her a mirror, she doesn’t recognize herself. Her face, her tired eyes. Another day, she might laugh and call herself an egg. Now, all she has the strength for is to ache. To feel the way her throat chokes up and her eyes grow wet.

“Thank you,” she says, all shaky, lowering the mirror because she doesn’t want to look at herself anymore. She loved her hair. Oh, how she loved it. How she misses it now.

A warm hand squeezes her shoulder. Eleni offers the beanie she set aside for this, and she takes it with trembling hands. The cold goes away when she puts it on. She can’t manage to stifle a sob.

Chapter End Notes

More tidbits(!): Cyrene tries to be very strong when it comes to Phainon. After their parents died in a house fire, they had to take care of each other. They were both closer than ever and fighting more than ever. Moving away from each other was good for both of them and their relationship. They both feel a bit responsible for the other, so they both try to put on a tough front so the other won't worry. Cyrene is also a voracious reader and frequent grass-toucher. Her screen time is like less that 3 hours a day for all devices, but now she's stuck with nothing to do but lay in bed and watch shitty TV all day.

chapters.title: Chapter 6
chapters.html:
“Your head doesn’t even hurt this time, does it?”

Phainon cracks an eye open. Mydei looks down at him, thumbs sweeping over his temples, fingers just a little bit cold. His crossed shins make a pillow as he leans against the headboard, Phainon laying flat, one leg hanging off the side of the bed. “Are you going to stop if I say no?” he asks.

“Fucking liar,” Mydei snorts, but he just skims his nails along Phainon’s scalp, raking his hair off his forehead so he can rub his small knuckles just above his eyebrows.

“I never lied,” Phainon protests. “You sat down. I took advantage. It’s not the same thing.”

“Oh, so it’s my fault for sitting down, then?” Mydei asks, and his ministrations stop so he can cup a hand beneath Phainon’s chin and tip him up so they can look at each other. His fingers are a bit warmer now, from contact and motion. His knees against Phainon’s shoulders, hand settling like it’s rather comfortable on Phainon’s exposed throat. He swallows, and he’s sure Mydei can feel it right there in his palm.

“Now you’re getting it.” The weight of his gaze. He’s… he’s kind of obsessed with Mydei’s eyeliner. His mouth is dry. One of Mydei’s fingers slips under his choker. “Don’t get mad at me for taking opportunities when I see them.”

“Opportunities,” Mydei repeats. He lets Phainon go, but the imprints of his fingers stay hot on his neck. “You saw me sitting down as an opportunity?” But he pets Phainon’s hair again, so he can’t actually be annoyed. Not when his touch is this gentle. Not when his expression is this soft.

“Well… Yes,” Phainon agrees, shutting his eyes again before too much heat can gather in his face. Not embarrassment. Something else. He can still feel Mydei’s fingers on his throat, can still see the smallest hint of his smile, and it’s moments like these where this tiny part of him whispers, he’d probably let you kiss him. Now, with a foot caked in mud, on his car under the night sky. He might even like it if you held his hand. “And I took it. I’m a go-getter like that.”

Fucking liar. Mydei’s voice in his head. Oh, he could laugh. How many opportunities has he had by now? How long has he made Mydei wait?

Why is it waiting now, if he’s never had plans to do anything about it?

“Sure, you are,” Mydei says, softly sarcastic, carding his fingers through Phainon’s hair, pulling it up like he’s measuring its length. A little longer, his hands fall away, but he lets Phainon remain where he is. “How much longer are we staying?”

He opens his eyes, first to the ceiling, then to Mydei as he leans a little bit back. There’s not much to see in his expression. He’s just patient, just asking. Running out of time off. Phainon is too. They can’t stay forever, he knows, as much as he’d like to. A sigh. “There’s just two more days of this round of treatment,” he says, holding his elbows. “Cyrene is coming home after that, so we’ll have to be out of here by then anyway, but… I get it, if we need to leave sooner.”

Mydei brushes Phainon’s hair behind his ears. “I’m not rushing you.”

“How much PTO do you have left?” If they leave tomorrow, they won’t have to take any of next week off. Phainon will keep three days of PTO for the rest of the year. If they wait until treatment is over, that’ll drop down to one. Mydei might have more than that, but it’s still early enough in the year that using it all up is less than ideal.

“Enough,” is all Mydei says.

Phainon studies him, trying to decide if he means that or if he’s just saying it. He pulls the inside of his cheek between his teeth and finds it already sore. A warm hand folds over his eyes.

“Stop that,” Mydei says.

Phainon blinks. His eyelashes brush Mydei’s fingers. “Stop what?” he asks. He hadn’t been doing anything but looking at him, but overthinking.

“I’m not worried about my PTO,” Mydei says after a moment. There’s something odd about his voice. “I’m worried about my laundry. I’m running out of clean clothes.”

Phainon laughs weakly. “I don’t think Cyrene will cry if you use her washing machine,” he says. “But I don’t believe you at all. We can leave tomorrow, alright? I’ve seen her and the treatment seems to be working… She— She’s okay. I’ll be fine.”

“Phainon.”

Phainon pulls his hand off and sits up, crossing his legs and trying to smooth down his hair where it’s all messed up from Mydei’s touch. “It’s smarter for both of us,” he says. “I’ve been trying not to think about it, but you and I both know I can’t really afford to stay out here much longer.”

Mydei is silent for a while, thinking about it, maybe. Marveling in the fact that Phainon is being reasonable for once in his life. God, what a mess he is. “Are you sure?” Mydei finally asks. “I don’t mind staying, and Cyrene will be happy to have the support.”

Phainon sighs. Pulls his knees into his chest like some scared child. “I’m broke, Mydei,” he sighs. “I can’t afford unpaid leave if I get sick later in the year when I’m out of PTO. I really shouldn’t stay.”

The mattress shifts behind him. A hand settles on his shoulder. “What about Cyrene?”

Phainon exhales, leans back until he falls against Mydei’s chest, one leg shifting to make way for him, an arm banding around his waist. They’re close enough that he’s still sitting upright, but he leans his head against Mydei’s shoulder, feeling the rise and fall of his chest against his back, his breath in his hair. “She’s fine,” he says, and tries to believe it. “She’ll be fine. And I’ll probably shit my pants from worrying about her, but what can I do? It’s not like me being here is going to kill her cancer cells. She already knows I can’t stay long.”

Mydei is warm, warm, warm. He always runs hot; Phainon always runs cold. His hand settles on Phainon’s thigh, squeezes lightly. “If you’re sure.”

An oil spill in his chest. “I’m sure,” Phainon says. “We can visit her in the morning and then head out. I can make due with that. And… she still has all her friends out here, it’s not like she’ll be alone. We can— Maybe we can leave some meals for her in the fridge for when she gets home; I doubt she’ll feel well enough to cook. Stelle—one of her friends—said she’d be around to take care of her when she comes home, but I don’t know if I trust her in the kitchen the way I trust you, and Cyrene deserves the best so…” The chest against his back shakes silently. “...Are you laughing?”

Mydei does for real now, shifting to wrap both arms tight around Phainon, pressing his forehead in the space between Phainon’s neck and shoulder, laughing. Laughing like some sort of maniac, hot like some kind of furnace. 

“Mydeimos,” Phainon tries. He sets a hand on Mydei’s forearm over his belly, turning his head to try and look at him. All he can see is Mydei’s hair, strawberry blond and cut in shaggy layers, dyed red at the tips. The shell of his ear, red too. He stops laughing after a bit, but he stays. His hold is so tight, but it’s comfortable. Like being held up, held together. “Would you care to tell me what was so funny?”

“Nothing,” Mydei answers, easing up a little. He sounds like he’s smiling. “I can cook some stuff for her before we go.”

Phainon just squints at the side of his head until they’re making eye contact when Mydei looks at him too. They’re close, a bit too close. A breath away, but Phainon is used to the fluttering feeling in his chest. It would take more than this to make him shy away, after god knows how many years of this. “I’m holding you to that,” he says. “Dessert too, since you laughed.”

And Mydei just laughs again. “Sure,” he says, smiling a little, rolling his red-lined eyes. “Dessert too.”

△

Between the two of them, there’s enough dirty clothing to start a load of laundry. Mydei wants to separate the darks and lights, which Phainon has never bothered with all his life. In the end, he wins that argument, if only because a light load would consist of only three pairs of underwear, a shirt or two, and their towels, so they put everything in together. Phainon tosses in detergent and starts the cycle, listening to the sound as it fills with water, the way the clothes thump, thump, thump against the metal sides of the washer when the cycle properly starts.

“Is there anything else you wanted to see while we’re here?” he asks Mydei, who stands in the doorway with his arms crossed, supervising like he thinks Phainon is going to toss bleach into their darks. But it’s laundry, and Phainon has been doing his own since he was a teen and the only consequence he’s ever come across is the fact that his white socks are tinged a tiny bit gray.

“You’re the one that knows the place better,” Mydei says. Cyrene had moved away from their hometown too, and Phainon only visits. He and Cyrene never do much when he does; in all honesty, he doesn’t know the place well at all. They’ll go to the beach a half dozen times or more, they’ll watch movies at a local theater, they’ll go on walks to see the sunset. They’ve always been content to do not much at all, so he doesn’t know what else there is to do out here.

“Cyrene and I never do anything,” he says. “If it’s up to me we’ll just go to the beach again. Do you want to look for another museum or something?”

A scoff. “You hate museums.”

“I…” Phainon pauses as he closes the box of laundry detergent. Organic, Plant Based and Vegan, it advertises. Fresh Lavender Scent. It does smell quite nice. Halfway like Cyrene, just missing the rose scent of her conditioner. “I don’t hate them.” He taps on the lid, likes the way the cardboard sounds under his nails. Tap, tap, tap, to go with the thump, thump, thump of the washing machine.

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “You don’t do well with them,” he amends. “You don’t like standing around and reading signs and looking at stuff.”

Phainon frowns but can’t refute it. They’d gone to one yesterday and he’d been vibrating out of his own skin trying to concentrate on sign after sign, thing in glass case after thing in glass case. “Maybe if there was like… an audio tour, or more things to watch I would like it. Maybe that was just a bad museum yesterday.”

Mydei laughs at him for this too. “I like the beach,” he says, and straightens up from where he’d been leaning. He flicks off the laundry room light while Phainon is still inside, turning himself into a silhouette, backlit by the living room. “We can go to the beach.”

“We already went to the beach,” Phainon says, following him out. “Is there really nothing else you want to do?”

Now, Mydei navigates to the kitchen, pulling open the fridge to check its contents, checking the pantry too. “Is there nowhere else you want to go?”

“Well, no,” he says. Cyrene is the one that always wants to go to the beach. She likes the sound of the waves, she likes the seashells, she likes the sand beneath her feet. That’s a big part of why Phainon loves it too. He has so many memories there, so many smiles, so much laughter. But he can’t take her, so he wants to tell her about it. How hot the sand is, how cool the water, how fast the wind. “But I want you to have fun.”

“And I am,” Mydei says, shutting the pantry. “Is it really so surprising that I might like the beach too?”

“Alright,” Phainon says, raising his hands in surrender. “We’ll go to the beach, then. Cyrene is having a hairdresser come in so she wants us to come a bit later again, so whenever you want to go…”

Now, Mydei ducks to check Cyrene’s bottom cabinets. He has to look through two before he finds the pan that he’s looking for. “I’ll make lunch,” he says, straightening up and setting the pan on the stove. He stops at the sink to wash his hands. A full twenty seconds, like you’re supposed to. He rubs his fingernails into his palms, works the suds up his wrists and between his fingers. “That way we have time to switch the laundry before we go. She’s cutting her hair?”

Phainon shifts from foot to foot. Leans against the counter and finds that he doesn’t like the way it digs into his hip. “Yes,” he says, watching Mydei pull out ingredients. Bread, eggs, cheese. Fuck if he doesn’t make a damn good egg sandwich. “She’s… getting it out of the way.” They cried over it together yesterday. Cyrene’s beautiful pink hair. It’ll grow back. It isn’t even Phainon’s hair, but he feels grief over this too. So much grief over things he has no business grieving. Things that are temporary or still right here.

Mydei’s tank top is cut to show some of the tattoos on his back. The beginnings of bold red lines. He gets ticklish when Phainon tries to trace them to the dip of his spine where they converge. “Brave choice,” he says, “How does she feel about that?”

“Sad, obviously,” Phainon says. He pushes himself up to sit on the counter instead of leaning against it, heels tapping the cupboards when he swings his feet. He’s out of Mydei’s way, or he’s sure he’d get a talk about being a nuisance in the kitchen. For now, he just watches Mydei crack and open an egg in one hand and tries not to find it impressive. “She kept saying she just wants to rip off the bandaid. Let it hurt now so she doesn’t have to prolong it by losing it slowly.”

Mydei hums. It’s an approving sound, because he was raised on bravery and strength of body and mind. Most of his native Kremnoan culture has been lost to time and diaspora, but he still has this love of courage like no other. Sometimes it’s funny, alongside how safe he is. He’ll never pride himself or others on taking needless risk, but he’ll always stick up for doing the hard thing as long as it’s the right one. “And she doesn’t want anyone with her while she rips that bandaid off?” he asks over the bubbling sound of the cooking eggs.

“No.” Phainon shakes his head. “She wants to do it on her own, and I get that. I think if it were me I’d just be ugly crying the whole time, and that’s not really something you want your sibling to see.”

“Fair enough.”

He watches Mydei’s back. Feels that stupid sticky oil spill sensation come back. He swallows around the way it crawls up his throat. Not his business to grieve, not his turn to be sad over this. A breath. He practices smiling over the feeling.

Mydei prepares the bread with mayo and a tiny bit of mustard. They’re both quiet as he works, listening to the sizzle of the stove, Phainon’s feet bumping the cupboards. Mydei finishes with the bread and moves to flip the eggs. He points with his elbow to the ingredients on the counter. “Put those away if you’re going to sit and watch.”

Phainon slips off the counter. “Alright,” he says softly, reaching for the bread, twisting the bag so he can fit the plastic clip on it and return it to the cupboard it belongs in. Next are the eggs and condiments, all tucked in his arm so he has a hand free to open the fridge. Mydei’s eyes are on him as he shuts it, but he doesn’t say anything.

“What?” Phainon asks.

“Nothing,” Mydei says back, but Phainon gives him a look. Mydei gives one back, frowning a little and raising an eyebrow. It makes Phainon laugh weakly and flip him off, and then his expression smooths out. “You’re allowed to be sad about this too, you know,” he says. “It’s empathy; it’s not like you’re pitying yourself.”

“Fuck off,” Phainon says, but he folds his arms around himself and feels so small. “I know that.”

Mydei turns the stove off and moves the pan from the burner. His eyebrow lifts again, and he opens his arms with an expectant expression. Phainon steps forward and falls into him, trying to laugh, trying to feel upset, but he’s so goddamn warm, and he smells like he’s been stealing Cyrene’s shampoo the same as Phainon has, and he looks like a total asshole but he’s the best hugger Phainon has ever met.

“I’m gonna kick your ass one day,” Phainon says, pressing his face into Mydei’s shoulder. “You’ll have to stop being so smug.”

“Smug?” His arms around Phainon’s back. He always hugs tight like he knows Phainon won’t break.

“That look on your face,” Phainon says, squeezing back. “I hate you.”

“Sure,” Mydei says, warm and sarcastic, the same way he says it when Phainon tells him he loves him. “You hate me so fucking much.”

△

After lunch and switching the laundry, they get dressed for the beach. Shorts and t-shirts, because neither of them thought to bring swim trunks. Phainon dresses in blue and green, Mydei in black and gray, both of them coated in coconut-scented SPF 50. The drive is about fifteen minutes, a lot of that by the water, so Phainon plays some nice acoustic guitar music he thinks suits the occasion. Something soft and percussive. Mydei comments again, and Phainon tries to convince him to learn it with no success.

“I’m no good at fingerstyle stuff or percussion like that,” Mydei tells him dismissively. “I know chords and that’s about it.”

“And how will you ever change that if you don’t try?” Phainon shoots back. Mydei looks over just so Phainon can watch him roll his eyes before he turns back to the road.

“Sure,” he says, “so why don’t you learn it?”

“Well…” Phainon did have a little stint with guitar back in high school. He thought it was cool that Mydei was learning, spent a week with blisters on his fingertips, and gave up when the calluses they turned into peeled off and playing hurt all over again. Mydei stuck with it, somehow. He isn’t impulsive in the way Phainon is, though. When he picks up something new, it’s with careful deliberation and persistence. So he kept it up and is pretty good at it now, though he’s no professional, and admittedly inexperienced in fingerstyle, but he spends a few hours practicing in his room every week, and Phainon listens to him play through the walls and develops a keen understanding of why women are 18% more likely to accept the advances of a guy with a guitar compared to one without.

“Skills are more easily built upon than learned from scratch,” he answers easily. “You’re already comfortable with guitar; picking up fingerstyle would be way easier for you than it would be for me.”

“Remind me why you’re so invested?” Mydei asks. One of his fingers taps the beat into the steering wheel, and he doesn’t just do that the way Phainon does. No, it means he likes this song. Instrumentals might just be their common ground; Phainon isn’t a big fan of Mydei’s old school rock and often finds his ballads a bit boring, and Mydei hates Phainon’s cutesy girl groups and complains about how dramatic showtunes are. He doesn’t comment when Phainon plays folk music most of the time, but his nose tends to wrinkle when the singer has a strong accent. He’s been doing his best to compromise with the softer songs on his playlists, but nothing seems to charm Mydei quite like instrumental guitar.

“Because I like listening to you play,” Phainon answers. “And because you like playing, obviously. Don’t you think you’d have fun learning something like this?”

“You are severely overestimating my capabilities once again,” Mydei says. “But sure. I’d have fun. Find something easier and maybe I’ll let you win this argument.”

They pull into the parking area, driving past a handful of cars before they find a spot. It’s not too busy today; some people in the water, a couple of boats. Kids playing in the sand, adults sunning and chatting in foldable beach chairs.

“Don’t say that if you don’t mean it, Mydeimos,” Phainon says, unbuckling his seatbelt. The music stops when Mydei opens his door, slipping out and turning to look at Phainon through the car. “You’re sending me on a mission, you know. I’m going to find you something.”

“Sure,” Mydei says, sighing for show. He shuts the car door, and Phainon is quick to slip out and follow him to the trunk. He pulls the door open to get to the cooler, digging out a couple of drinks. Lemonade for Phainon, kiwi strawberry Propel for Mydei, the only flavor they both rank in the top three. Grape is Mydei’s favorite, like some kind of cough syrup drinking maniac. “Just know I’ll probably reject a dozen choices before I agree to one. Your ability to gauge difficulty is terrible.”

And Phainon isn’t the one who plays, so he can’t argue with this. “...Good music is often difficult to produce,” he tries, but Mydei just shakes his head and snorts as he shuts the cooler and hoists himself to sit on the lip of the trunk and pull off his shoes before they can get filled with sand. Phainon follows suit, though there isn’t space for him to sit, so he stands on one leg for a bit. They leave their shoes and balled up socks in the trunk, and then Mydei is locking the door and they’re hobbling to the beach, wincing as they walk over rocks and asphalt and bits of broken shells.

“Why’s it gotta be so damn rocky?” Phainon complains as something stabs the arch of his foot.

“Because they don’t dump sand all the way up here,” Mydei tells him, unruffled or steel-footed, because he doesn’t limp at all on the way. They reach the soft, sandy part of the beach and Phainon relaxes.

“Don’t kill the illusion,” he protests, feeling the heat of the sun-baked beach. It’s almost hot enough to hurt. It’s warm and blinding and a little bit windy today, stirring up Phainon’s hair, making him squint. He takes a breath of the air, sea-scented and fresh, listens to the rush of the waves. “Beaches like this are gifts from mother nature, not man-made at all.”

“It’s not like they’re fake,” Mydei says. It’s a long walk to the water. Something prods Phainon in the arm. The sunglasses, held out without a word, Mydei avoiding eye contact like it’s a criminal thing for him to be nice. “They just add more sand when erosion washes it away.”

“Shh,” Phainon shushes him, taking the sunglasses. He puts them on, feels his lips quirk at the corners.

Mydei huffs. A bit further, the waves brush their ankles. “...Quit smiling,” he grumbles. Phainon just smiles wider.

“I can’t help it,” he says. “It’s cute when you pretend not to be nice to me.”

△

Mydei doesn’t have the same attachment to the beach that Phainon does. He’s been few enough times to count on his hands; Phainon has probably been enough times to need a dozen extra to count. He still likes the beach, though. He likes the sound of the ocean, the cool feel of it on a hot day, the sand, the smell, the way it looks. He’s not the picture taking type, but he has a few of the beach in his photo gallery, and if they can find a good spot without many people, he might be tempted to take a couple more.

“What do you think?” Phainon asks, walking close enough for their shoulders to brush, a little clumsy as his feet sink into the sand.

“About?”

Phainon gestures vaguely. “I dunno. The city, the beach, the wind, any of it.”

“I like the city,” Mydei answers. Water laps at his shins with the next wave. It’s cold as ice, but the sun is molten. “The beach is beautiful. The wind keeps blowing my hair into my face.”

“Hah.” Phainon smiles a little, looks at him. Mydei is reflected back in the sunglasses. Hair in his face, expression too soft. Is that what he looks like next to Phainon? Embarrassing. “I guess it’s worse for you, with how long your hair is,” Phainon says. “Did you bring a hair tie?”

“I forgot,” Mydei says. He’d thought of Phainon first, like some kind of fool. He grabbed the sunglasses instead.

Something tickles his arm. Phainon turns away and whistles conspicuously like they do in cartoons. His hand is held out. Between his forefinger and thumb, a black band and a bit of lint he’d dug out of his pocket.

“Fuck off,” Mydei says, snatching it with a laugh and shoving Phainon’s shoulder. He stumbles a step further into the water, and maybe they’re both only as bad as each other, because his expression is embarrassing too. Maybe if he said it this time, Mydei would actually believe him.

“See!” Phainon says triumphantly. “I can do it too! ‘Look at me, I’m not nice to people at all. I don't think of others and do sweet things for them ever, no sir! I just happened to have this hair tie in my pocket—’ Ah!” Mydei kicks water at him, but all it does is make him laugh and laugh, dancing away, kicking some back. “Don’t hate the player, hate the game,” he says nonsensically, backing up as Mydei pursues him, made unsteady by the waves.

“I could push you in,” Mydei threatens. They’re in up to their knees now, and Mydei wasn’t planning on getting his clothes wet. They didn’t even bring towels. “I could push you in so easily.”

“You wouldn’t,” Phainon says. Mydei starts to pull his hair back, sticking his drink between his legs and gathering it out of his eyes and into a ponytail as Phainon shakes his head. “Oh no. Mydeimos, you don’t want to do this.”

“Oh, but I do,” Mydei tells him, advancing until the water is too high for Phainon to avoid him without getting his shorts wet in the process. He grabs Phainon by the wrist, and then they’re struggling, splashing, laughing.

It ends with them drenched and searching for Phainon’s lost lemonade somewhere in the sea. It’s Mydei who finds it, but he makes Phainon bend to fish it out of the water and soak himself more in the process. He takes a sip of his own drink while he watches, safely held onto during their fight, and the withering look Phainon gives him is almost enough to start him laughing again.

And then they’re standing halfway up their thighs in the ocean, and the sun isn’t enough to keep them warm every time a breeze blows by. The smell of salt and sunscreen. Water drips from the ends of Mydei’s hair, bangs that slipped out of his ponytail, too short to stay in. Phainon starts to rock a little in place.

“What are you doing?” Mydei asks. They’ve sobered a bit now, as they tend to after messing around like that, energy worked off.

“Burying my feet,” Phainon answers. He’s kicked up the sand around him, so Mydei can’t see when he looks into the water. A stronger wave rewets the ends of his shorts and makes Phainon wobble a little. “It’s fun if you can get in deep. Cyrene and I used to try to get stuck.”

Mydei doesn’t reply, just watches him do it a little longer, watches the way he glazes over with this soft, nostalgic expression. That one shows up a lot lately. Mydei starts to work his feet into the sand too. It takes a moment, but by the time the tops of them are covered and all he can see are his ankles in the water, he feels rooted in deep. It’s a bit harder to correct his balance when the waves hit him. The sand is cool and comfortable as he wiggles his feet further down, moving sand and shells and rock out of his way to see how far he can stick himself.

“What happens if you get stuck?”

Phainon gives a soft laugh. The tired one, the nostalgic one. “It’s pretty hard to,” he says, “but once I buried myself to my knees. Cyrene couldn’t pull me out, so she got our mom. She liked to play along with all that bullshit about me growing up to be a hero, so she pretended to be some grand warrior tasked with assisting me on my journey. And then she just… grabbed me by the armpits and pulled me out.” He chuckles a little, kind of smiling. “God. You think your parents are so strong when you’re a kid. And then you grow up and realize they’re way stronger than even that.”

He’s looking out at the water, still trying to dig himself deeper. The water around him has cleared, and he’s stuck past his ankles. “My dad would have made me get myself out if I got stuck,” Mydei says. “Call it a test of strength. Maybe pretend to leave to create urgency.”

“Your dad was an asshole,” Phainon tells him. A pause. “Sorry. May he rest in peace.”

Mydei laughs at this. “No,” he says. “Good fucking riddance. He got way too much good for someone who gave so little. My mom didn’t deserve to rot with that guy. I didn’t either.”

Another beat of silence. He’s killed the conversation. “I’m glad you had parents that would pull you out,” he tries, though it’s weird on his tongue the way these kinds of things always are.

“Me too,” Phainon breathes. He stills now, not quite stuck, waves lapping at his thighs, still too soaked to start drying. He sighs, and Mydei gets this odd kind of relief knowing he’s letting himself feel whatever he needs to feel.

“You’re thinking about them a lot lately, aren’t you?”

“I always am,” Phainon admits. “Hard not to.”

Mydei hums in reply, giving him the space to speak.

“My mom loved the ocean a lot too. I think that’s why Cyrene does. She would take us all the time, so when I think of being a kid, I think of her smile and getting myself stuck in the sand.” Phainon pauses for a bit, taking a sip of his lemonade. Sun glints off the glass bottle, dripping with seawater. His hair is damp and curling up at the ends. He sighs, pulls one foot out of the sand, then the other. “This is me not being stubborn,” he says, facing Mydei now. “Are you sure you want it?”

Mydei holds his gaze, unsticks himself from the sand too. It clings to him and tries to suck him back down as he removes himself, an odd sensation, but… fun, in a way. He can see it, a kid Phainon and a kid Cyrene burying themselves side by side and cracking up as they pull themselves out because of how weird it feels. It’s strange, then, that this is the first time Phainon has done it with him, in all these years. He could say something weird. I want you however you are, maybe. I’d listen to anything you have to say if it means there's even the slightest chance of seeing you smile. “I can’t help much,” he says instead, “but I have functional ears.”

“Sure,” Phainon says, and it sounds like his walls are down, like he’s unlocked his doors and come out to sit on the porch, bruised heart in his hands. Another sigh. They start walking back to shore. There’s a breeze, and goosebumps rise on Phainon’s arms. “I just… miss them, you know?”

And he does. Mydei still has his mother, but he knows what it’s like to lose someone. What that feels like. An ache that might ease once the shock of it is gone, but never quite goes away. The memories stay, and humans are dreadfully nostalgic creatures. “I know,” Mydei says.

“I keep thinking about the fire,” Phainon continues, turning them to walk along that line separating wet sand from dry, one foot on each side. Cool and wet, hot and sunbaked. The waves don’t even reach their ankles here, just lapping the sides of their feet. “How sudden it was. How one minute I’m just this happy kid that’s never lost anything, and the next, my house is gone and my parents are too.”

Phainon is a tactile creature. He likes physical comfort, easy enough when Mydei is no good at words, but he might cut off whatever Phainon is trying to say if he goes for a hug now. His free hand is closer to Mydei. How easy it would be to reach out and take it, but they don’t do that, they’ve never done that before without some kind of pretense.

“I guess I’ve been stuck on that all my life. Reliving it over and over and always having this fear that things are temporary. And I never got over that after Livia and Piso passed.”

Childhood friends of Phainon’s, though this particular circle didn’t overlap with Mydei. They’d been a few years younger, neighbor kids Phainon used to babysit until they grew up and turned into friends. Mydei remembers, though. Livia died first in a traffic accident. Piso half a year later to suicide. “That’s not the kind of thing anyone gets over,” he says.

“Maybe,” Phainon admits. Those stupid sunglasses hide his eyes, and his eyes are how to read him. He’s sad, obviously, but… “You know what I just realized?”

His free hand, swinging at his side as he walks. Mydei switches his drink to the opposite side. “What?” he asks.

“Everyone I’ve ever lost has died so fast. One minute they’re there, and the next they’re just… gone. This is the first time I’ve ever had any notice that there’s something wrong, and it’s just throwing me straight into panic mode.”

Mydei reaches for his hand. Phainon’s head angles to look, and after a breath he laces their fingers together, lukewarm and covered in grains of sand. “Thanks,” he says, so softly.

“Keep talking,” Mydei prompts, and this comes out soft too. Phainon squeezes his hand. He squeezes back.

“I think I’m past the point of thinking Cyrene’s going to die, what with her treatment going well and her being young and healthy, but… I can’t shake that feeling, that fear that I’m going to lose her too.” His exhale is shaky. He clears his throat, and maybe his eyes are watery and wet. “It just spreads the pain out, you know? Knowing that something is wrong. Because now I’m like… pre-grieving someone who isn’t even dead, who isn’t even going to die and I just— I don’t have room for that. I’m still not over my parents, still not over Livia and Piso. What will I do if I lose her too?”

The rush of the waves is like a sigh. “You keep grieving,” Mydei answers, squeezing his hand. Phainon squeezes back. “It fucking sucks but that’s all you can do. You grieve, and then you grow enough for the memories to be warm instead of painful.”

Phainon laughs wetly, weakly. “That’s some poetic shit right there,” he says. “I didn’t know you had it in you, Mydeimos.”

“Shut up,” Mydei tells him. Their joined hands get trapped between them as Mydei wraps his other arm around Phainon’s shoulders. “Not everything needs to be a goddamn joke.”

△

They walk around on the beach a little bit longer, freezing in the wind, baking in the sun. Phainon finds a single seashell bigger than a half inch, something tinged blue and steeply ridged. Their clothes are only half dry by the time they’re trying their best to get the sand off their feet so they can put their shoes back on and head back.

Phainon plays more guitar music on the drive. They argue over who gets to shower first and end up playing rock, paper, scissors to decide. Mydei wins best four out of seven and refuses to let Phainon wheedle him into any more rounds. He showers first, Phainon second, and when he gets out he heads to the kitchen to decide on dinner.

He ends up making butternut squash and ginger soup with enough leftovers to leave two servings of it for Cyrene in the fridge and a third to take with them to the hospital. He isn’t sure how much time he’ll have to cook in the morning, but they’ll also leave behind the bread and fruit they’d gotten for themselves. Phainon wants to do more, but too many leftovers will only go bad in the fridge, and they never taste quite as good in the freezer.

So Mydei makes this soup—and it’s damn good soup—and they pack up three servings so they can eat with Cyrene this time. Phainon holds the bag in his lap on the drive, taking the job of making sure they don’t spill unnecessarily seriously, a new book plucked from Cyrene’s shelves on top since she finished the last one.

The receptionist lets them head up right away. They take the stairs and make their way through the sterile-smelling hallway to room 216, and then Phainon pauses at the door. He takes a breath and sets his shoulders, lifting his hand to knock, hesitating some more.

“Phainon,” Mydei rasps.

“I know.” Phainon raps on the door three times, and Cyrene calls for them to come in. He rolls the door open and steps inside first, Mydei close after him, shutting the door behind them.

And there she is. Cyrene propped up on her bed, looking a little more comfortable than the last time he saw her, a journal in her lap and a pink and gold pen between her fingers. She’s still hooked up to an IV to get her treatment, but she looks used to this now, not quite so tired. But the biggest difference is the beanie on her head in place of pink hair. He watches Phainon take it in. The tiniest hint of a sigh on his breath.

“Hey,” Phainon says, kind of hovering in the middle of the room. His voice breaks, just a little.

“Hey to yourself,” Cyrene says back, closing the journal and reaching to set it on her bedside table. Her hand quivers slightly. Still sick, still struggling. They’re fighters, both of these siblings. Now, she stretches her hand toward them. “What did you bring? I’ve had nothing to read all day.”

Phainon snaps out of whatever stupor he’d fallen into upon seeing her and steps further into the room, producing the book he’d taken off her shelf. It’s thick, maybe six hundred pages or more, the cover printed in deep blues and yellow, accented with gold. For the Sun is Set to Die is the title, and she takes it gratefully. “I’ve been meaning to read this one forever,” she says, setting it aside. “Hopefully it’s good.”

Phainon still doesn’t say anything, even as Mydei takes the bag from him and nudges him in the direction of the guest chairs. He just sits heavily and stares, taking the container Mydei passes to him on autopilot, the soup still warm.

“Cyrene,” he finally says as Mydei takes up the task of helping her with the tray table. She looks at him, clear blue eyes meeting clear blue eyes. So alike, these two, yet so different. “Your hair.”

She exhales. “Yeah,” she says. The glass of the container clacks lightly as Mydei sets it down. He’s softer with the spoon, so it doesn’t make a sound. “What do you think? Do I look like an egg without it?”

Mydei sinks into the seat next to Phainon, passing him the last of the spoons in the bag, engraved with little curlicues on the handle. “Maybe more like a mushroom with that hat,” Phainon tries to joke, and then he sobers again. “Are you…?”

“I’m still getting used to it,” she answers his unspoken question. “I’ll admit, I did cry a lot after they cut it, but… It’s alright. It was cathartic. I’ve come to terms with it.”

“You look fine,” Mydei offers, and immediately regrets speaking. Cyrene smiles and turns her gaze to him. She’s different without her hair, but anyone would be. Anyone would look like a new person with half as drastic a haircut.

“Thank you, Mydei,” Cyrene says, chuckling a little. “And thank you for cooking again. I really hope it’s not a bother.”

“Not at all,” Mydei says. He nudges Phainon’s foot with his own, looks at him. “I meant it before; I have to cook anyway or this one will wither and die.”

“I can cook for myself,” Phainon protests, frowning a little. And he can, it’s just terribly mediocre.

“Sure,” Mydei says, and turns back to Cyrene. Something about the exchange has her smiling. He gestures to the soup. “It’s butternut squash and ginger. The broth might be a bit thick, but I made it a bit blander so it should be easy to keep down.”

“Thank you,” Cyrene says again. And he already knows she can’t taste much. He’s seen that in her expression, in the way it takes her so long to finish a bowl of anything. She won’t say so, but she’s easy to read the same way Phainon is, even if Mydei isn’t half as practiced with her.

“There’s some more in the fridge too, for when you go home. Hopefully you like it.”

Phainon sucks in a breath. “Right,” he says, pulling the lid off his own container. “We’re leaving tomorrow. I wanted to stay until this round of treatment is over, but we need to get back to work.”

“That’s alright,” Cyrene says. “I’m happy you were able to make it at all. It’s been nice seeing you. Both of you. It’s a lot less lonely with you coming around.”

Phainon stirs his soup. He has yet to try it, caught up in conversation as he is. Mydei chews on a spoonful. “Are you going to be okay?” Phainon asks. “I know you said Stelle was going to come over and help out, but if there’s anything I can help with, or anything I can do—”

“Phainon,” Cyrene interrupts, somewhere between amused and exasperated. It’s a feeling Phainon is an expert at bringing out in people. “I’m okay. I’m not a kid, yeah? I’ve taken care of myself while sick a dozen times; I can take care of myself through this too.”

“Yeah,” Phainon breathes. He wipes one hand on his pants, then the other. He flushes slightly, embarrassed. “Yeah, sorry, I’m just… worried.”

“It’s nice being cared about,” Cyrene tells him. “But I don’t need to be babied.”

“I know,” Phainon says, ducking to finally try the soup, spoon clinking against glass.

“Just let us know if there’s anything we can do to help,” Mydei says. “And keep us updated. I’ll try to make sure he doesn’t shit his pants.”

Phainon kicks him. “Shut the hell up; I’m fine.”

“Sure you are.” Mydei kicks back, and Cyrene laughs softly at their exchange.

“I’ll keep you updated,” she agrees. “And I’d like it if you did too. I’m so sick of everything being about me and my cancer. Share whatever you guys get up to.”

Phainon gives up on squabbling with Mydei to turn an earnest expression on her. “We will,” he promises. “And we’ll be back in the morning before we leave tomorrow, so don’t worry about us, alright? Just focus on getting better.”

“I’m doing my best,” she says. “Try not to worry about me either.”

“No promises,” Phainon laughs. “It’s chronic.”

△

It’s late by the time they leave, dirty dishes packed back into the bag swinging from Phainon’s hand. 8:43, seventeen minutes before the hospital’s visiting hours close, as late as they could push it before Cyrene’s energy started to flag and she melted into her bed with her eyes barely staying open.

Phainon’s mood dims the moment they shut the door, as it often does, but he’s usually like that. He gets sad once a party is over, lonely after a guest leaves for the night. It doesn’t matter how much time they spend together. It’s… part of why Mydei moved in with him. A Phainon left in solitude is rarely a happy creature.

As they approach the car, Phainon switches the bag from one hand to the next, twisting the handles in his fingers. Mydei unlocks the doors, and he hesitates.

“Do you mind if we walk?” he asks. At Mydei’s glance, he adds, “just for a little while. To… see the sunset, or something.”

“Or something,” Mydei repeats. He studies Phainon’s expression. Not drowning in worry or grief, just… he doesn’t have the words for the way Phainon seems to feel. A little bit tired. Lonely but not, sad but content. Mostly, he’s just kind of quiet, kind of contemplative. “Leave the bag,” Mydei says, so Phainon stows it in the car and they walk.

The sun is behind the hospital, so they make a slow loop. It’s quiet out, but for the hum of the hospital’s power and the occasional passing of cars. Mydei looks to the sky and finds that this might be the most average sunset he’s seen in his life. Just a splash of muted orange, cloudless and textureless, but Phainon wants to walk, so they walk.

“I like this,” he says after a while.

Mydei looks at him, gold cast and ruffled by the wind. “The sunset or the walking?”

“It’s not a very good sunset,” Phainon points out. Their shoulders bump. He always walks so close. “I guess the walking. Or the way my brain is kind of quiet for once.”

“You seem sad,” Mydei tells him.

“I don’t think I am.”

He doesn’t think. What does that even mean? “Alright,” Mydei says. He’s out of things to say. They’ve been glued to each other for the better part of a week now. Most people would probably be grating on his nerves by now. Phainon, well… he’s always grating on Mydei’s nerves, but he’s alright company. Mydei wouldn’t follow him everywhere if he wasn’t.

They finish their loop, the sun at their backs, the car in view a handful of seconds away, butter yellow and coated in water spots and a glob of bird shit. Phainon takes a deep breath of air that smells a bit polluted and steers them back toward the parking lot. “We can head back now,” he says. “I’m so ready to go to bed.”

“So early?” Mydei asks, but all he does is follow. He’s good at that, when it comes to Phainon. He’d probably follow him over the edge of a cliff if it came to it. There are words for that, but he’d rather not say them.

“Yeah,” Phainon answers. “I think the sun gave me a bit of a headache.”

Chapter End Notes

obligatory tidbits (5th edition): I said it in another chapter but Mydei's love language is 100% acts of service, which translates into other love languages when he thinks someone he cares about would appreciate it. He's touchy with Phainon because Phainon likes it, he begrudgingly says sweet things when he knows Phainon needs it, he spends so much time with Phainon because he knows Phainon doesn't like to be alone. He gets absolutely mortified when attention is drawn to it, but he lives to make the people he cares about happy, particularly his mom and Phainon. He's a big mama's boy. Phainon, on the other hand, has every love language in the book, and he's very free with his affection. He's puppy like that.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.html:
The dessert Mydei makes at Phainon’s insistence is a fruit cobbler with strawberries, peaches, plums, and nearly expired corn muffin mix from the back of Cyrene’s pantry. It sounds a bit odd, but Phainon trusts the process, and when it comes out sweet-smelling and hot, he douses it with whipped cream and stifles an indecent noise at the taste when he bites into it.

“This is good,” he says, pointing at it as Mydei watches with an amused expression. It’s past breakfast time at the hospital already, so Cyrene will have eaten already, but they’ll leave the rest for her in the fridge with the leftover soup as promised. “I like this a lot.”

They’re running late because of how long it had taken to make. Phainon doesn’t even care. Seven pieces out of nine from the square pan are probably too many to leave behind for Cyrene anyway. They’ll have to take some of the leftovers too. The flavor is light and honeyed, and the texture is surprising but it works. Phainon isn’t even the one with the sweet tooth; what did Mydei put in this?

“Cool,” Mydei says. “I wasn’t sure about the corn muffins.”

“It’s good,” Phainon says, stabbing another bite with his fork. “Goddamn is it good.”

Mydei huffs a laugh. “Hurry and eat so we can get out of here,” he says, brushing off the compliments as he tends to. But the smile is there, so Phainon knows it’s appreciated. “Did you pack up your shit?”

Phainon covers his mouth as he talks with it half full. “My toothbrush is still drying, but I think I got everything else.”

“Double check,” Mydei tells him. “Don’t forget your charger and whatever else.”

“Yes, mother,” Phainon says, swallowing. God, he loves peaches. “I take it you’re packed too?” Mydei’s hot pink duffle bag sits on the floor beside the couch, zipped up and ready. He packed up while the cobbler was baking, quick and efficient as always. He points at it with his thumb but doesn’t bother with a verbal response.

Phainon leans toward him and squints. “But did you double check?”

Lazily, Mydei lifts his fork between two fingers, pointing it at Phainon, then at himself. “Which one of us forgets things?” he asks. “You or me?”

Phainon laughs, flips him off. “You suck,” he says.

“And who made that goddamn good cobbler you’ve been drooling over all morning?”

Now, Phainon puts his hands together and pretends to bow. “You did, Your Highness,” he says. “God of the kitchen. This mortal one can only bow before your talents and grovel for your blessings.”

“Submit or starve,” Mydei tells him, chair screeching as he pushes it back to stand and grab a cup of water. As he sits back down, glass clinking, he asks, “Did you tell Cyrene we’re running late?”

“Yeah, she knows,” Phainon answers, finding his piece almost gone. He’s tempted to go for another. A glance at Mydei, then his plate. He scoops the last bite into his mouth and stands to get another. “She called us stupid.”

“Shut up with your mouth full,” Mydei scolds. “And she’s right. We’re going to get to the hotel in the middle of the night again.”

“But cobbler,” Phainon says, mouth still full. He tops this second piece with a smiley of whipped cream, then fills in the gaps because it isn’t quite enough. He sits back down, and Mydei’s mouth wavers before he purses it to hide a smile. He’ll never admit it, but every now and then he loves flattery. He only ever pretends to be humble.

“Yeah, yeah,” he says. Another bite. He chases it with water. “Hurry up.”

△

Cyrene is glad to see them. She’s tired again today, mentioning aches and bruises and lethargy, though she doesn’t complain much. Only ever in small doses, and never in a way that generates real concern. But Phainon knows her well, and worries anyway like he’ll get withdrawals if he doesn’t.

On the bedside table, Cyrene’s sunflowers are already wilting, dropping petals and sagging under their own weight. They must’ve spent too much time without water. Cyrene herself sits cross-legged in bed with her hat on and both her journal and the book Phainon brought her the day before in the blankets with her. Her bookmark sticks out from between the pages, already a fourth of the way through.

“Call if you need anything,” Phainon tells her.

“I will,” she says, half smiling.

“Mail me the paperwork for the trust.”

“I will.”

“And make sure—”

“Phainon,” she interrupts him. He stops short, chastened, and holds his tongue. “I’ll be fine. You’ll know if things go south and you need to come back out. Unless that happens—and that’s a big if, mind you—you don’t need to worry about me so much, okay? I’ll update you.”

Phainon lets the inside of his cheek go from where he’d been chewing on it. Mydei’s foot nudges against his softly. “Alright,” he says. “Sorry if I’m being overbearing.”

“A little,” Cyrene admits, softening. “But I probably would be too in your place. Just… try not to worry about me too much.”

He brings a hand to his brow in a salute. “Aye aye,” he says, and it makes her smile. “I’ll call you sometime on the way home too, okay? If you can handle me being annoying for a little longer. We’ve got thirty hours of driving and not much else to do either way.”

“And I’ve got a couple more days of this and not much to do either, so I think I’ll be glad to have the distraction.” Again, Mydei’s foot taps his. He leaves it there, close. Cyrene sighs a little, taps her fingers on the hard cover of her journal. “Stelle and Dan Heng are visiting again, so probably don’t call later today.”

“Noted,” Phainon says. He glances at Mydei, who just sits and listens, sits and listens. He’s done his eyeliner differently today, just on the lower lid of one eye. It would probably look weird on anyone else, but he makes it work as good as he made that goddamn cobbler. “There’s soup and fruit cobbler in the fridge for you. You go home the day after tomorrow, right?”

“Yes, finally,” she confirms.

“We changed the sheets and stuff for you too; everything should be ready so you can just relax when you get there.”

“I have done way too much relaxing,” she says, smiling, “but thank you. I appreciate it a lot. You guys coming to see me, cooking for me, all of it. It’s been… really nice.”

“Hug?” Phainon asks.

Her eyes smile more than her mouth. “Hug,” she confirms, gingerly sliding herself off the bed to be in a better position for it. Phainon wraps her up, fighting the urge to squeeze her tight in case it might hurt, mindful of the IV tube stretching behind her. She smells like hospital linens and he misses the tickle of her hair, but she’s warm and she laughs a little against him. “I’ll miss you,” she says, and tiptoes to peer over his shoulder. “You too, Mydei. Thanks for coming out with him.”

“Any time,” Mydei says, kind of soft.

Another breath, and Phainon pulls back. “Alright,” he breathes. “We’ll get out of your ha— ah…” They look at each other for a moment, Cyrene expressionless, just staring enough that guilt squirms in his stomach, and then she’s laughing, she’s laughing so hard it seems to hurt her, sitting back down and shaking her head.

“Get out,” she says, still laughing, and the sound of it has him laughing too. “Get out, you’re banished!”

“Sorry!” Phainon tries, but she kicks him toward the door, grin straining her face. “Really, that was in terrible taste and I didn’t mean it, I’m sorry!”

“Bye, Phainon. You have like, ten hours to drive today; leave.” Her eyes sparkle. Phainon grabs his bag and heads toward the door.

“Bye, Cyrene,” he says, rolling it open. “Talk to you soon.”

“Yeah, yeah,” she says. “Bye Phainon, Mydei. Keep in touch or whatever.”

Mydei lifts a hand to her on his way out, and then the door rolls shut between them and the hallway is uncomfortably silent. Phainon sighs and follows Mydei down the familiar path to the stairs. Warmth in his chest, the way it eases into something soft and bittersweet. God knows when he’ll be able to make it out here again. Christmas, if they follow the usual plan. Knowing she’s sick, he’s afraid to wait that long.

A glance at Mydei. He’s got this half smile going when their eyes briefly meet. “You guys are fucking weird,” he says.

Phainon bumps him. “Like you’re so normal,” he says. At the top of the stairs, he pauses, stretches an arm in front of Mydei to make him pause too. He smiles before that bittersweet feeling can take over. “Race you.”

“Not helping your case,” Mydei tells him, but he gears up for it as Phainon counts down. At go, he drops his arm and they thunder down the stairs neck and neck before Phainon pulls just a bit ahead since he has the inside of the bend. At the bottom, he laughs, heart beating hard in his chest.

“I believe the victory is mine,” he says, ignoring the looks they get from the noise they must have made, the annoyance on Mydei’s face. He pretends to think for a moment. “As my prize, we’ll be listening to girl group music for the first hour of the drive.”

“I swear to god,” Mydei sighs. “You fucking suck.”

△

Contrary to popular belief, Phainon is not a complete menace. He keeps the obnoxiously cutesy stuff to the first fifteen minutes of the drive, just to see the way it makes Mydei frown. He doesn’t even play some of the super high-pitched stuff he has buried in his playlists. Only the best of the best, only the classics. At the last song he picks, something upbeat and deeply danceable, Mydei either gets tired of scowling or can actually tolerate this song, because his expression smooths out as he drives.

The second chorus comes on, and one of his fingers starts to give a traitorous tap to the beat. Phainon watches, just for a bit, just to make sure it isn’t some kind of fluke. But no, Mydei keeps it up, tapping out the beat to this song belonging to a genre he’s sworn again and again is his mortal enemy.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon says. A grunt. “Have you, by chance, taken a fancy to this song?”

And oh, he can feel the way Mydei sighs. He stops tapping the beat. “No,” he says, long suffering and sick of Phainon’s bullshit. “I have not.”

“You were tapping the beat,” Phainon teases, lips pulling up. “You don’t do that unless you like the song. Admit it.”

Mydei’s mouth presses into a firm line. He doesn’t spare Phainon a glance. “It’s way too cutesy for a bunch of grown ass women,” he says, but it isn’t a denial.

“Sure, sure,” Phainon waves that off. “But do you like it?”

“Crashing the car is an option readily available to me.”

It startles a laugh out of him, knee bouncing, fingers tapping on his phonecase. The last chorus of the song starts, and there’s tension in Mydei’s jaw. “So stubborn,” Phainon notes. “Didn’t we already have this discussion? We’ll both die if the car crashes.”

“Yes,” Mydei agrees, and his finger lifts on the steering wheel before he deliberately sets it back down off beat. “The afterlife sounds much kinder than this hell.”

“You’re such a hater,” Phainon tuts. “Well, if it’s all the same to you, should I play that song where they bark and sing about wanting to be dogs? I can always put that on next.”

“So we’re off to the afterlife together, is what I’m hearing,” Mydei says.

“It’ll be a good bonding experience.”

A little longer and the song comes to an end. Phainon has mercy and chooses something fairly normal to play next because he’s kind and benevolent like that. Mydei props one elbow on the edge of his window and drives one-handed for a while. The air conditioning works overtime as the sun beats down on them. Phainon snags the sunglasses out of the center console and slides them on. In the sun visor mirror, his reflection looks a bit silly. Somehow, Mydei always makes these look cool. Hell, he makes everything look cool. No point in acting surprised.

“This is fun,” he says after a while. Not the driving, but the road trip, the time together in a setting so different from their home. Mostly, he likes the fact that he isn’t alone. He’ll crash later and cry, he’s certain of it. He'll think of Cyrene’s hair and her exhaustion, and his long dead parents and friends and he’ll fall apart, but right now he’s about as happy as a person can be with a lifetime of grief stored in their chest. 

“Fun,” Mydei repeats dryly. Mydei, who isn’t upset with him, hasn’t been. Mydei, who has stuck around longer than anyone Phainon’s ever known, aside from Cyrene, who doesn’t quite count because she’s his sister.

“Are you insinuating that you don’t love sitting in a hot car for hours on end with only your best friend and his delightful music taste to keep you company?”

“Delightful is a word for it,” Mydei retorts.

“It certainly is,” Phainon agrees, “One you used, even.”

“You’re just saying shit at this point,” Mydei says. “Either let the important stuff out or shut up.”

He must be clearer than water, than glass, than crystal. Mydei can smell sentimentality like a shark can smell blood in the water. “Everything I say is important,” Phainon tells him.

“Sure.”

“You suck,” Phainon laughs, and he can’t even pretend to be offended. “And here I was about to say nice things about you.” Mydei’s nails digging into the steering wheel. His eyeroll, the dismissive grunt he lets out.

“Don’t hold back on my account,” he says.

He’s such an asshole, but he isn’t at all, really. They’re just like this. Phainon flip flops between feeling scared and feeling secure, but right now that emotion in his chest is warm and settled. This is it. This is them. They have a long way to go to get home, but Phainon doesn’t mind it at all.

“Thirty more minutes,” Mydei says. “Play whatever dumb shit you want now, because I’m only putting up with it for another thirty minutes, and then you’re driving and I’m controlling the music.”

Phainon laughs through his nose. “Got it,” he says, and scrolls through his playlist for the worst songs he can possibly find.

△

Phainon lasts a surprisingly long time before they swap. He makes it three and a half hours, tapping his foot and his fingers, and talking about whatever random things come to mind the whole while. Mydei lets him go on about Antiques Roadshow, which he’s had a very strange obsession with for a few months now. He wants to get into antique appraisal and collecting, and always gets pouty when Mydei tells him he’s just going to get scammed.

But he listens, because Phainon needs someone to listen to his shit or he’ll wilt like Cyrene’s flowers did. So much of Mydei is dedicated to keeping him happy. It’s getting embarrassing.

They stop for lunch at a ramen restaurant, and Phainon bets that he can’t handle the spiciest thing on the menu, which means they both end up ordering it and suffering. Mydei’s nose runs and his mouth feels lit on fire, but he manages to finish his bowl before Phainon does. As his prize, Phainon—who just sits there, red as a lobster, tearing up a little from the spice—must comply with his demands for the music for the entirety of his shift driving.

Mydei’s turn passes pretty uneventfully, aside from Phainon’s complaining every time he makes him put on yet another Metallica song. They fill up on gas and end up in the middle of nowhere for a while, driving eighty-five on a road they have pretty much to themselves. Phainon would probably be going over a hundred.

Eventually, they lose service and are left with only the music Phainon has downloaded on his phone, which means Mydei has to forfeit his prize, but he still has skipping rights every time Phainon tries to turn on something atrocious.
